0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
The message. First John is written to give believers assurance, as it says near the end: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). John’s Gospel was written “so that you may believe” (John 20:31); this letter is written so that those who believe may know. The word “know” comes more than thirty times. Yet this assurance is never cheap. God is light and love, and those who truly know him begin to look like him: they walk in the light, love their brothers and sisters, and hold to the truth about his Son.

Background: the writer. The letter names no author, but it opens with the voice of an eyewitness: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life” (1:1). From the second century the church received it as the work of John the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved (John 13:23; 19:26). Polycarp, who had known John, echoes it, and Irenaeus quotes it as John’s. Its language is that of the Fourth Gospel: light and darkness, truth, abiding, new birth. Tradition places John in old age at Ephesus, the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, and the letter was probably written there about AD 85–95, perhaps soon after the Gospel. With no greeting or farewell, it reads like a pastoral sermon to churches whose members the old apostle calls “my little children” (2:1).

The first readers. They were probably congregations in and around Ephesus, mostly converted Gentiles in cities full of temples, where the letter’s last words, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (5:21), would not have sounded abstract. But the danger John faces came from within, from a group that had left: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (2:19). The faithful were left shaken, wondering whether those confident teachers, to whom “the world listens” (4:5), had found a deeper truth.

What the false teachers said. They denied “that Jesus is the Christ” (2:22), would not confess “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (4:2), and claimed fellowship with God while walking in darkness (1:6; 2:4) and freedom from sin (1:8, 10), with no love for those they left. Behind this probably lay the idea, later developed by the Gnostics, that spirit is pure and matter low, so that God could not truly take a body and what one does in the body hardly matters. Irenaeus tells of Cerinthus, a teacher in Asia in John’s day, who said that the divine Christ came upon the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross; John’s insistence that Jesus came “not by the water only but by the water and the blood” (5:6) answers exactly that kind of teaching. John’s opponents may not have held exactly his views, but they were of that family.

Who wrote it? Many modern scholars, noting its anonymity and small differences from the Gospel, credit a later leader among churches shaped by John’s teaching, or a “John the elder” whom Papias, an early bishop in Asia, seems to distinguish from the apostle. But the letter claims eyewitness knowledge in its first lines (1:1–3; compare 4:14), it speaks with authority over many churches, the differences suit its different purpose, and the early testimony is consistent. This commentary holds that John the son of Zebedee wrote it, as he wrote the Gospel and the two short letters from “the elder”.

How the letter makes its case. John circles rather than marching in a line, returning to the same themes and going deeper each time, like a spiral staircase. The prologue (1:1–4) announces the life “made manifest” and the fellowship it opens with the Father and the Son. The first movement (1:5–2:29) begins from “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1:5): sin is to be confessed, not denied (1:5–2:2); knowing God shows itself in keeping his commandments (2:3–6) and in loving one’s brother (2:7–11); the world, which is passing away, is not to be loved (2:15–17); and the antichrists who went out are exposed, while the faithful abide in what they heard (2:18–27). The second movement (2:28–3:24) turns on being children of God: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us” (3:1). God’s children do not make a practice of sin (3:4–10), they love in deed as he laid down his life for them (3:11–18), and they find confidence before God (3:19–24). The third movement (4:1–5:12) tests the spirits by their confession of Christ come in the flesh (4:1–6), rises to “God is love” (4:7–21), and shows faith overcoming the world, resting on God’s testimony to his Son (5:1–12). The close (5:13–21) gathers it up: assurance, confident prayer, the sin that leads to death, three “we know” statements, and the warning against idols.

Three tests. Through the whole run three marks, often called the tests of life: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for being saved but signs that one has been, the fingerprints of new birth. Those born of God will obey, love and confess, not perfectly, for John also says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1:8), but truly and persistently.

Where it leads: to Christ. The cross stands at the centre. “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1:7). “He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world” (2:2): the sacrifice, foreshadowed on the Day of Atonement, that turns away God’s just wrath, offered not for one people only but for people of every nation. “He laid down his life for us” (3:16). Love itself is defined by it: “he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (4:10). Now he is our “advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (2:1). He came “to destroy the works of the devil” (3:8), undoing the story of sin that runs from Eden through Cain (3:12). And he will appear again: “we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (3:2). Near its close the letter names him plainly: “He is the true God and eternal life” (5:20).

For us. First John gives settled, humble, joyful assurance to those who have truly come to Christ, and that assurance, far from breeding complacency, fuels a life of love. It teaches you to rest first on what God has done, and to see a changed life as evidence of his work, not the price of his favour. It warns that spiritual talk without obedience, love and the truth about Christ is a lie. It tells the anxious that “God is greater than our heart” (3:20), and it calls every believer to love not “in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (3:18). “We love because he first loved us” (4:19).

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—<sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—<sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.<sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.<sup>6</sup>If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.<sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.<sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.<sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.<sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the letter without a greeting: a prologue on the Word of life made visible (vv. 1–4), then the first great statement about God, “God is light” (vv. 5–10), a thought that runs on into 2:2.

The message. Fellowship with God is open to you, because the eternal life of God came near enough to be heard, seen and touched in Jesus. But God is light, so that fellowship can only be enjoyed in honesty. Those who pretend about their sin shut themselves out; those who own it find the blood of Jesus cleansing them, and a faithful and just God forgiving them.

Why it was said. A group had walked out of the churches claiming a higher knowledge of God that sat lightly to the body, to the real humanity of Jesus and to sin (see the introduction). Those left behind were shaken: had they missed something deeper? John answers as an eyewitness, and names the claims by which people, then and now, try to have God without the light.

How the chapter makes its case. The prologue piles up the evidence: what was from the beginning was heard, seen, looked upon and touched (vv. 1–2), and it is proclaimed so that readers may share the apostles’ fellowship with the Father and his Son, and joy be complete (vv. 3–4). Then the message heard from Jesus: God is light (v. 5). Three false claims follow, and grace answers them. Claiming fellowship while walking in darkness is a lie, but those who walk in the light have fellowship and the cleansing blood (vv. 6–7). Claiming to have no sin is self-deception, but those who confess find God faithful and just to forgive (vv. 8–9). Claiming never to have sinned makes God a liar (v. 10), and the answer, an Advocate with the Father, follows at once (2:1–2).

Where it leads. The chapter begins with hands touching the Son of God and ends with sinners washed in his blood. Because the eternal life became truly human, he could truly die; because he is God’s Son, his blood cleanses from all sin. The light that would expose us came down to wash us.

For us. Our faith rests not on feelings or private insight but on what was seen and touched. And fellowship with a holy God is kept up not by pretending to be clean but by honest confession. You never need to hide from him: the light is where the washing happens.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fellowship with God is open to us because the eternal life of God was heard, seen and touched in Jesus. Before any command or warning, John rests the whole letter on this one fact, and he writes as a man who was there. The life that was with the Father became visible (vv. 1–2); it is proclaimed so that readers may share the apostles’ fellowship with the Father and his Son (v. 3); and the letter itself is written so that joy may be complete (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Incarnation as the Ground of Fellowship

The eternal life was heard, seen and touched. A Christ who did not truly come in the flesh could not truly die for our sins, and without that death there is no fellowship with God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Teachers were spiritualising Christ out of his humanity.

Now: The gospel is not a philosophy but a report of what was heard and seen.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eternal life of God became a man whom the apostles heard, saw and touched, and they bear witness to what they handled. Christ is not an idea or a vision but the eternal Son, come in real flesh.

A sentence that cannot wait for its verb. The letter opens with one long, breathless sentence in the Greek, and its main verb, “we proclaim”, does not arrive until verse 3. No greeting, no name, no thanksgiving: like a witness who has waited decades to be asked, John piles up the evidence first.

That which was from the beginning. An echo of John 1:1, “In the beginning was the Word”, and behind that Genesis 1:1: the eternal Son, who existed before creation (on the wording, see below). John writes “that which”, not “he who”, because he has in view the whole message about Christ, who he is and what he did. The letter begins in eternity and moves straight to fingertips.

Which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands. The senses rise in intensity, as though John were walking closer. Hearing can be done from the edge of a crowd; seeing needs line of sight; “looked upon” is a long, careful gaze, the word in “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). “Touched” is a strongly physical word, used of groping in the dark, and the risen Lord used it: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see” (Luke 24:39). Against those who denied that Jesus had a real body, John says the apostles touched him, before and after the resurrection (John 20:27).

The head on his chest. This is the disciple who reclined next to Jesus at the last supper and leaned back against his chest to ask a question (John 13:23–25). He had felt the Lord breathe. Faced with teachers who said Christ only seemed to have a body, he does not argue from philosophy. He says, in effect: I put my head on him. A man does not lean his weight on an appearance.

Concerning the word of life. Christ himself, the Word who is life and gives life (John 1:1–4; 11:25), and also the message about him. John will not let the two be separated: the message is not a set of ideas a man once taught; it is the man.

The life was made manifest, and we have seen it. “Made manifest” means made visible: the incarnation. Eternal life was invisible, as God is invisible; in Jesus it walked into Galilee, not a teaching about life but the life itself, with a face and a voice and calloused hands. The eternal life of God did not stay where it was safe.

And testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life. “Testify” is the courtroom word from which martyr comes; “proclaim” is to bring news. The apostles are witnesses in a court and heralds in a street. Early tradition says John alone of the twelve died old; his brother James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2). Men do not die for what they know they invented (see the question below).

Which was with the Father and was made manifest to us. “With the Father” is face to face with him, as in John 1:1, “the Word was with God”: distinct from the Father, yet eternal and divine. The life that appeared to fishermen had come from the Father’s side, where it had been for ever.

The setting. The writer is John, son of Zebedee, writing as an old man to churches shaken by those who had left them teaching a false Christ (2:19; see the introduction). Some held an early form of docetism (from the Greek dokein, to seem): that matter is evil and the divine Christ only seemed to have a body. Others followed Cerinthus, who taught that the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before his death. Irenaeus, passing on a story from Polycarp, tells how John ran out of the baths at Ephesus on seeing Cerinthus inside, saying the building might fall because the enemy of the truth was in it. Hence the letter’s first words: we heard, we saw, we touched.

Near enough to be nailed. The hands that flung the stars into place were held out to be touched; fishermen jostled him in a boat, and Thomas put a finger in the wound. The eternal life of God came near enough to be handled, near enough to be nailed, and it is in that flesh, risen and glorified, that he sits now at the Father’s right hand. The Word of life has a human face, and he has not put it away.

How can I know the apostles were not mistaken or lying? They did not describe private visions no one could check, but things done in public, within living memory, among hostile witnesses; and as far as our sources tell us, no one ever produced the body, though that would have ended the matter. Barely twenty-five years later Paul could point to more than five hundred who had seen the risen Lord, most still alive to be asked (1 Corinthians 15:3–8): no legend invented generations later.

Why their witness holds. They gained nothing by it but beatings, prison and death, which rules out deliberate fraud, though not by itself sincere error. Their accounts have the untidiness of real testimony: the disciples look slow and frightened, and women are the first witnesses, which an inventor in that culture would hardly have chosen. This is strong evidence, not a proof, the kind people rightly trust in a court; and the Spirit who inspired the apostles still bears witness through their words (John 15:26–27; 1 John 5:6). Faith is not a leap in the dark but trust in reliable witnesses about a real man.

I never saw or touched him: is my faith second-hand? Not second-class. John writes so that people who never saw can share exactly what he had (v. 3), and the Lord pronounced a blessing over you in the room where Thomas touched him: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). You know him through the same Word and the same Spirit. The apostles’ eyes were the window God built once, so that everyone afterwards could see through it.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases can be read more than one way. Elsewhere in this letter “from the beginning” often means the beginning of the gospel as the readers first heard it (2:7, 24), and some take it so here; but the life “which was with the Father” (v. 2) and the echo of John 1:1 point back before creation, which is the likely meaning. “The word of life” may be the personal Word, Christ himself, or the life-giving message. John probably means both, with the person in front, for in v. 2 it is the life itself that was “made manifest”.
verseByVerse.note: The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that it has long been received as the apostle John’s, written late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. Some had left the church denying that Jesus the Christ truly came in the flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John proclaims Christ so that his readers may share the fellowship the apostles have with the Father and with his Son. He writes not only to inform but to bring people in.

That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you. He repeats seen and heard: this is not rumour. And “also to you”: what began in a small circle on a lake shore is not to stay there.

So that you too may have fellowship with us. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) is sharing, partnership. Luke uses a related word for James and John as Simon’s partners in the fishing (Luke 5:10), sharing the boat and the catch. Christian fellowship is not a pleasant hour after the service but a common life in Christ, a shared inheritance.

And indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. The Father and the Son are named together as equal partners in this fellowship, which no mere man could be. Fellowship with God and with other believers go together (v. 7), and the way in is the apostles’ message about Christ: those who reject it, as the false teachers did, have no fellowship with God (2:22–23).

A circle that was turning before the world began. Before there was a world, the Father loved the Son and the Son delighted in the Father, in the Spirit (John 17:24). The gospel draws us into that circle. Jesus prayed for exactly this on his way to the cross: “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us” (John 17:21). Fellowship is God opening his own life and setting places at his table for rebels: the Son came from the Father’s side to fetch them, and went to the cross to make them clean enough to sit down. Strangers to God now call him Father, and the eternal Son their brother.

What does fellowship with God look like on an ordinary day? It is quieter than people expect: speaking to him in prayer and hearing him in Scripture, as friends talk; bringing him the day’s worries (1 Peter 5:7); confessing sin quickly (v. 9); loving what he loves and grieving what grieves him; and enjoying all this with his people, at his table. It is a shared life, not a feeling of closeness: the feelings come and go, but the sharing does not stop.

Can I have fellowship with God without a church? Not in the way John means: “fellowship with us”, and “our fellowship is with the Father”. The road into the Father’s company goes through the apostles’ message, and that message gathers people. A Christian alone is like a coal taken out of the fire: it does not stop being coal, but it goes cold. Some cannot attend for illness or persecution, and God meets them where they are. But choosing to stay away cuts you off from the very means God uses to keep you warm (Hebrews 10:24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes so that the joy he shares with his readers may be full, as it can be only when they share the fellowship he has described.

And we are writing these things. The letter is itself part of the proclamation. Every time you open it, the eyewitness is still speaking.

So that our joy may be complete. “Our” includes writer and readers: the apostle’s joy is bound up with theirs (on the wording, see below). “Complete” means filled to the brim. John cannot be fully glad until those he loves are fully in the fellowship of verses 1–3, as a father is not at peace while one of his children is missing from the table.

The joy of the upper room. Jesus spoke of the same full joy on his last night: “These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11; see also 16:24; 17:13). John was in the room, and decades later is still passing it on. This joy comes from sharing the Son’s own life, and no one can take it away (John 16:22). God is not a reluctant giver of gladness: he is the happy God, and he means to make us happy in him for ever.

What if I do not feel joyful? You are not unusual, and not disqualified. Christian joy is deeper than mood. It can sit alongside grief, as Paul was sorrowful yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10), and it can be buried for a season under illness, depression or loss. It is not manufactured by trying to feel happy but grows from its sources: God’s word, honesty with him about sin, the company of his people. Keep going back to the spring, even when the cup feels empty. The Lord who wants your joy full knows how to fill it, and he knows how to wait.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “your joy”; “our” is better supported.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — God Is Light: Walking in the Truth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God is light, fellowship with him cannot be had by pretending, only by honesty, and the light that exposes sin is where sin is washed away. John states the message he heard from Jesus (v. 5), then exposes three things people say to live comfortably without facing that light: that they have fellowship with God while walking in darkness (v. 6), that they have no sin (v. 8), and that they have not sinned (v. 10). Grace answers at once: the blood of Jesus cleanses (v. 7), and God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Light

The three claims of vv. 6, 8 and 10 keep people from the light; the remedy is confession (see the note on v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers claimed an enlightenment that placed them above sin.

Now: Honest confession, not self-defence, keeps a believer in fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is pure light, holy and true through and through, with no darkness in him at all. Everything John says about sin and fellowship rests on this.

This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you. “From him” is from Jesus, who called himself the light of the world (John 8:12) and whose life made the claim visible. This is what the God we seek fellowship with is like.

That God is light. In Scripture light stands for God’s holiness, truth and glory (Psalm 27:1; 36:9; Isaiah 60:19–20): he is not merely a source of light but light in his very nature. His first words into the dark of creation were “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and the Bible closes with a city that needs no sun, “for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). Between those pages he shone in a pillar of fire over Israel and on the face of Moses, and then, fully, in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

What light does. Light shows what is there, the dust and the stain you had not noticed. It warms and makes growth possible. And it is pure: shine it into a sewer and the light does not become dirty. All of that is God. He sees everything as it is, he gives life, and he enters our filth without being stained by it, which is why the Son could touch a leper without becoming unclean, and the leper was made clean instead (Mark 1:41–42).

And in him is no darkness at all. A strong double negative: none, not any. Darkness stands for sin, falsehood and evil. God is absolutely holy: no shadow of sin, no mixture of good and evil, no hidden corners, no moods in which he is less than himself (James 1:17). Every human being has a dark room somewhere; God has none. His eyes are too pure to look on evil with approval (Habakkuk 1:13), and he cannot be talked into thinking sin is small, whatever the teachers who treated sin as compatible with knowing God supposed. You will never discover something about him that makes you trust him less.

He entered our night. The burning purity no one can approach (1 Timothy 6:16) came down into a stable and walked our roads: holy and never compromised, yet stooping to the darkest places to bring his people out. He did not shine on us from a safe distance. He entered our night, and at noon on the day he died darkness covered the land while he bore the judgment our sins deserved (Mark 15:33), so that people of the dark might stand in his light and not be consumed.

If God is light, why does my life sometimes feel so dark? Because the darkness John means is sin, not hard circumstances. A believer can walk through a dark valley of grief, illness or confusion and still be walking in the light, because he is walking honestly with God. Scripture expects such seasons: “Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10). When you cannot see his face, you can still lean on his name. The darkness around you is not a darkness in him, and it will not have the last word.

Does this make God frightening rather than loving? It makes him trustworthy. A love with dark corners could never be relied on; because God is light, his love is exactly what it appears to be. John will say just as plainly that God is love (4:8), and the two are not rivals. At the cross the light did not dim and the love did not hold back: sin was exposed and judged, and sinners were embraced, in the same act.

In everyday life. Pick one thing you would not want God to see: a resentment, a rehearsed conversation. He has already seen it, and has not turned away from you. Say so to him today; verse 7 tells you what waits for you in the light.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To claim fellowship with God while living in the dark is a lie, however correct the words.

If we say we have fellowship with him. The first of three false claims (vv. 6, 8, 10), perhaps the false teachers’ slogans. But John says we, not they: saying the right words over a wrong life is a temptation in every human heart, an apostle’s included.

While we walk in darkness. “Walk” is a settled way of life, not an occasional stumble: a man keeping to the unlit side of the street because he does not want to be seen. Jesus named the motive: “the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil” (John 3:19).

We lie and do not practice the truth. To claim intimacy with the God who is light while life runs toward darkness is not merely an error; it is a lie. “Practice the truth” (literally, do the truth) is one of John’s most striking phrases: truth is not only believed but done (John 3:21).

The lie we tell with our lives. Most who live this verse have never said anything false aloud. The lie is in the distance between their mouths and their days: the husband who leads family devotions and is cruel when the door is shut; the businesswoman who tithes on money she obtained by deceit. God hears not only what we say but what our lives say, and the two do not match.

Whoever follows me. John learnt the language of this verse from Jesus, who stood in the temple and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). The world that loved the darkness put the light out, for three days, but could not hold him: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (John 1:5). So walking in the light is not first a moral standard but walking behind a person, and no one can follow someone while walking the other way. The remedy is not trying harder in the dark but turning round to follow him.

What it does not mean. Not that any sin in a believer proves he is not a Christian: verses 8–10 show that believers do sin. It is the settled pattern that contradicts a claim to know God.

How do I tell the difference between stumbling and walking in darkness? Ask what you do with your sin. A believer stumbles, sometimes badly and often, but he hates the sin, confesses it and turns back toward God. The person walking in darkness has made peace with it: he hides it, excuses it, renames it, and has no intention of changing. Ask too whether you want God to see: a stumbling Christian, ashamed, still runs toward the light; a man in darkness avoids it. If your sin grieves you and drives you to Christ, that grief is itself a sign of light.

In everyday life. Is there an area of your life you keep in the dark? Name it to God plainly this week, where his Son’s blood waits to wash it (v. 7), and if it grows in secret, tell one trusted believer. Darkness loses most of its power the moment it is spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who live openly before God share a real fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus keeps cleansing them from every sin.

But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light. The counterpart to verse 6, with two gifts: fellowship and cleansing. To walk in the light is to live openly before God, hiding nothing and letting his light expose and correct us: not sinlessness, but transparency. “As he is in the light”: the light is not a standard we must reach before we may come; it is the place where he lives, and we are invited to live there with him.

We have fellowship with one another. We might expect “with him”. But pretence and hidden sin destroy relationships: two people who are both hiding cannot be close, only polite. When each is honest with God, the masks can come off.

And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. “Blood” is Christ’s sacrificial death, his life poured out (Hebrews 9:14, 22; 1 Peter 1:18–19). “Jesus his Son”: against those who separated them, the human Jesus is the divine Son. It was the blood of a man who bled like any man, and of God’s Son, which is why it can cleanse not some sin but every kind. “Cleanses” is present tense: it keeps on cleansing. Not that we are justified again each time: justification is a verdict God pronounces once, declaring a believer righteous for Christ’s sake (Romans 5:1). Rather, believers’ ongoing sins are continually covered by Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10–14), which needs no repeating.

A spring, not a bucket. The present tense pictures a stream that runs continuously, washing whatever is dropped into it. The hymn’s fountain filled with blood is the right image: what Christ did once at Calvary flows on, precisely because the work was finished.

Why the light is not to be feared. You might expect the light, where everything shows, to terrify a sinner. John says it is the place of cleansing: the darkness is where sin festers; the light is where it is washed. We hide because we think exposure means condemnation, but where the blood of Jesus is, exposure means cleansing. We walk in the light, not because we are clean enough to stand in it, but because he keeps us clean while we are there.

Do I have to tell other people my sins to walk in the light? Not everyone, and not everything. Walking in the light is first honesty with God, but it includes being willing to be known by fellow believers rather than keeping up a performance. Confess to those you have wronged and ask their forgiveness. Have one or two trusted, mature believers to whom you can admit your struggles and who will pray for you (James 5:16). Some things would harm others if broadcast, and public confession is for public sins. The aim is not display but freedom from pretence.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims that sin no longer lives in him has fooled himself, and the truth has no place in him.

If we say we have no sin. The second false claim: not “I have never sinned” (v. 10) but a denial that sin still lives in us now. The false teachers may have claimed that their knowledge put them beyond sin, or that what the body does cannot touch the spirit.

We deceive ourselves. We lead ourselves astray, fooling ourselves though not others. It is a terrible blindness, because the man who has deceived himself has no one left to tell him: everyone else can see it; he alone has stopped seeing it.

And the truth is not in us. To deny our sin is to have no grasp of the truth about God or ourselves: the word that diagnoses every human being as a sinner (Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:23) has not taken up residence. The gospel begins with acknowledging our sin.

The holiest people feel it most. Not the beginners: Isaiah, the prophet of the holy, cried out that he was lost, a man of unclean lips, when he saw the Lord (Isaiah 6:5). Paul, near the end of his life, called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The nearer you come to the light, the more of the dust you can see. A Christian who thinks he has little sin left has usually wandered further from the light, not closer.

The one man of whom it is true. There is one person of whom “I have no sin” is simply true: “in him there is no sin” (3:5). Jesus could ask his enemies which of them could convict him of sin (John 8:46), and none could. He did not keep that as a boast: the sinless one appeared to take sins away (3:5), carrying ours to the cross, and his whole life of perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). So the Christian who says “I have no sin” is not only deceiving himself. He is claiming the one title that belongs to the Saviour, and leaving himself no need of him.

What it does not mean. It does not excuse sin or make it inevitable in every moment: John writes so that we may not sin (2:1). But when we do, we must not deny it.

If I still have sin, am I really a new creation? Yes. The Christian is a new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), with a new heart that loves God, and sin no longer rules him. But sin still lives in him as an unwelcome tenant, and he fights it until he dies (Galatians 5:17). You are a saint, set apart and loved, and a sinner who still needs cleansing; admitting your sin is how the new man behaves. Only the new heart hates the old sin enough to confess it.

In everyday life. Ask someone who lives or works with you what fault of yours they notice most. You can bear to hear it, because the blood of verse 7 has already covered it. Do not defend yourself; thank them, and take it to God.

Where Christians differ: can a believer become free of all sin before glory? Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state in which they no longer sin knowingly. Those who hold it are often deeply earnest about holiness, and every Christian should share their longing; the question is whether Scripture promises it before glory. This commentary’s view: John says plainly that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself, and he includes himself and every believer in the we, promising in the same breath forgiveness to those who keep confessing (1:9). When he later says that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning (3:9), he means the settled direction of a life, not sinlessness: the believer still sins, but no longer lives in it at peace. Believers are freed from sin’s dominion (3:9; Romans 6:14) and grow in holiness, but sin remains in them until glory (Romans 7:14–25; James 3:2; Philippians 3:12). We should strive for holiness while daily confessing sin and trusting Christ’s blood.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we honestly own our sins before God, he forgives them and cleanses us completely, and he can be relied on to do it.

If we confess our sins. The chapter’s great promise, against the self-deception of v. 8. “Confess” (homologōmen) is literally to say the same thing: to agree with God, calling sin what he calls it, without excuse. The present tense means keep confessing, as a habit of life. And it is specific, as David found: while he kept silent his bones wasted away, and when he acknowledged his sin and did not cover his iniquity, God forgave (Psalm 32:3–5; 51:3–4). Hidden sin does not prosper, but sin confessed and forsaken finds mercy (Proverbs 28:13).

He is faithful. He has promised to forgive (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12) and staked his name on it. Your forgiveness depends not on how sorry you managed to feel or how well you worded it, but on whether God keeps his word.

And just. We might expect “merciful”. But forgiveness is just because Christ has paid for sin (2:2; Romans 3:25–26). When God forgives the one who confesses, he is not setting justice aside: justice has already been done at the cross, and God would be unjust to punish the same sin twice. The attribute that once stood against us now stands for us: a sinner who comes in Christ’s name can appeal not only to God’s kindness but to his fairness.

To forgive us our sins. “Forgive” means release, cancel the debt. The sins are not filed for future use: he casts them into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19), and as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove them (Psalm 103:12).

And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. “Cleanse” is the word of verse 7. Forgiveness removes guilt; cleansing removes defilement. Both are complete: all unrighteousness, the deeper contamination beneath the surface acts, including the sins we have not yet noticed.

Justice and mercy kiss each other. God does not forgive by looking away from sin but by having looked straight at it on the cross, where he poured out on his Son what we deserved. Every honest sinner who comes finds the door already open and the Father already running. He is faithful, because he cannot lie; he is just, because Christ has paid; and he is glad to forgive.

What it does not mean. Not that believers lose their justification when they sin and regain it when they confess (Romans 8:1). Confession restores the enjoyment of fellowship: a child before a father, not a criminal before a judge.

Must every sin be specifically confessed before it is forgiven? No. The believer’s standing before God was settled once for all when he believed: the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (v. 7), and there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Confession keeps short accounts with a Father; it is not a ledger in which any sin forgotten remains unpaid. Confess specifically the sins you know, and trust him with the ones you do not; David prayed, “Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12).

And what of sins unconfessed at death? A believer is not lost because he dies with a sin he did not name: this verse describes the pattern of a Christian’s life, not an exam at the end. Our advocate is Jesus Christ the righteous, whose propitiation covers all our sins (2:1–2, opened in the next verses): he has already borne in full what his people’s sins deserved.

What if I keep confessing the same sin? Keep confessing it, and keep fighting it. The promise has no limit; Jesus told Peter to forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22), and he is not less patient than he asks us to be. But confession is agreeing with God, who hates the sin, so true confession includes turning from it: removing what feeds it, asking for help, taking practical steps. Repeated failure is not proof that you are not a Christian. A besetting sin can be loved and hated at once, and the hating and fighting are the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:19–25; Galatians 5:17). Giving up the fight would be the danger; each return to him is a sign that grace has not let you go.

I have confessed, but I do not feel forgiven. Then believe the promise rather than the feeling. John does not say we will feel forgiven; he says God is faithful and just to forgive. Feelings may lag for weeks after a serious sin, and the accuser will happily remind you of it. Answer him with the cross: the debt was paid there, and God does not collect twice. Put right what can still be put right with the person you wronged, and thank God for his forgiveness before you feel it. The feeling usually follows the faith.

Does this not make sin cheap: do wrong, say sorry, carry on? Only if you misunderstand confession. To confess is to agree with God about your sin, and God thought it so serious that the only just way to forgive it was the death of his Son; no one who has understood that price treats forgiveness as a revolving door. The religious person makes the opposite mistake, thinking he must earn the pardon by feeling bad enough first. The cross answers both: sin is too costly to be cheap, and grace is too free to be bought. Real forgiveness does not make a person careless. It makes him grateful, and gratitude hates the sin that cost so much (Psalm 130:4; Romans 6:1–2).

In everyday life. Before you sleep tonight, name to God specifically where you sinned today, without arguing for yourself. Then read this verse aloud and believe it. If your sin wronged someone, put it right tomorrow.

Where Christians differ: must we confess to a priest to be forgiven? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest, who absolves not in his own name but on Christ’s behalf, as his minister, so that the penitent hears Christ’s own pardon spoken to him. This commentary’s view: John directs confession to God: he is faithful and just to forgive. Christ is our only mediator and advocate (2:1; 1 Timothy 2:5). Confessing sins to one another is good and healing (James 5:16), but forgiveness comes directly from God through Christ, not through priestly absolution.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To claim that we have never sinned is to call God a liar, and shows that his word has never taken root in us.

If we say we have not sinned. The third and most extreme claim: not only that sin no longer lives in us (v. 8), but that we have never committed it, in the whole of life or since conversion.

We make him a liar. God has declared that all have sinned (Romans 3:23; Psalm 14:3; Isaiah 53:6). To deny our sin is to call God a liar and make the cross unnecessary. Pride, in the end, always accuses God.

And his word is not in us. Someone who claims never to have sinned has never really heard God’s word. The good news has not yet reached him because the bad news has not yet landed.

Two men in the temple. One, a Pharisee, stood and thanked God that he was not like other men, and listed his virtues. The other, a tax collector, stood far off, would not lift up his eyes, beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). The first made God a liar without realising it; the second agreed with God and went home justified. Each of us goes into the temple as one of those two men.

The beginning of every mercy. God’s word about us is severe and true, and it is the beginning of every mercy. He tells us we have sinned because he has come to forgive sinners; he will not let us hide from the diagnosis because he is holding out the cure. The Physician came for the man who will say, in agreement with God, I have sinned; and to that man he gives his own righteousness, his Father’s welcome, and a word that lives in him for ever.

How do I take sin seriously without being crushed by it? Look at your sin long enough to confess it, and at Christ for much longer. John never mentions sin in this chapter without the remedy in the same breath: the blood that cleanses (v. 7), the God who forgives (v. 9), and, as the letter runs on, the Advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1). A Christian who only examines himself will despair; one who never does will become proud. Be honest about sin and glad about grace, with the gladness the larger of the two. For every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's four verbs in verses 1–2 (heard, seen, looked upon, touched) answer docetism (see the note on vv. 1–2). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. God became graspable so that we could grasp him, and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" shapes how we live. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light is searching, and also liberating (see the note on v. 7). God's holiness is the backdrop against which his grace shines. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had broken bread with had walked out, leaving wounds and questions: had those who stayed missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats feelings and spiritual experiences as the surest guide to what is real. John’s answer is the incarnation: Christianity is tied to history, to flesh, to an empty tomb, and our fellowship with God is a fact, not a feeling. Confession, agreeing with God about what we are, is the daily discipline that keeps it real: not earning forgiveness, but receiving what has already been purchased.

keyVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the chapter together: the God who is light (v. 5), the fellowship the apostles proclaimed (v. 3), and the remedy for the sin the rest of the chapter refuses to hide (vv. 8–10). It shows that walking in the light does not mean being sinless but being honest, and that the light is the place of cleansing, not condemnation. And it names what makes that possible: the blood of one who was both the man Jesus and the Son of God.

1.reflection:
John grounds the whole letter on what the apostles heard, saw and touched (vv. 1–3). Why does it matter that Christianity rests on a real man in history rather than on spiritual experience? How would you answer someone who says faith is a private feeling?

John says that fellowship with the Father and the Son comes through the apostles’ message and is shared “with us” (v. 3). What does fellowship with God look like on an ordinary day, and what part do other believers play in it for you?

Verses 6, 8 and 10 each begin “If we say”. Which of these three ways of avoiding the light is most tempting for you, or for churches like ours, and what does it sound like in practice?

Verse 9 says God is not only faithful but “just” to forgive. Why is that good news, and how could it help someone who has confessed a sin but still does not feel forgiven?

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.<sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.<sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.<sup>4</sup>Whoever says “I know him” but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him,<sup>5</sup>but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:<sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.<sup>8</sup>At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.<sup>9</sup>Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.<sup>10</sup>Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.<sup>11</sup>But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.<sup>12</sup>I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.<sup>13</sup>I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.<sup>14</sup>I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.<sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.<sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.<sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.<sup>18</sup>Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.<sup>19</sup>They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.<sup>20</sup>But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.<sup>21</sup>I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.<sup>22</sup>Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.<sup>23</sup>No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.<sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.<sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.<sup>26</sup>I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.<sup>27</sup>But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.<sup>28</sup>And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.<sup>29</sup>If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 completes the letter’s first movement, which began from “God is light” (1:5): it finishes the answer to sin begun in chapter 1, then brings the light to bear on obedience, love, the world and the teachers who have left.

The message. If you belong to Christ, your failures will not undo you: when you sin, Jesus Christ the righteous speaks for you before the Father, and his sacrifice has turned God’s wrath away. And the life he gives is real, so it shows: in keeping his word, loving your brother, refusing your heart to the world, and holding to the truth about the Son. So abide in him until he comes.

Why it was said. The teachers who had gone out (v. 19) claimed to know God while shrugging at his commands, looked down on ordinary believers, and denied that Jesus is the Christ (see the introduction). Those left behind needed a way to tell real faith from its imitation, and the assurance that their own struggling faith was real.

How the chapter makes its case. Grace comes first: an advocate and a propitiation for believers who fail (vv. 1–2). Then the tests: knowing God shows in keeping his commandments and walking as Jesus walked (vv. 3–6), and being in the light in loving your brother, a command as old as Moses and made new by Christ (vv. 7–11). Lest anyone tremble, John tells them what is already theirs (vv. 12–14). He warns against loving a world that is passing away (vv. 15–17), and exposes the antichrists, whose leaving showed they never belonged and whose lie is the denial of the Son; against them every believer has the Spirit’s anointing and the word heard from the beginning (vv. 18–27). He ends: abide in him, so as to meet him unashamed, for those who do right are born of him (vv. 28–29).

Where it leads. The chapter opens with Christ pleading for us in heaven and closes with Christ appearing from heaven, and everything between is how to live in the meantime. The one who stands for us before the Father is the one whose walk we copy, whose name forgives us, through whom alone we have the Father, and whose face we shall see: the righteous one, who met every test in our place and whose life now begins to show in us.

For us. These tests are not hurdles for getting in but a family likeness to look for. Do not use them to torment yourself, or to excuse yourself. Look first to the advocate, then for the signs of his life in you: a care for his word, a love for his people, a loosening grip on the world, a firm hold on the truth about him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Advocate and the Test of Knowing God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Knowing God is real when it changes how we live, and it rests on a Saviour who covers our failures. John wants his people not to sin, yet sets the remedy beside the command: an advocate with the Father who is himself the propitiation for our sins (vv. 1–2). On that ground of grace comes the first test. Those who know him keep his commandments, and in them love for God reaches its goal (vv. 3–5); those who say they abide in him walk as Jesus walked (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology:
Advocate and Propitiation

Jesus Christ the righteous pleads for us, and he is the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers separated the divine Christ from the suffering Jesus (see the note on v. 22).

Now: Knowing God shows itself in keeping his commandments and walking as Jesus walked.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes so that his children will not sin; but if they do, Jesus Christ the righteous is already speaking for them before the Father.

My little children. “Little children” (teknia) is a tender term, used seven times in the letter. Whatever hard things follow are said by a grandfather with his hand on a child’s head.

I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. “May not sin” (hina mē hamartēte) points to single acts: not even one. Chapter 1 might be misused (if everyone sins and God forgives, why worry?), so John says plainly that forgiveness is not a licence. Lose the aim and grace becomes an excuse; lose the provision and holiness becomes despair.

But if anyone does sin. “If” (ean): John knows believers will sin (1:8, 10). Not “when”, which would sound resigned, nor “never”, which would be a lie, but “if”, with the remedy in the next breath.

We have an advocate with the Father. “Advocate” (paraklētos) is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7): one called alongside to help, especially a defence lawyer in court. The Spirit is our advocate within us; Christ is our advocate before the Father. When Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), Christ speaks for us. “With the Father” is face to face with him, as in 1:2: our advocate is in the Judge’s presence and is the Judge’s Son. And “we have” is present: he is not sent for after we have sinned; he is already standing there.

Jesus Christ the righteous. “The righteous” (dikaion): Christ is perfectly righteous, and that is why he can speak for us. An ordinary lawyer argues that his client did not do it. This advocate admits everything, and wins, because he pleads not our righteousness but his own: a life of perfect obedience and a death in our place, both counted as ours (v. 2; Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He has never lost a case, and the Father who sent him delights to hear him.

The scene in Zechariah. The prophet Zechariah saw it centuries before. Joshua the high priest stood before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to accuse him. The accusation was true; the clothes were filthy. But the LORD rebuked the accuser: “Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?” And the filthy garments were taken off, and he was clothed in clean ones (Zechariah 3:1–5). That is what happens in heaven when a Christian sins. The charge is not disputed. It is answered.

What it does not mean. Christ’s advocacy does not mean the Father is reluctant and must be persuaded. The Father sent the Son in love (4:9–10). The Son’s advocacy is his presence there as the one whose sacrifice covers our sins (Hebrews 7:25).

Does having an advocate make sin less serious? It makes it more serious. The eternal Son stands in the Father’s presence with the marks of the nails in his hands, and his plea is his own death. No one who understands that can treat sin lightly. But it changes what sin does to a believer. It no longer threatens his standing, so he is free to stop hiding it. A child who knows his father will not disown him is not more careless; he is more honest. And honesty is where holiness begins.

What does this mean in the moment after I have sinned? Go straight to him, not away from him. Do not wait until you feel sorry enough or have earned the right. Your advocate is already speaking for you. Name the sin to the Father, plainly, and thank him that Jesus has answered for it. Jesus told Peter that Satan had demanded to sift him like wheat, and then said, “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). He prays for you before you fall and while you are down.
verseByVerse.note: “Advocate” is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit (“Helper”) in John’s Gospel; here it is Jesus himself pleading for us.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is himself the sacrifice that has turned away God’s wrath against our sins, and there is no other, for people anywhere in the world. The advocate of verse 1 does not merely plead; his advocacy in heaven rests on an atonement finished on earth.

He is the propitiation for our sins. “He is” (autos estin): he himself is the propitiation, not merely its provider. A propitiation (hilasmos) is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. To expiate is to remove the sin; to propitiate is to turn away the wrath. Christ’s death does both, and this word is the stronger one: the holy anger of God against sin has been absorbed, not overlooked. The word is related to the mercy seat in the tabernacle (Hebrews 9:5), the lid of the ark where, on the Day of Atonement, the blood was sprinkled between God’s presence and the broken law. Christ’s death satisfied God’s just wrath by bearing it in our place (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 2:17), which is why the Father can be both just and forgiving (1:9). This is penal substitution: penal, because what Christ bore was the penalty sin deserves; substitution, because he bore it in the place of others.

Not a pagan bribe. Pagan propitiation meant men trying to calm a moody god with gifts. The biblical propitiation is the reverse at every point. It is not man appeasing God but God providing the sacrifice himself: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (4:10). God’s wrath is not a bad temper but holiness meeting evil with steady justice, and the one who bears it is the Son, who came willingly and is himself God.

And not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. “Ours” means John and his readers. The words “the whole world” have been argued over for four centuries (see the box below), but first see what the verse is for: to keep a failing believer from despair, and on every reading the person who trusts Christ is covered.

The wrath fell on him. The wrath that should have fallen on us fell, and it fell on him. God did not lower his justice to save us; he satisfied it himself, at his own cost, in his own Son. The cup that was ours he drank to the bottom, and when he cried that it was finished, it was. So the mercy seat is no longer a box hidden in a curtained room but a cross lifted up before the nations, and a multitude from every tribe is being gathered whom he bought. There is a man in heaven who never needs to be reminded of our names; he saves completely, and his blood has never failed for one of those for whom it was shed.

What both sides agree on. It is more than what they disagree on, and it is what changes how you live. The death of Christ is of infinite worth, insufficient for nobody. The offer is genuine and goes to everyone without exception. No one who comes is turned away, ever, for any reason. And nobody at all is saved by any other means.

Then can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for him? Tell him what the apostles told people: not the extent of the atonement, but that Christ died for sinners, is a perfect and sufficient Saviour, and forgives everyone who repents and believes (Acts 2:38; 13:38–39). You can say with complete sincerity: Christ is offered to you; there is room for you; if you come to him he will never cast you out (John 6:37). That is a real offer from a real Saviour, the most generous sentence a human being can hear.

How do I know he died for me? Not by searching the secret decrees of God, but by coming to Christ: everyone who comes finds that he was expected. If you trust him, rest on him and want him, you have every right to say with Paul that the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). The doctrine was given to comfort believers that their salvation was actually accomplished, not to keep seekers at the door.

Where Christians differ: did Christ propitiate the sins of every person? Arminians (Christians who hold that God’s choice of his people rests on his foreknowledge of their faith) and others read the whole world as every individual without exception, so that Christ’s death was a propitiation for the sins of all people, including those who are finally lost. Universalists conclude that all will be saved. The wider reading’s strength is the plain force of sentences like this one: he gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6); he tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9); one has died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14). Read without a system, this verse does look as though it is widening something. Godly, careful men have stood on both sides, and neither side holds its view in order to shrink the cross. This commentary’s view: Propitiation means God’s wrath is actually turned away. If Christ propitiated God’s wrath for every individual, no one would face God’s wrath, which Scripture denies (John 3:36; Revelation 14:10). So the whole world must mean something other than every individual. In John’s writings, world often means people of every kind and nation, not just Jews. In John 11:51–52 Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad: the same shape of sentence, from the same author, with the same widening. John’s point is that Christ’s sacrifice is not limited to one group, John’s churches or Jewish believers; it is for people throughout the whole world, of every nation (Revelation 5:9). It is also the only propitiation there is: no other sacrifice is available anywhere in the world. This is definite atonement: Christ’s death actually and effectively propitiated God for all his people, from every nation. Scripture’s language about the cross points this way throughout: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21); the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11, 15); Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25); God obtained the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). Its value is infinite and sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to all.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We can know that we truly know God, because those who know him keep his commandments. Obedience is not the price of knowing him but the sign of it.

We have come to know him. A knowledge gained in the past and still held. The false teachers claimed special knowledge of God; John shows how the true kind is recognised. And knowing, in John, is never just having information. It is knowing a person, the knowing of which Jesus said, “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God” (John 17:3). It is astonishing that God can be known at all: the Maker of galaxies is not a theory but a person, who has made himself known in his Son, so that fishermen and children can say, “I know him.”

If we keep his commandments. “Keep” means observe, guard, obey, and the tense is habitual. “His commandments” are God’s moral will, summed up in love for God and neighbour (3:23; John 13:34; 15:12). This is the first test, obedience. John is not setting up salvation by works; he is describing what a genuine relationship produces (John 14:15, 21). You cannot live for years with someone you love and not begin to care about what he cares about.

In the flow. The claim of 1:6 is now tested by obedience (vv. 3–6), love for the brother (vv. 7–11) and belief about Jesus (vv. 22–23): not hurdles for getting in, but marks of those already in (5:13).

The Son who kept his Father’s commandments. John did not invent this test; he watched it lived. Jesus said, “I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love” (John 15:10), and his whole life, from the carpenter’s bench to the cross, was knowledge of the Father worked out in obedience. The commandments a Christian keeps are a path the Son has already walked. Obedience is the family likeness of the obedient Son.

How much obedience is enough to be sure? John gives no percentage, because he is not grading a performance. He is looking for a direction. The question is not whether you ever fail, since you do, but whether obedience is the settled direction of your desire and effort. Do you want to do what God says? When you disobey, does it trouble you and send you back to him? A real but weak obedience is evidence of real life. What contradicts the claim to know God is not stumbling but a life that has stopped caring what he commands.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims to know God but ignores his commands is lying; in the one who keeps his word, love for God reaches its goal.

Whoever says “I know him”. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10, perhaps the false teachers’ slogan. The words are right; the question is what stands behind them.

Is a liar. The claim and the life cannot both be true. He has the vocabulary of faith without its substance, like a man who can describe a country in detail from the guidebook and has never set foot in it. John is describing someone who claims God and shrugs at his word, not a believer who fails and grieves over it; that grief is the opposite of what he condemns.

Whoever keeps his word. “His word” is broader than commandments: the whole of God’s revealed will, treasured and obeyed, not merely a list.

The love of God is perfected. Probably our love for God, which shows itself in obedience (5:3; see below). “Perfected” means brought to its goal. Love that never reaches the hands has not finished its journey.

That we are in him. Easily missed: keeping his commands assures us that we are joined to Christ, not just that we agree with him.

Words first spoken by Jesus. To men who claimed God as their Father while plotting to kill him, Jesus said: “you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word” (John 8:55). All of John’s terms are there: knowing, lying, keeping his word. The true knower of God is Jesus himself, in whom knowing the Father and obeying him never parted by a hair.

What if I obey out of duty, not love? Then keep obeying, and ask God for the love. Duty is often the scaffolding inside which love is built. A husband who keeps his vows on the days he feels nothing is not a hypocrite but faithful, and the feelings usually return. Jesus said, “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15), and the road also runs the other way: those who obey come to know him better, and knowing him they love him more (John 14:21). Tell God honestly that your heart is cold, and do the next right thing.

Uncertain wording. “The love of God” could mean God’s love for us, our love for God, or the love that comes from God; the Greek allows all three. The parallel in 5:3 (“this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments”) makes our love for God the likeliest, though it is a love he first gives (4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims to live in Christ should live the way Jesus lived.

Whoever says he abides in him. “Abides” means remains, dwells, continues, John’s word from the vine and the branches (John 15:4–10): not visiting Christ but drawing life from him all the time.

Ought to walk. “Ought” means owes it, a debt; “walk” is to live; and “he” is emphatic: that man, the one we saw (John 13:15; 1 Peter 2:21). The likeness does not come by willpower but grows out of being joined to him: those who abide in the vine bear the vine’s fruit.

The man John watched walk. John is not recommending an abstract virtue. For some three years he had walked behind Jesus and watched him stop for a blind beggar the crowd wanted silenced, eat with tax collectors, rise before dawn to pray, weep at a friend’s tomb, wash twelve pairs of dirty feet, and set his face to go to Jerusalem knowing what waited there. When John writes “the same way in which he walked”, he is seeing it. We follow footprints made by the Son of God in the dust of our world.

Is this not an impossible standard? As a way of earning God’s favour, yes. But John writes to people who already abide in him, and the standard is the direction of the life, not the measure of its success. A child learning to write copies the teacher’s letters and makes a mess of them, and the teacher is delighted, because the child is copying the right letters. And Christ lives by his Spirit in those who follow his pattern. Where a life runs in a quite different direction from his and stays there, the claim to abide in him should be questioned. Where it is stumbling after him, it is the real thing.

In everyday life. Pick one encounter in the Gospels: the woman at the well, the washing of feet, the leper he touched first. The one who walked that way now lives in you by his Spirit. Look this week for the person in your path whom everyone else is stepping round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The Old-New Commandment: Love and Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To be in the light is to love your brother. The command is old, given through Moses and heard from the beginning (v. 7), and new, because Christ has kept it all the way to the cross and the true light is already shining (v. 8). So the claim to be in the light is tested by the person on the next chair: love keeps a believer from stumbling, while settled hatred shows a man still in the dark and blind to where he is going (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Old-New Commandment

Why the command is old is treated at v. 7, and why it is new at v. 8.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The split in the church showed where the darkness was.

Now: Nursed grudges blind; love keeps the path clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The command to love is nothing new: it is the old command the readers heard when they first heard the gospel.

Beloved. The first time John uses the word: about to talk about love, he begins by calling them loved.

An old commandment. Familiar, theirs “from the beginning” of their hearing the gospel. This is the command to love, rooted in Moses (Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18) and taught by Jesus. Unlike the false teachers with their advanced insight, John keeps returning to the original. His word is old because he is eternal, and it is never stale because he is never tired.

The word that you have heard. The answer to teachers offering something new is not cleverness but deeper roots in the message already received.

The oldest command in the mouth of Christ. Asked which commandment was the greatest, Jesus did not produce a new one. He reached back to Moses for the two oldest, love the Lord your God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself, and said that all the Law and the Prophets hang on them (Matthew 22:37–40). Then he did what no one before him had done: he kept them, all the way to the cross. So John’s readers learnt what love is by hearing about him.

The old man’s one sermon. Jerome tells a story about John in extreme old age at Ephesus. Too frail to walk, he was carried into the meetings and could manage only one sentence: little children, love one another. At last someone asked him, wearily, why he always said the same thing. He answered that it was the Lord’s command, and if this alone were done, it would be enough. Whether every detail is exact or not, the story fits the man who wrote this verse: he had spent a long lifetime discovering that he had not finished obeying it.

Does this mean Christians should not learn anything new? No. We should grow in knowledge all our lives (2 Peter 3:18). What John warns against is new content: a gospel beyond the gospel, a secret level of truth the apostles did not teach. Growth digs deeper into what was given; error builds somewhere else. A good test of any teaching that excites you: does it send you back to the Christ of the apostles with fresh wonder, or does it make the plain gospel seem elementary and leave it behind?

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet the old command is also new, because in Christ it has been lived out, it is now being lived out in believers, and the new day has dawned.

A new commandment. New here means new in quality, not merely recent (John 13:34): old in its source, but new in its standard, which is Christ’s love, and in its power, because Christ has brought in the new age and given his Spirit. Moses said love your neighbour as yourself. Jesus said love one another as I have loved you, and then went out and was crucified. The cross is now the measure and the pattern of love.

Which is true in him and in you. “True” here means made real, actually happening. Fulfilled in Christ, who embodied it perfectly, and being fulfilled in believers by his Spirit: the command was a description waiting for a person, and now it has one.

The darkness is passing away. Is going by, disappearing, even now: the present tense pictures it in progress. The old age of sin and darkness is ending.

The true light is already shining. The true light is Christ (John 1:9; 8:12). With his death and resurrection the age to come has already broken in, though this present evil age has not yet ended (Galatians 1:4; Hebrews 6:5). Light and darkness overlap now, but the darkness is fading. So when we love, we are not straining against reality but living by the new age that has already arrived. Hatred belongs to the night that is ending; love belongs to the day that is coming. When you love, you are living in tomorrow.
