The grey before dawn. Anyone up before sunrise knows the moment: still dark, nothing visibly changed, yet the sky in the east has thinned, and you know the sun is coming. That is where the church lives: in the grey before dawn, with the first light on the hills.

The world seems to be getting darker. John reads history by its centre, not by the evening news: Christ has risen, and the light cannot be put out. Darkness can still rage as its time runs short (Revelation 12:12), but every person brought out of darkness into his light (1 Peter 2:9) is the dawn spreading, and since the resurrection it has spread to every continent. The darkness is losing, even when it is loud.

In everyday life. Measure your love this week by the new standard, not the old one: not as you love yourself, but as he loved you. What would love cost you today if it looked like his: time, pride, money, the right to be proved right? Pay it somewhere specific.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims to be in the light while hating a fellow believer is still in the dark.

Whoever says he is in the light. Another claim, as in verses 4 and 6, now tested by the most uncomfortable measure: the treatment of a fellow believer.

And hates his brother. Keeps on hating: not a flash of anger but a settled contempt, resentment or ill will. His brother is a fellow believer, the person on the next chair on Sunday; the false teachers apparently despised ordinary believers. It is easy to love humanity at large. John points at someone with a name.

Is still in darkness. Whatever he claims, he has never left it. This is the second test, love, and it will not let our relationship with God be separated from how we treat his people.

The brother Christ has made. Hatred of a brother proves a man still in the dark because the light is Christ (v. 8), and the brother is someone that light has claimed: born of God (5:1), cleansed by the blood of Jesus (1:7), and called brother by the Son himself (Hebrews 2:11). No one can stand near the Lord and keep his back turned on the Lord’s family. When we were enemies, God did not wait for us to become likeable. The love that refuses to hate a brother is only the overflow of a love that refused to give up on us.

What it does not mean. Not that a believer can never feel anger or have conflict with another believer. John describes a settled attitude of hatred and contempt.

Who is my brother, and may I hate those outside the church? Your brother here is your fellow believer, because John is giving a test of genuine membership in God’s family. But it does not follow that you may hate anyone else. Jesus commands love for enemies and persecutors (Matthew 5:44), and the neighbour of Leviticus 19:18 is whoever is in front of you (Luke 10:29–37). John narrows the focus because love inside the family is the first proof of belonging to it. If you cannot love a Christian who shares your Lord, your claim to love the unbeliever down the road is unlikely to be real.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves his brother lives in the light, with nothing on his path to trip him or others.

No cause for stumbling. A cause for stumbling (skandalon) was originally the stick in a trap that springs it. Love keeps us from tripping and from tripping others (Romans 14:13; Psalm 119:165).

How hatred trips us. Resentment distorts judgment, so that you misread the other person’s every move. It makes you avoid church or a family gathering, cutting you off from grace. It hands the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Behind many spiritual falls there is a grudge. The loving person simply has nothing on the path for his feet to catch on.

Twelve hours in the day. John had heard this picture from Jesus. When the disciples begged him not to go back to Judea, he answered: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world” (John 11:9). He was going to Bethany because Lazarus, whom he loved, had died (John 11:5), and that walk of love led in the end to the cross. Love made his road plain, though not safe, and the loving believer walks the same road behind the same Lord.

The one who never stumbled. The one who never stumbled holds the hands of those who do. He walked every step of his Father’s will without a slip, and goes before his people as the shepherd who knows every stone on the path. He is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24), and he will not loosen his grip on one of us between here and there.

What does love for a brother look like when he is difficult? Love is not mainly a warm feeling but a settled will for his good, shown in action (3:18). With a difficult brother that means praying for him, speaking to him rather than about him, giving him the benefit of the doubt, and forgiving when he wrongs you. It may mean telling him a hard truth gently. It never means pretending wrongs did not happen or putting yourself in danger. You can love someone you do not naturally like, because the love comes from God, not from your temperament.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hatred keeps a man in the dark, lost and blind, however sure of himself he feels.

Position and practice. John piles up four statements: he is in the darkness, walks in it, does not know where he is going, and has been blinded.

Does not know where he is going. He thinks he knows, with strong opinions about everybody, but he is walking in circles.

Blinded. Hatred blinds, about God, oneself and others (2 Corinthians 4:4). Like a man who has lived in a cellar for years, the soul that hates finds the daylight it needs is the very thing it cannot bear, and turns back to the dark.

While you have the light. Jesus spoke these words first, in the last days before the cross: “The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12:35). And he gave the remedy with them: “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light” (John 12:36). A blind man cannot cure his eyes by staring harder into the dark. The cure for hatred’s blindness is faith in the Light himself, while he is near. Jesus spat on the ground, made mud, and gave a blind beggar his sight; he can do the same for a heart blinded by bitterness. No darkness is too long-standing for him, and no grudge too old.

Can I hate someone and not know it? Yes: blindness does not feel like blindness, and hatred rarely calls itself by name. It calls itself justice, discernment, honesty, or just being realistic about him. Some signs: you feel pleasure when he fails; you replay his offences; you cannot pray for his blessing or bear to hear him praised. If any are true, do not argue with the diagnosis; ask God to open your eyes, and begin praying for that person’s good. And take heart: the dismay you feel at finding these signs is itself the light at work, and the Lord who prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) is able to teach you to forgive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Assurance for Every Stage of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tests are not meant to frighten God’s children, and John stops to tell them so. He writes because they are already forgiven for Christ’s sake (v. 12). Fathers know the eternal Christ, young men have overcome the evil one, and children know the Father (v. 13); and John says it all again, adding the source of the young men’s strength, the word of God abiding in them (v. 14). Every stage of faith has something to stand on.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance for Every Stage

Before further commands, John tells every believer what is already his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were being told they needed something more.

Now: The newest believer needs first to hear that his sins are forgiven for Christ’s name’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes to his readers because their sins are forgiven, for the sake of Christ’s name.

I am writing to you, little children. Three groups follow: either three stages of maturity, or “little children” addresses all believers (as in v. 1), and fathers and young men are two groups within the church, older and younger.

Because your sins are forgiven. They have been forgiven and remain forgiven, as the tense shows. John writes to them because they are genuine believers.

For his name’s sake. “His name” is Christ’s name, his person and work (Acts 4:12; 10:43). Forgiveness is on account of who Christ is and what he has done, not anything in us; it is the first word to every believer because it is the ground of every other. He has staked the honour of his Son’s name on the pardon of sinners, and he does not forgive grudgingly or provisionally, keeping a file in case we disappoint him.

Why the reassurance comes here. After searching tests, a sensitive believer begins to tremble. So John stops: I am not writing because I doubt you, but because you are forgiven. The tests expose the counterfeit and let the real children see the family likeness in themselves.

What if I am not sure my sins are forgiven? Then look away from yourself to the ground of forgiveness: his name’s sake. If forgiveness rested on the depth of your sorrow or the quality of your faith, you could never be sure. It rests on Christ. Ask yourself: am I trusting him, and him alone, to be my righteousness? If the answer is yes, however weakly, God’s word says you are forgiven (Acts 10:43), and it is not humility but unbelief to doubt it. Assurance grows by looking at Christ more than at yourself.

In everyday life. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not reopen the case. Say aloud: forgiven, for his name’s sake.

Uncertain wording. The little Greek word (hoti) that begins each reason in verses 12–14 can mean “because” or “that”. “That” would make John’s purpose to announce their forgiveness; “because” makes it the reason he writes. Either way the readers are told they are forgiven, and “because” (as in the ESV) fits verse 21, where John writes “because you know” the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mature believers know the eternal Christ, younger believers have conquered Satan, and the newest know God as their Father.

Fathers. Mature believers, perhaps older in years. “Him who is from the beginning” is Christ, the eternal Word of the letter’s opening (1:1). Long years have not made Christ stale to them but rooted them more deeply in him. John praises not their achievements or offices but that they know him.

Young men. Believers in the vigour of spiritual life, perhaps younger in years. “Have overcome” means have conquered and remain victorious. The evil one is Satan (5:18–19). Young believers are in the thick of battle, and they have won by Christ’s victory (4:4; 5:4–5; John 16:33).

Children. Probably those newer in faith, as the different word from verse 12 suggests (paidia). Their knowledge is the simplest and most precious: God as Father (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The newest believer, who could not explain a single doctrine, knows the one thing the false teachers with all their learning did not: that the God of the universe is his Father. The one who has walked with him fifty years has not exhausted him, and the one who met him last week is not kept at a distance.

Which group am I in? Probably more than one. If you are new, you are not second-class: you know the Father, which is the heart of everything. If you are in the thick of the fight, you have overcome, even on days when it does not feel like it. If you have walked with Christ for decades, the goal is not to retire but to know him more deeply still. And every church needs all three. Older believers should seek out younger ones to encourage, and the young should seek out the fathers to learn from.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John repeats his assurance to fathers and young men, and names the young men’s strength: God’s word living in them. A father repeats what he most wants his children to remember.

Fathers, again. To the fathers John adds nothing new. What could be added to knowing the eternal Son?

The word of God abides in you. This is the source of the young men’s strength: God’s word dwelling in them (John 15:7; Colossians 3:16; Psalm 119:11). The word is not the reward of strength but its cause.

You have overcome the evil one. Strength through the word leads to victory over Satan (Ephesians 6:17). Scripture is not information about spiritual warfare; it is the weapon itself, the sword of the Spirit.

The Word with the written word. Jesus overcame Satan in the wilderness by quoting Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11), three times, all from Deuteronomy. The eternal Word defended himself with the written word, and won the battle his people now share.

How does the word actually make me strong? By changing what you believe in the moment of temptation. Every temptation is a lie: this will satisfy you, God is holding out on you, no one will know, you cannot help it. The word that abides in you answers the lie with the truth, as Jesus answered with written words. That works only if the word is already inside you, read, remembered and believed. If reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud, sing it, and learn a few verses well. A small sword in the hand is better than a large one left in the cupboard.

Uncertain wording. Why does John say it all twice? In Greek the first three lines (“I am writing”) are present tense (graphō), and from the line to the children, which the ESV puts at the end of verse 13, the next three (“I write”) are past tense (egrapsa). Probably John is looking back over what he has written so far, or using the letter-writer’s past tense, written from where the reader will stand when the letter arrives. Either way he is not turning to new groups but saying the same assurance twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — Do Not Love the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not give your heart to a world that is passing away. The world John means is not God’s creation or its people but human life organised without God, and love for it cannot share the throne of the heart with love for the Father (v. 15). Its pull comes in three forms, the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, none of them from the Father (v. 16). And all of it is fading, while whoever does God’s will abides for ever (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Do Not Love the World

The three desires are traced at v. 16, and why the world cannot last at v. 17.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Wealth and religion were on public display in the cities of Asia.

Now: Receive created things as gifts, but enthrone none of them (see v. 15).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not give your heart to the world and what it offers, because love for the world and love for the Father cannot rule together.

Do not love the world. Do not give the world your heart: the tense speaks of a settled affection. The world here is not the created earth, which is good (Genesis 1:31), or the people of the world, whom God loves (John 3:16), but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values, desires and priorities (James 4:4; 1 John 5:19).

The same word, two loves. “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). “Do not love the world.” The difference is not the word but the direction. God loves the world as a rescuer loves a drowning man: to save it. We are forbidden to love it as the drowning man loves the current: to be carried by it.

Or the things in the world. The things it values and offers: possessions, pleasures, status, power, when sought as ends in themselves, in place of God.

The love of the Father. Love for the Father. No one can give his first loyalty to both (Matthew 6:24). Everything in the world may be enjoyed as God’s gift; nothing in it may be enthroned.

What the world did with the Son. To see what the world is, watch what it did with the Son: it did not know him (John 1:10), it hated him without a cause (John 15:25), and it nailed him to a cross. To love the world is to take its side. And the cross is also the cure: by it, Paul said, the world had been crucified to him, and he to the world (Galatians 6:14). A heart that has seen the Son of God die for it finds the world’s prizes losing their shine. He did not ask us to give up the world and get nothing; he gave us himself.

How do I know if I love the world? Enjoying films, sport or nice things is not worldliness; God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). The question is what rules the heart. Some tests: what do you think about when your mind is free? What could you not bear to lose? What do you spend on most gladly? Do you laugh at what dishonours him? Does it make you want God less? Worldliness is not a list of activities but a direction of love; anything, even good things, becomes worldly when it replaces the Father. If these questions show you a strong pull toward the world, that alone does not prove you have no love for the Father: believers feel both loves, and the struggle to put the Father first is itself his work in you.

In everyday life. Name the thing the world offers that most tempts your heart. The next time you want it badly, stop and thank God for something you already have in him. Love is retrained by gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything the world offers in place of God comes down to three cravings, and none of them comes from the Father.

For all that is in the world. Three streams, which between them water every temptation the world offers.

The desires of the flesh. Flesh is sinful human nature, craving physical gratification: sexual immorality, gluttony, drunkenness, laziness, comfort above all. The world treats appetite as king: if the body wants it, that settles it.

The desires of the eyes. Cravings aroused by what we see: covetousness, greed, envy, materialism, pornography. The eyes lead the heart (Genesis 3:6; Joshua 7:21; 2 Samuel 11:2). Achan saw, coveted and took; David saw from the roof and sent. And we carry screens built by brilliant people to make the eyes want.

The pride of life. A braggart’s pride: the word (alazoneia, as in James 4:16) belongs with the word for a braggart, the travelling pedlar who promised more than he could deliver. Life here means livelihood: arrogance about what one has or does, the self-sufficiency that needs no God.

Not from the Father. God made us able to enjoy, to see and to achieve, and he made those abilities to serve him. Sin has bent them towards self, and these three desires are the result.

The oldest temptation. Many commentators, Augustine among them, have seen the same three in Eden. The fruit was good for food (the flesh), a delight to the eyes (the eyes), and desirable to make one wise (pride) (Genesis 3:6). And in Jesus’ temptation: bread (the flesh), the kingdoms of the world shown in a moment (the eyes), and throwing himself from the temple (pride) (Luke 4:1–13). The world’s system is very old, and so is its remedy. The first Adam fell at all three points in a garden. The last Adam met all three in a wilderness and did not fall.

Are sexual desire and ambition the desires of the flesh and pride of life? Not in themselves. Sexual desire is God’s gift for marriage (Genesis 2:24; Proverbs 5:18–19), and working hard to do well can be obedience (Colossians 3:23). They become the desires of the flesh and the pride of life when they rule: when desire demands satisfaction outside God’s design, or ambition wants glory for self rather than for God. The test is the master. Hunger is good; gluttony is hunger on the throne. Excellence is good; pride is excellence worshipped.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world and all its wanting are passing away, but whoever does God’s will lasts for ever.

The world is passing away. As in verse 8, it is already in motion. To love the world is to invest in a structure already collapsing (1 Corinthians 7:31). And John adds: along with its desires. Not only the things pass, but the wanting of them. The appetite that seemed so urgent at twenty is gone at eighty, and what it sacrificed for is gone with it.

Every empire passes. When John wrote, the Roman Empire looked eternal, its emperors worshipped as gods. Today tourists photograph its ruins. Every fashion, fortune and name in lights will go the same way. A man who builds his life on any of them is building a house on a tide.

Whoever does the will of God. Doing the will of God is living in obedience (Matthew 7:21; 12:50). Not that obedience earns eternal life: those who do God’s will already share that life, and they will last when the world is gone.

The one who did the will of God. There has been one man of whom this sentence is perfectly true. Jesus came saying, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7), and he did it all the way to the cross; by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10). The believer who does God’s will abides for ever, not because his obedience can outlast the world, but because he is joined to the Son who did the Father’s will perfectly.

What it does not mean. Not that the world will be annihilated. The present order will be renewed (2 Peter 3:13). What passes away is the world as a rebellious system.

How do I know what the will of God is? Mostly, by reading it. God’s will in John’s sense is not a hidden plan to decode but his revealed will in Scripture: to believe in his Son and love one another (3:23), to be holy (1 Thessalonians 4:3), to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). For decisions Scripture does not settle, such as which job or which house, obey what is clear, pray for wisdom (James 1:5), seek counsel, and then choose freely within his commands. A believer who is doing the revealed will of God is in the will of God, whichever good option he picks.

In everyday life. A calendar and a bank statement are quiet confessions of what we think will last. Most of what fills them is good, but ask now and then how much of a month went into God’s word and God’s people, the things that will outlast the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Antichrists, Apostasy, and the Anointing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who deny the Son have no hold on you, because you have the Spirit and the truth. Many antichrists have come, a sign that the last hour has struck (v. 18), and their walking out showed they never belonged (v. 19). Every believer has the anointing and knows the truth (vv. 20–21), and the lie is plain: to deny that Jesus is the Christ is to lose the Father as well (vv. 22–23). So let the message heard from the beginning abide in you, with its promise of eternal life (vv. 24–25), and trust the anointing, which teaches you to abide in him (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointing

On those who left, see v. 19; on the anointing every believer has, see vv. 20 and 27.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers offered superior knowledge.

Now: Beware any teaching that says Scripture, the Spirit and the church are not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last hour has come, and the many antichrists who have appeared prove it. What frightened the church is a sign that God’s timetable is running as foretold.

Children, it is the last hour. The last hour is the final period of history before Christ’s return, which began with his first coming (Hebrews 1:2; 1 Peter 1:20). Every hour since has been part of it.

Antichrist is coming. The word appears in the Bible only in John’s letters (2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). The prefix anti carries two senses at once: against, an opponent, and in place of, a counterfeit substitute. The antichrist is both: an adversary of Christ and a usurper who offers himself as an alternative Christ. The readers had been taught that a great opponent of Christ would come at the end (Mark 13:22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12).

Many antichrists. Before the final antichrist come many smaller ones: all who deny Christ, especially false teachers within the church (vv. 19, 22). And the shock: they are former insiders, not pagan outsiders. The enemy had sung in their meetings and eaten at their tables.

Therefore we know. Their presence shows that the final period has begun. The true Christ is not anxious about the counterfeits. He has already won, and the last hour is simply the time he is taking to gather his own.

What it does not mean. “Last hour” does not mean John expected the end within months. It describes the kind of time we live in: the final stage before Christ returns. Nor should believers be fearful; antichrists cannot snatch Christ’s sheep (John 10:28).

Is it right to call a false teacher antichrist today? John did, so the category is real, and it is defined by the denial of Christ’s true identity (v. 22; 4:3), not by politics, personality or how much we dislike someone. Any teaching that denies that Jesus is the eternal Son of God who came in the flesh, died and rose, is of the spirit of antichrist, however warm its tone. But the label is not for throwing at fellow Christians with whom we disagree about secondary matters, nor at every leader we fear. Use it seldom and with sorrow, to protect the sheep, not to win the argument.

Where Christians differ: who is the antichrist? Some identify the antichrist with a specific future world ruler who will appear during a seven-year tribulation after a secret rapture; the Reformers often identified the papacy as the antichrist; others see the antichrist as a principle only, not a person. Each view is held by believers who love Christ’s appearing, and the hope they share, his personal and visible return, is far larger than their disagreement. This commentary’s view: John teaches both: the spirit of antichrist is present throughout the church age in the many who deny Christ, and Scripture also foretells a final, personal climax of opposition before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8). This fits the amillennial view, which reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of the whole present age, with Christ reigning now, rather than as a later earthly reign; this commentary holds it because the New Testament speaks of one return of Christ, bringing resurrection and judgment together (John 5:28–29), though many faithful Christians read the prophecies differently. On that view, throughout the age between Christ’s comings, antichrists arise, culminating in a final great deceiver whom Christ will destroy at his single, visible return. Believers should not speculate about identities but test every spirit by its confession of Christ (4:1–3).
verseByVerse.note: “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who left the church showed by leaving that they had never truly belonged, for those who belong stay.

They went out from us. The false teachers had left the church, perhaps forming a rival group, and some were now teaching against what they had once confessed. It was painful: people they had prayed with were gone.

But they were not of us. “Of us” means truly belonging, sharing the same life. Their membership was outward only.

That it might become plain. True believers persevere, so the departure revealed what had always been true. Even apostasy (falling away from the faith) serves the purpose of God, separating what only appeared united.

John had seen it happen at the table. The first man to go out from the apostolic circle went out from the Last Supper. Judas had walked with Jesus for three years; then he took the morsel from Jesus’ hand and went out, and it was night (John 13:30). Peter fell the same night, more loudly, and came back weeping, because he was one of them; Judas went out, and showed that he never had been. The difference lay not in the size of the sin but in the keeping of the Lord, who had prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

What it does not mean. Not that everyone who leaves a particular church is an unbeliever. People move, churches err, and believers sometimes leave for good reasons. John speaks of those who left the apostolic faith and fellowship, denying Christ (v. 22).

Someone I love professed faith and has now walked away. What do I make of it? First, grieve; John did. Then remember that you cannot see the end of the story. Some who wander are true believers in a terrible backslidden season, like Peter after his denial, and they come back. Others, if they never return, will show that they did not truly belong, and that is the sorrow of this verse. You do not have to decide which today. Your part is to pray, to keep loving them, to keep the door open, and to speak the truth when it can be heard. God is able to bring back the lost, and he often does it years later.

Could I be one of those who leave? The people who ask this anxiously are rarely the people in danger of it. The warning is real, and it is meant to keep you close. But the promise is just as real: no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Your perseverance rests on his keeping, not on the strength of your grip. Stay where his grace is given: in his word, at prayer, among his people, at his table. Those are the very means by which he keeps you.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer fall away and be lost? Arminian Christians hold that true believers can fall away, pointing to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). They hold it out of a desire to take those warnings with full seriousness, and many of them are devoted followers of Christ. This commentary’s view: This verse is one of the clearest statements of the perseverance of the saints. Those who finally depart from Christ and his people show that they were never truly of us, never genuinely regenerated; if they had been, they would have continued. True believers may stumble, backslide and need restoring, but they will not finally fall away, because God keeps them (John 6:37–40; 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The warnings of Hebrews are real, and they are one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. This is a cause not for complacency but for assurance, and for testing ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unlike those who left, every believer has been anointed with the Holy Spirit and knows the truth.

Anointed by the Holy One. In contrast with those who left, you have an anointing (chrisma), a word related to Christ, the Anointed One, and to antichrist. The wordplay is unmistakable: the anti-anointed ones have gone; you are the anointed ones of the Anointed One. The anointing is the Holy Spirit, given to all believers (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).

You all have knowledge. Against the false teachers who claimed knowledge for an elite, John says every believer has the Spirit and knows the truth (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11).

In the Old Testament, oil was poured on few heads. Prophets, priests and kings were anointed, a handful in each generation. Moses longed for the day when all the LORD’s people would be prophets, and the LORD would put his Spirit on them (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised it (Joel 2:28). Now John says to an ordinary congregation of slaves, tradesmen and widows: you have the anointing, all of you.

Do I need a special experience to have this anointing? No. John says all his readers have it. The anointing is the Holy Spirit himself, given to every Christian at conversion (Romans 8:9; Ephesians 1:13). You may not have felt anything dramatic when you came to faith, but if you trust Christ, love him, and find the gospel true and precious, the Spirit is at work in you, for no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Some believers have vivid experiences and some quiet ones; the anointing is the same.

In everyday life. Do not be intimidated by people who sound more spiritual or more learned than you. You have the same Spirit. Open your Bible today, ask him to teach you, and trust that he will.

Uncertain wording. “The Holy One” is most likely Christ, who is called by this title (John 6:69) and from whom the anointing is received (v. 27, “from him”); but it could be the Father, and John does not say. Either way the anointing comes from God himself.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “you know all things” (panta); “you all” (pantes) is better supported.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes not to tell his readers something new but to confirm the truth they already know, and truth can recognise a lie. This is a letter of assurance, not a course in basics.

Because you know it. Most of the Christian life is not learning new things but remembering old ones at the right moment.

No lie is of the truth. Truth and lies have different sources. Because they know the truth, they can recognise lies (John 8:44; 14:6). The false teaching is not a different angle on the same reality; it is incompatible with the truth. Bank clerks are said to learn counterfeit notes not by studying every forgery but by handling the real thing until anything else feels wrong in the hand.

The truth has a face. In John’s writings truth is not first a list of correct statements but a person: Jesus said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and the false teachers’ lie was a lie about him (v. 22). A believer who has spent years with the Christ of the Gospels may not answer every clever argument, but he knows when the Jesus he is being offered is not the one he loves.

The Truth once stood on trial. Pilate looked at him and asked what truth is, while the Truth stood in front of him, bound, soon to be handed over to be crucified on the word of liars (John 18:38). But no lie could keep him in the grave. He rose, and the world’s verdict was overturned by the verdict of God. He is the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), and he will not let his children be finally deceived.

How can I tell truth from a lie when both sides quote the Bible? Ask: does this teaching agree with Scripture read in context, or depend on one verse twisted away from the rest? Does it exalt Christ as fully God and fully man, the only Saviour, or does it shrink him? Does it agree with what the church has confessed across the centuries, or does it claim that everyone was wrong until now? Does it produce humility, holiness and love, or pride and division? And ask mature believers and faithful pastors. A lie usually fails at least one of these.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great lie is to deny that Jesus is the Christ, and whoever denies the Son denies the Father too. This is what makes a teacher antichrist.

Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? “The liar” (ho pseustēs) means the liar above all others, and this is the lie above all lies. The false teachers apparently separated the human Jesus from the divine Christ, claiming the Christ spirit came on Jesus at his baptism and left before his death (the view associated with Cerinthus; see the introduction). That would leave only a man to die on the cross, and a death that saves no one. To deny that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah, the eternal Son come in the flesh (4:2), is the ultimate lie. The confession about Christ is not optional theology; it is the load-bearing wall of the gospel.

Denies the Father and the Son. You cannot deny the Son without denying the Father, because the Father is known only through the Son (John 14:6–9). Claims to know God while rejecting Jesus as the Christ are false.

What it does not mean. Not that everyone with a confused view of Jesus is the antichrist. John speaks of a deliberate denial of the apostolic truth about Christ, by those who once knew it.

Who denies that Jesus is the Christ today? Anyone who denies who Jesus really is, whatever words he keeps. Some deny his full deity, making him a created being or a great teacher; some deny his real humanity or bodily resurrection. Some keep the name Jesus but empty it of the Christ of Scripture, so that he becomes a symbol of their own values. The test is not whether someone speaks warmly of Jesus but whether he confesses the Jesus of the apostles: the eternal Son of God, truly man, crucified for sin and risen bodily, the only Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has the Father without the Son, and whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.

No one who denies the Son has the Father. To have the Father is to be in relationship with him. There is no access to the Father apart from the Son (John 5:23; 14:6; Acts 4:12), however sincere the seeker. The Son is not a signpost we may remove and still keep the Father; he is the only way the Father is known and reached.

Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also. To confess is to acknowledge publicly, and confessing the Son brings the Father with him. Whoever has the Son has not part of God but all of him: Father and Son together, in the Spirit.

What about those who never hear of Christ? Scripture gives us no other way, and we must not invent one. People are not condemned for failing to believe in a Christ they never heard of, but for their sin against the light God has given them in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Infants who die in infancy, who are elect, are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). Parents who have buried a little one may entrust that child to a Judge who is both just and very tender, and many Reformed pastors have found good hope for such children in David’s words about his son: “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23). But for everyone who can hear, Paul’s logic stands: “how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (Romans 10:14). That is why we send missionaries, not why we stop.

Is it proud to say that whoever denies the Son has no Father, and Jesus is the only way? Pride would be the right word if Christians had invented the claim or thought themselves better for holding it. But a messenger who passes on a warning he did not write is not arrogant; he would be cruel to keep quiet. Every view excludes something: to say that all religions lead to God is to tell Christians, Muslims and Jews that they are wrong about their own faiths. And the Christian way is the one way that leaves no room for pride. It is not a summit reached by the good but a gift handed to the undeserving, because God came looking for us in his Son (Luke 19:10).

Where Christians differ: can people be saved through other religions? Inclusivists hold that people of other faiths may be saved through Christ without knowing him; pluralists that all religions lead to God. This commentary’s view: John’s statement is absolute: no one who denies the Son has the Father. Salvation is found in Christ alone, received through faith in him (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must take the gospel to every nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold on to the gospel you heard at the start, and you will go on living in the Son and in the Father.

Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. “What you heard from the beginning” is the original apostolic gospel (v. 7). Hold on to it, rather than drift to novelties.

You too will abide in the Son and in the Father. The “if” carries a promise: those who hold on to the apostles’ message will go on living in union with God. Holding fast to true teaching is not just tidy thinking; it is how we hold fast to God (John 8:31; 15:7). The gospel we first believed is not the shallow end of the faith; it is the whole ocean.

What it does not mean. Not that we keep ourselves saved by holding onto doctrine in our own strength. God keeps us (5:18), through his word abiding in us.

What if what I heard at the beginning was wrong? “From the beginning” in John means the apostolic gospel, not whatever you happened to be taught first. Some people were raised on a distorted message: a gospel of works, of prosperity, of fear, or of a Jesus who was merely an example. Abiding in what was heard from the beginning means going back past your own beginning to the apostles’ beginning, the gospel written in the New Testament. If your first teachers were wrong, let Scripture correct them, and you will find yourself not drifting from the faith but arriving at it.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Christ has promised those who abide in him is eternal life.

The promise. Made by Christ, and secured not by our faithfulness in holding it but by his in keeping it.

Eternal life. Not merely endless existence, which the lost also have, in a tragic sense, but the life of the age to come, the life of God himself, knowing the Father and the Son (John 17:3), now and for ever (5:11–13; John 10:28). The life is in the Son (5:11–12), so the false teachers, in leading people away from the Son, lead them away from the life itself. When everything we have known has passed away, we will still be just beginning, and the life that started the day we believed will open out into an eternity of knowing him.

If I have eternal life now, why does it not feel like it? Because eternal life is first a relationship, knowing God (John 17:3), not a sensation, and it is as real on dull days as on bright ones. It is like a seed in winter ground: alive, growing roots you cannot see. It shows itself in small ways: a love for God’s word, a hatred of sin, a care for his people, a hope that will not quite die. And the full flowering is still to come. Jesus said whoever believes has eternal life and has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Trust his word over your mood.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes plainly about those who are actively trying to lead his readers astray. Naming the threat is an act of pastoral love.

Those who are trying to deceive you. Leading astray, and actively trying to: so the verb and its tense say. It is the word used in “we deceive ourselves” (1:8): fooling ourselves and being fooled by others are the same disease. Naming the threat clearly helps the church resist false teaching instead of taking it in out of a mistaken kindness.

Words John heard on the Mount of Olives. John was one of the four who asked Jesus privately about the end (Mark 13:3), and the Lord’s first words were a warning: see that no one leads you astray; many will come in my name and lead many astray (Mark 13:5–6). Decades later the old disciple uses the same verb, naming the danger before it strikes.

How do I recognise a deceiver if he seems sincere and kind? Most deceivers are sincere, deceived first themselves (2 Timothy 3:13); but sincerity is not truth, and kindness is not sound teaching. The most dangerous deceptions arrive wrapped in spiritual language. Watch what is said about Christ, about sin, and about Scripture. Ask whether the teaching draws you to Christ and his people, or to the teacher and his group. Be wary when you are told the church has missed something only this teacher sees. And do not judge alone; take it to faithful pastors.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit who lives in every believer teaches them the truth, so they need no new teachers with a new message; they need only to remain in Christ.

The anointing abides in you. The Spirit remains permanently (John 14:16–17), not a visitor for good meetings only. The same Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation, who overshadowed Mary, who raised Jesus from the dead, has made his home in us to teach us Christ.

No need that anyone should teach you. You do not need the false teachers’ higher knowledge; you already have the Spirit and the apostolic truth (see the box below).

His anointing teaches you. The Spirit teaches believers, guiding them into the truth (John 14:26; 16:13), not by giving new revelation, but by making the apostles’ message clear to them, confirming it in their hearts, and enabling them to recognise error.

True, and no lie. The Spirit is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17). His teaching is the opposite of the deceivers’.

Abide in him. That is, in Christ. The remedy for every form of false teaching is not winning arguments but staying joined to the Son, kept by the Spirit and holding to the word received from the beginning.

What about when I feel the Spirit has told me something? Test it by Scripture, humbly. The Spirit who inspired the Bible does not contradict it, nor add to it now that it is complete. He does give conviction of sin, assurance, comfort and wisdom, and he guides through his word and providence. But an inner impression is not a revelation with authority over anyone else, and it can come from our own desires. If a feeling leads you toward something Scripture forbids, it is not the Spirit. If it leads you to obey what Scripture says, follow it gladly, and say “I believe God wants this”, not “God told me”. Christians who believe the gift of prophecy continues today usually agree that any such word must be tested by Scripture and never binds the conscience as Scripture does, and on that shared ground believers on both sides can stand together.

In everyday life. Before you read Scripture today, pray a short prayer for the Spirit to open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Then read slowly, expecting him to teach you, and write down one thing he shows you about Christ.

Where Christians differ: does this verse mean believers do not need teachers? Some have used this verse to reject all church teaching, or to claim private revelations from the Spirit. This commentary’s view: John himself is teaching them in this very letter, and Christ gave teachers to the church (Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 2:2). John means they do not need the false teachers’ new knowledge, because the Spirit has given them the true knowledge through the apostolic gospel. The Spirit does not give new revelation that contradicts or adds to Scripture; he illuminates Scripture and confirms its truth to the heart. Every claim to Spirit-given teaching must be tested by the apostolic word (4:1–6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stay in Christ, so that you can meet him gladly when he comes. Abiding in him now means confidence, not shame, at his appearing (v. 28). And a life that does what is right is the family likeness of those born of God, the theme that the next chapter takes up (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Abide in him

On abiding and confidence at his coming, see v. 28; on the family likeness, see v. 29.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Christ’s appearing was still ahead.

Now: Live now as someone who will meet him face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remain in Christ, so that when he comes again we can meet him with confidence instead of shrinking back in shame. The call to abide, gathering force through the chapter (vv. 6, 10, 24, 27), now has its final reason: he is coming back.

What it means to abide. “Abide” can sound like a technique for advanced Christians, a feeling of closeness to work up and hold on to. It is simpler: to stay where you have been put. And everyone abides somewhere. Each of us has a place the heart goes home to when the day goes wrong: someone’s approval, a clean record, the next success. Whatever that place is, it shapes us, and none of it will hold us up when he appears. John’s call is to make Christ that home, and the wonder is that he made room for us first. “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4): he joined us to himself before we took a step, and he keeps hold when our grip slips. Timothy Keller often pointed out, in Center Church and elsewhere, that the gospel is not just the ABCs of the Christian life but the A to Z of it: we never move on from Christ to something more advanced; we only go further in. In practice, abiding means going back to him first. When you fail this week, bring it to him before you start repairing your image; when something goes well, thank him before you lean on it. See also In Christ in the Theological Dictionary.

So that when he appears. “Appears” means is revealed, made visible: the same word as 1:2, where the life appeared in the incarnation. He appeared once in humility; he will appear again in glory, visibly and publicly.

We may have confidence. Confidence was a citizen’s right to speak freely in the assembly, with nothing to fear. Here it is a child running to greet a returning father, not hiding. John includes himself.

Not shrink from him in shame at his coming. Coming (parousia) is the word used of a king’s official visit to a city. The shame is not only a punishment imposed from outside. It is the horror anyone must feel on meeting the one whose commands he spent his life ignoring.

He is coming. The one who appeared in a manger will appear in the sky, and for his own it will be the homecoming they have waited for, when the bridegroom comes for the bride and the king enters his city. Those who have stayed close to him will run to meet him unashamed, because the one they meet is the one who covered all their shame.

Will I be ashamed when he comes because of my sins? Not if you are in him. Your sins were judged at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The confidence John speaks of is not earned by perfection but rests on abiding: trusting him, staying near him, walking in the light with your sins confessed. There may be things you will wish you had done differently, and some work may be lost (1 Corinthians 3:15). But the believer will meet his Lord as a child meets a father coming home, not as a criminal meets a judge. Live now in the way you will be glad of then.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since God is righteous, everyone who habitually does what is right shows that he has been born of God.

If you know that he is righteous. Righteous means perfectly upright, always doing what is right (on who “he” is, see below).

Born of him. To practise righteousness is to do it habitually, and “has been born” means born at a point in the past and still God’s child now. This is the first mention of new birth in 1 John, the theme chapter 3 unfolds, and the order matters: birth first, righteousness as its evidence. The new birth is a change of nature, not only of status. Children resemble their Father.

The likeness of the Son. John does not stop to say whether the righteous one is the Father or the Son (2:1), because their righteousness is one. The family likeness God is producing in his children is the likeness of his Son, whom he has made the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). When a child of God does what is right, it is the life of the Firstborn showing in a younger brother. His children do not yet look much like him, but they will. He has never yet failed to raise a child to his likeness, and he will finish what he started.

Must I have had a dramatic born-again experience? No. New birth is God’s work, done once, often silently: “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8). Some can name the day; many raised in Christian homes cannot remember a time when they did not trust Christ. What matters is not the memory of the birth but the evidence of the life. A man does not prove he was born by remembering his birthday but by being alive. If you trust Christ and are growing, however slowly, in doing what is right, you have been born of him.

Uncertain wording. “He is righteous” could refer to Christ, called “the righteous” in verse 1 and the “he” of verse 28, or to the Father, since “born of him” must mean born of God (3:9; 5:1). John moves between them without marking the change, and the meaning is the same either way.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The two words of 2:1–2 look at Christ’s saving work from two sides. As advocate, he represents us before the Father (see the note on v. 1). As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation (see the note on v. 2). The atonement was finished once, in history, and Christ goes on pleading it for us now. Together they give the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John’s three tests, obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11) and belief (2:22–23), are not a checklist for earning assurance but signs of new birth, as a doctor looks for signs of life. The question is not whether I have been good enough but whether the Spirit’s fruit is growing in me. And they belong together, because obedience, love and right belief about Jesus grow from the same new life.
2.examples:
Then: The teachers who had left claimed a superior knowledge of God. John answers that by leaving they showed they had never truly belonged (2:19), and that those who remained, perhaps confused and fewer, had the anointing from the Holy One and knew the truth (2:20).

Now: Every generation is offered new spiritualities and new paths to a better self, and the church is tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more current. The gospel does not need updating; it needs to be lived in. We go deeper not by moving beyond the cross but by going further into it.

keyVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the chapter’s two halves in one breath: the call to holiness that the tests of obedience, love and truth spell out, and the grace on which every one of those tests rests. John will not let either swallow the other. Before he asks anything of his children, he shows them who is standing for them before the Father.

2.reflection:
John puts the command “that you may not sin” and the provision “if anyone does sin” side by side (v. 1). What happens to a Christian who keeps only the first? Only the second? What do you do in the first hour after you know you have sinned?

John’s tests are obedience, love for the brother, and the truth about Jesus (vv. 3–11, 22–23). Why does he give tests at all, and how can we use them to strengthen assurance rather than to torment ourselves or to judge others?

Verse 16 names the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life. Where do you see each of them in the world around you, and which pulls hardest at you? What does it mean in practice that “the world is passing away” (v. 17)?

John tells ordinary believers that they have the anointing and know the truth (vv. 20, 27). How should that give us confidence when we meet persuasive teaching, and how does it fit with our need for pastors and teachers?

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.<sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.<sup>4</sup>Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.<sup>5</sup>You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.<sup>6</sup>No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.<sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.<sup>8</sup>Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.<sup>9</sup>No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.<sup>10</sup>By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.<sup>11</sup>For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.<sup>12</sup>We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.<sup>13</sup>Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.<sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.<sup>15</sup>Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.<sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.<sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?<sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.<sup>19</sup>By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him;<sup>20</sup>for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.<sup>21</sup>Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;<sup>22</sup>and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.<sup>23</sup>And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.<sup>24</sup>Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 is the heart of the letter’s second movement, which opened at 2:28–29 with the call to abide in Christ until he appears and the first mention of being born of God. John now turns from the tests of chapter 2 to the family behind them.

The message. You are God’s children, really and now, because the Father has loved you; and children grow like their Father. The Son appeared to take away sins and undo the devil’s work, and God’s own life is planted in you, so you cannot make peace with sin. The cross has shown you what love is, so you will love your brothers and sisters in deed, not only in talk. And when your heart accuses you, God is greater than your heart.

Why it was said. The teachers who had left claimed a higher knowledge of God while treating sin lightly and showing no love for those they left behind (see the introduction). The faithful needed to hear that such “spirituality” bears the devil’s likeness, not God’s, and that their own struggling hearts were not the final word about them.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens in wonder: the Father’s love has made us his children now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him, a hope that makes us pure (vv. 1–3). Then come two families, known by how they live: the Son appeared to take away sins and destroy the devil’s works, and God’s seed abides in those born of him, so they do not keep on sinning (vv. 4–10). The second mark is love: not Cain’s hatred, which the world still shows the righteous, but love defined by the cross and shown in an open hand to a brother in need (vv. 11–18). Last comes rest for the anxious: God is greater than our heart, prayer is free, his one commandment is faith and love, and his Spirit assures us that he abides in us (vv. 19–24).

Where it leads. Christ “appears” three times in the chapter: to take away sins, himself without sin (v. 5); to destroy the works of the devil (v. 8); and at the end, when we shall see him and be like him (v. 2). At the centre stands the deed that defines love: “he laid down his life for us” (v. 16). Before the chapter asks anything of God’s children, it shows the Son who became one of us to make us children, carried our sins away, broke the devil’s hold, and will finish what he began on the day we see him as he is.

For us. This chapter is meant to settle true believers and to unsettle those at ease in sin. If you are fighting your sins, loving God’s people imperfectly and trusting Christ, see in it the family likeness; and when your conscience still accuses you after you have confessed, let God’s verdict outweigh your heart. Then love one brother or sister in need this week, in deed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Father’s love has made us his children, really and now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him. John stops to point at the wonder of it: we are called children of God, and so we are, though the world does not recognise us any more than it recognised him (v. 1). What we will be is still hidden, but we know whom we shall be like, for we shall see him as he is (v. 2). And the hope is not idle: everyone who has it is already getting ready, purifying himself as he is pure (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology:
Children Now, Like Him Then

On being children now, see v. 1; on being like him when we see him, v. 2; on the hope that purifies, v. 3.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some claimed they had already arrived.

Now: We become what we behold (see v. 2); set your hope on his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father’s love has made us his children, truly and now, though the world cannot see it, just as it could not see his Son.

See what kind of love. “See” is a cry of wonder: John is stopping in the road and pointing. “What kind of” is used of things out of the ordinary, as when the disciples asked what sort of man even winds and sea obey (Matthew 8:27): this love comes from outside the world. And “has given” means the gift remains, handed over and not taken back.

Called children of God. Children here means born ones: not merely adopted (though that is true, Romans 8:15), but born of God (2:29) and sharing his life. Not that we become God, but that he gives us a new heart that begins to love what he loves (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Peter 1:4). A king might adopt an orphan and give him his name, but he cannot give him his blood. God does both.

And so we are. John interrupts himself with the two most important words in the verse. The calling is not a courtesy title but a fact, true now, with all our failures in plain view.

The world does not know us. The world did not recognise Jesus as the Son of God (John 1:10–11), so it does not recognise his likeness in his children. Think of the old stories of a king’s son who travels his father’s kingdom in disguise. No one guesses, and he is no less the prince for it; the day will come when he rides back through the same towns with his father’s banners, and everyone who pushed him aside will know. That is the believer in the world.

It cost him his only Son. The Son himself came like that: born in a borrowed stable, a carpenter in a despised town, crucified as a criminal, and the world did not know him. The God who needs nothing has chosen to have children. He looked at rebels who had run from his house and wasted his gifts, and did not merely pardon them; he brought them into his family, gave them his name, put his life in them and seated them at his table. It cost him his only Son, who became a child of man so that the children of men might become children of God.

What it does not mean. Not that all people are God’s children by nature. All are his creatures, but only those born of him by faith in Christ are his children (John 1:12–13; 8:42–44).

What if I do not feel like a child of God? John does not say, see how you feel, but see what love the Father has given. Your sonship rests on his gift, given to those who received his Son and believed in his name (John 1:12). If you trust Christ, you are God’s child on the bad days as fully as on the good; children do not stop being children when they are sulking, ill or ashamed. Say to yourself, “and so we are”, and speak to God as Father, even if the word feels strange. The Spirit teaches us to say it (Romans 8:15).

Should I want the world to like me? Peace with people is good (Romans 12:18), and Christians should be the kindest neighbours on the street. But being understood by the world cannot be your aim, because the world did not understand your Lord. If people misread you because you will not join in their sin, or love a Christ they do not know, that is the family likeness showing. Be gentle, be honest, and be content to be known by your Father.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, omit “and so we are”; the earliest include the words.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are God’s children already, and when Christ appears we shall see him as he is and be made like him.

Now, and not yet. “Now” is the present fact, but the full glory of being children is still hidden (Romans 8:18–19; Colossians 3:3–4). An acorn is a real oak in the making, but nobody looking at it would guess the tree.

We shall be like him. “When he appears” is Christ’s return (2:28), and “like him” means like Christ in his glorified humanity: holy, immortal, with resurrection bodies (Philippians 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:49; Romans 8:29). John does not know what we will look like, but he knows whom we will look like.

We shall see him as he is. The church has called it the beatific vision. Now we see dimly (1 Corinthians 13:12); then face to face (Revelation 22:4; Matthew 5:8). As Moses’ face shone after seeing God’s glory (Exodus 34:29), so seeing Christ will make us like him. The order matters: we do not become like him and then qualify to see him; we see him, and are changed, and that sight will finish in an instant what the Spirit has been working toward for a lifetime.

Becoming what we behold. People grow like what they gaze at: children pick up a parent’s laugh; a man who watches cruelty becomes cruel. Even now, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image (2 Corinthians 3:18). The psalmist saw the end from far off: “when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness” (Psalm 17:15).

Nothing between. The eyes that have wept at gravesides and strained to read the promises in the dark will look on the face of the Son of God, with nothing between: no mirror, no dimness, no faith struggling to hold on, but sight.

In everyday life. When the mirror shows age, weakness or the marks of sin, say: this is not yet what I will be. And spend five minutes today looking at Christ in a Gospel passage; it is how the likeness grows.

Will I still be me? Yes, more than you have ever been: the risen Jesus was recognisably himself, and being made like Christ completes everything God made you to be.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who truly hopes to see Christ is already getting ready for him, making himself pure as he is pure.

Everyone who thus hopes in him. Literally, has this hope set on him. Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but a sure expectation: an anchor, not a guess.

Purifies himself as he is pure. The tense means keeps purifying. It is the word used of ritual purification before a festival (John 11:55), when pilgrims went up to Jerusalem early to make themselves ready for the Passover. The target is Christ’s own purity, not the best we can manage. What we expect then shapes how we live now (2 Peter 3:11–14).

The bride before the wedding. Nobody needs to tell a bride to get ready in the week before her wedding. She is not afraid the groom will reject her; he has already chosen her. She gets ready because she is going to see him. That is the purifying of this verse: not fear of rejection but the joy of an approaching meeting. And our hope is not that we will make ourselves fit to meet him, but that he who is pure has promised to make us like him, and has already begun.

What it does not mean. Not that we purify ourselves by our own power: Christ’s blood cleanses (1:7) and the Spirit sanctifies, though we actively cooperate (2 Corinthians 7:1). Nor that we have reached sinlessness (1:8). It means a life turned towards his purity.

How does hoping in Christ’s return actually make me purer? By changing what you want. If you truly believe you will see him face to face, the things that compete with him start to look small, and the sins you cherish start to look like stains on a wedding dress. Hope also gives staying power: you can say no to a pleasure now because a greater joy is coming. Think about his return on purpose: read the passages about it (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; Revelation 21–22), sing about it, and ask of each choice whether you would be glad of it when he appears.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s children cannot make peace with sin, because the Son came to remove it and God’s own life is in them. Read carefully, the passage neither terrifies the true believer nor comforts the false one. In two matching waves John shows sin for what it is, lawlessness and the devil’s work, and sets against it why Christ appeared: to take away sins (vv. 4–7) and to destroy the works of the devil (vv. 8–9). So there are two families, known by how they live, by righteousness and by love (v. 10). This is not sinless perfection (1:8–10) but a new direction that will not be reversed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Birth

On God’s seed in those born of him, see the note on v. 9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Claimed spiritual knowledge was being used to excuse sin.

Now: Avoid both errors: tolerating sin as normal, and thinking that any sin proves you are not born again.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To go on sinning as a way of life is to live in rebellion against God, for at its root every sin is lawlessness.

Everyone who makes a practice of sinning. Literally, the one doing sin: habitually, as a way of life, the opposite of practising righteousness (2:29). The passage runs in two matching waves (vv. 4–7, 8–10), each resting on why Christ appeared, so it describes first what his coming does in his people.

Sin is lawlessness. Defiance of God’s law. Sin is weakness and does damage, but beneath both it is self-rule, refusing God’s right to command us. Lawlessness is the word Paul uses of “the man of lawlessness” revealed before the end (2 Thessalonians 2:3): every sin, however small, shares the spirit of that rebellion.

The small rebellion. We usually measure sin by its damage; John measures it by its direction. A child told not to touch the fire who touches it has done little harm if he was not burnt, but something serious: he has decided that his will outranks his father’s. That is the shape of every sin. It says to God, “I will decide.”

Not my will. The whole life of the Son of God said the opposite, and nowhere more plainly than in Gethsemane, with the cup of wrath before him: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The first Adam reached for the fruit to have his own way; the last Adam bowed to the cross to do his Father’s. Lawlessness is answered not by a better rule but by a perfectly obedient Son, who then took the place of the lawless.

If all sin is lawlessness, are all sins equally bad? All sins are rebellion, and any one of them is enough to condemn us apart from Christ (James 2:10). But some sins are more serious than others: in their effects, in how much the sinner knew, and in the hardness of heart they show (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48; the Westminster Larger Catechism, question 150). A flash of impatience and a lifetime of cruelty are both sin, but not the same. So we never call any sin small, and never treat a struggling brother’s weakness as if it were a monster’s crime.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ came to carry sins away, and because he himself is without sin he could do it.

He appeared in order to take away sins. This is why he came: his death for sin was his mission, not an afterthought. “Take away” means carry away, as in John 1:29: “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” He removes its guilt by his death and its power by his Spirit; to continue in sin contradicts the purpose of his coming.

In him there is no sin. Christ is sinless (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22), and his whole sacrifice rests on it: only the sinless one can bear the sins of others without being destroyed by them. A drowning man cannot rescue another drowning man.

The goat into the wilderness. Every year on the Day of Atonement the high priest laid both hands on the head of a live goat, confessed over it all the sins of the people, and sent it away into the wilderness, carrying their iniquities to a solitary land (Leviticus 16:21–22). That is what taking away means: Christ carried our sins out of sight, and they are not coming back.

Untouched, then laden. The holy one, in whom there was no sin, came into a world thick with it, walked through it untouched, and then took it all on himself. Those united to him cannot be at home in what he came to carry away.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ removed all sin from believers instantly. He removed its guilt completely, is removing its presence progressively, and will remove it entirely at his return (v. 2).

In everyday life. When a sin from your past comes back to mind, picture it carried away out of sight, as the goat went into the wilderness, and refuse to go out into the desert to fetch it back. What Christ has taken away, do not pick up again.

How could Jesus be truly tempted if he had no sin? Temptation is not sin; yielding is. Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and the devil’s offers were real. He felt the force of temptation more than we do, because he never gave way: a man who gives in after a minute never learns how heavy the pressure can become. That is why he can sympathise with us and help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever lives in Christ does not settle into sin, and whoever has settled into sin has never truly known him.

Keeps on sinning. A settled habit of sin, not a single lapse: that is what the verbs point to. Read the verse in the light of 1:8–10, or it will give false assurance to the person who sins at peace and claims to abide, or false despair to the struggling believer who concludes he cannot be born again.

Has either seen him or known him. Spiritual seeing and knowing. Nobody meets the Lord and goes on exactly as before: Zacchaeus met him, and that same day he was giving half his goods to the poor (Luke 19:8).

I have fought the same sin for years. Am I keeping on sinning? The key word is comfortable. John describes a person who sins and does not mind, who has made peace with it and stopped fighting. If you hate this sin, confess it, grieve over it and keep fighting it, even after many defeats, you are not the person in this verse; the fight itself is evidence that you have seen him. Paul describes exactly that war in Romans 7, and he was an apostle. Keep fighting with every means God gives, and keep running to Christ each time you fall. The person who has given up the fight is the one in danger.
verseByVerse.note: The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse (compare 1:8–2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be fooled: a righteous life is what shows that someone belongs to the righteous Christ.

Let no one deceive you. The false teachers taught that one could be righteous without living righteously. John will not allow the separation.
