As he is righteous. The one who habitually does right shows that he is righteous, like Christ. Doing right does not make him righteous (justification is by faith alone); it shows that he has been counted righteous and given a new nature (2:29). And the standard is Christ himself.

Not only on us but in us. Christ is righteous, wholly and without remainder, and he has not kept his righteousness to himself. He has wrapped his people in it as a robe, and then begun to make them what he has declared them to be. The one who clothed us will also fit us to the clothes, until his righteousness is not only on us but in us, and shines out of us for ever.

How can I be righteous and still sin? Because righteous means two things, both true of you. Before God’s court you are counted righteous, completely and for ever, because Christ’s righteousness is credited to you (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21); that never grows or shrinks. In your life you are being made righteous by the Spirit, and that does grow, unevenly. Luther summed it up: at the same time righteous and a sinner. The first is the root; the second is the fruit. Rest on the first, and pursue the second.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A life of settled sin bears the devil’s family likeness, and the Son of God came precisely to undo the devil’s work.

Of the devil. Belonging to him: sharing his character, as one of his family (John 8:44).

Sinning from the beginning. From the beginning of his rebellion, or of human history (Genesis 3). He has been sinning ever since, and those whose lives share that pattern bear his family mark.

To destroy the works of the devil. Untying a knot, breaking up a building, releasing a prisoner: that is the verb (lysē). Sin, deception, death and bondage: Christ came to undo all of it (Hebrews 2:14; Genesis 3:15). He won the decisive victory at the cross, and will complete it at his return.

The demolition in the Gospels. Watch the Son of God at work and you see the devil’s works coming apart. A woman bent for eighteen years, whom Satan had bound, was loosed and stood up straight (Luke 13:16), and Jesus’ word for “loosed” belongs to the same family as John’s word for “destroy”. Unclean spirits left, lepers were cleansed, a widow’s son sat up on his bier. Every miracle was a brick pulled out of the devil’s wall. Then at the cross the foundations went, and Christ went down into death and broke it open from the inside.

If Christ has destroyed the devil’s works, why is there still so much evil? Because the victory is decisive but not yet complete. A war can be won in one battle while fighting goes on for months. Christ disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15), he is dismantling the devil’s works in every life he saves, and at his return the devil will be thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10). So do not fear the devil as though he were Christ’s equal. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those born of God cannot make peace with sin, because God’s own life has been planted in them, and it remains.

God’s seed abides in him. The seed (sperma) is the life God implants at the new birth (on what exactly it is, see the box below), and it remains. A seed planted does not stay a seed; it grows, pushes through the soil, and in the end bears the likeness of the plant it came from.

He cannot keep on sinning. “Born of God” means born and remaining so, and the verb means that he cannot continue in sin as a way of life: God’s life in him resists it, so sin is never made at home. This is also a promise of perseverance: the seed remains, and in the weakest believer it is stronger than all the sin that remains in him. On the last day it will flower into the full likeness of his Son.

Kept by the one born of God. Why does the seed remain? John answers in 5:18: “everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him”. The one who protects is most naturally the Son, born of God in a unique and eternal sense. The seed does not survive because the soil is good; it survives because the Son of God stands guard over it.

In everyday life. When you sin, notice the discomfort that follows: the unease, the loss of joy in prayer, the desire to put it right. Do not drown it out. Thank God for it, because it is the seed refusing to let you settle, and follow where it leads, back to him.

What about a believer who falls into serious sin, like David? David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and for months covered it up. But God did not leave him there: he sent Nathan, and David was broken, confessed, and wrote Psalm 51. That is what the seed does. It does not stop a believer from falling, sometimes terribly, but it will not let him stay at peace in the mud. If you have fallen badly, the misery you feel is not proof that you are lost; it may be the seed at work. Come back the way David came: honestly, quickly, to the God of steadfast love.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach sinless perfection? Some read it as teaching that a born-again person is incapable of sinning at all, or that sinless perfection is possible in this life. This commentary’s view: John has already said that anyone who claims to be sinless is deceived (1:8, 10), and he provides for believers who sin (2:1). The present tense verbs in chapter 3 indicate habitual practice. A child of God cannot continue in a settled lifestyle of unrepented sin, because God’s seed in him makes it impossible. He may fall, but he will not stay down; he will be grieved, convicted and restored. This is the Reformed doctrine of perseverance (those truly born of God will be kept to the end) and of progressive sanctification (growth in holiness through life).

Uncertain wording. What “God’s seed” means is not certain: God’s life or nature imparted (2 Peter 1:4), the Holy Spirit, or the word by which we are born again (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18); a few take “seed” as offspring, meaning God’s children remain in him. Most likely it is the divine life itself, given through the word by the Spirit. On every reading, what God has planted stays.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are only two families, and they can be told apart by how they live: whoever does not do right or love his brother is not of God.

Two families. Every person belongs to one or the other (John 8:42–47); John allows no neutral ground.

Nor is the one who does not love his brother. Here the two tests meet: righteousness (vv. 4–10) and love, which John develops next (vv. 11–18). They are two aspects of one life, for love is the heart of righteousness (Romans 13:8–10).

The Son who remains in the house. It was Jesus who first spoke of the devil as a father, to religious men who were trying to kill him (John 8:44). In the same conversation he told them how anyone moves from one family to the other: “The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:35–36). No one changes families by trying harder. The Son, who belongs in the Father’s house by right, brings slaves in with him and makes them sons.

What it does not mean. Not that we can always tell for certain who is a child of God by outward observation; God alone knows the heart. But the general pattern of a life reveals its family.

What about decent people who are not Christians? Unbelievers can be kind, honest and brave by God’s common kindness to all (Matthew 5:45; Romans 2:14–15), and we should honour it. But John asks a deeper question: not whether a person does good things, but to whom he belongs. Outward decency does not make anyone a child of God; only new birth does (John 3:3). That is not an insult to our neighbours but the reason we must tell them about Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Love One Another: The Cain Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for the brothers is the second mark of God’s children, and the cross shows what it is. John brings love down to earth: the brother in front of you. Cain shows the opposite, hatred of a righteous brother, and why the world still hates believers (vv. 11–13). Love is the evidence that we have passed from death to life, as settled hatred is the mark of a murderer (vv. 14–15). Then John defines love by an event, Christ laying down his life for us, which obliges us to give ourselves for one another, beginning with an open hand to a brother in need (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Love Defined by the Cross

Cain’s hatred is traced at v. 12, and love defined by the cross at v. 16.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The world’s hatred was not to surprise the church.

Now: Love in deed and truth: an open hand to a brother in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for one another is not an extra for advanced Christians but the original message itself, heard from the very beginning.

The message that you have heard from the beginning. The first message (1:5) was that God is light; the second, that we love one another. “From the beginning” (2:7) means this is nothing new: it is the apostles’ message itself, which the false teachers had quietly left behind.

That we should love one another. Keep loving, as the tense shows. This is Jesus’ new commandment (John 13:34–35; 15:12, 17), what the gospel produces, and the badge by which he said the world would know his disciples: not their buildings or their size, but their love for one another.

What it does not mean. Not love only for believers. Christians love all people, even enemies (Matthew 5:44). But love for the family of God is a special mark of belonging to it.

Do I have to like every Christian? No, but you must love every Christian. Liking is natural affinity, and you will have it with some believers and not others; that is no sin. Love is a settled will for another’s good, shown in action, and it is commanded. You can love a brother you find tiresome by praying for him, helping him, defending his name, welcoming him and forgiving him. Often, over years, liking follows. Even when it does not, love has done its work.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and killed his brother because his brother’s goodness exposed his own evil.

Not like Cain. Cain is Scripture’s first example of hatred (Genesis 4:1–16). His was not a crime of sudden passion; it showed what he was, one of the evil one’s family (v. 10). The first child born in the world became the first murderer; the second became the first martyr.

Murdered his brother. Slaughtered (esphaxen), the word used of sacrificial animals, and in Revelation of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). Abel was slaughtered by hatred; the Lamb was slaughtered by hatred, and for haters.

And why did he murder him? Not for Abel’s wrongdoing but for his righteousness. God accepted Abel’s offering, which exposed Cain’s evil heart (Genesis 4:4–7; Hebrews 11:4). Evil hates good because good exposes it (John 3:19–20); righteousness does not have to speak to accuse. This is why the world hates believers (v. 13): those who have chosen darkness feel a righteous life as a rebuke, and their natural response is to put out the light.

God’s warning to Cain. Before the murder, God spoke to Cain gently. Why are you angry? If you do well, will you not be accepted? Sin is crouching at the door; its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it (Genesis 4:6–7). God saw the hatred while it was still a feeling and offered a way out. Cain went to the field instead. Hatred almost always gets a warning, and the warning almost always comes early.

A Brother who never asked it. Cain asked whether he was his brother’s keeper, with his brother’s blood still on the ground (Genesis 4:9). There is a Brother who never asked it. The firstborn Son of God took his brothers’ keeping on himself at the cost of his life; when they turned on him he did not curse them but died for them. In his family hatred is answered with blood that turns enemies into brothers.

In everyday life. Is there someone whose goodness makes you resentful: the colleague who is more conscientious, the sibling who visits your parents more, the Christian whose prayers sound more real? Confess it, and pray for them instead. You are accepted in Christ, the better sacrifice, so another’s goodness takes nothing from you.

Why did God accept Abel’s offering and not Cain’s? Scripture’s own answer is faith: “By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain” (Hebrews 11:4). The difference was first in the heart, not the gift: Abel brought the best of his flock in trust, while Cain’s life showed that his heart was not right with God (Genesis 4:3–5, 7). God looks at the person before the offering. That is why our worship is acceptable only through faith in Christ, the better sacrifice, whose blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers should not be surprised when the world hates them, for it hated Christ first. It is a sign not of failure but of belonging to the right family.

That the world hates you. As Cain hated Abel, the world hates the righteous (compare 1 Peter 4:12). Jesus warned of it: “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you” (John 15:18–20; 17:14).

The first centuries. The early Christians knew this verse in their bodies. They were accused of atheism because they would not worship the emperor, of cannibalism because they spoke of eating Christ’s body, and of hatred of the human race because they kept apart from the temples and the games. Tertullian complained that if the Tiber flooded or the Nile failed to rise, the cry went up at once: “The Christians to the lion!” They were not surprised. They had been told.

How to answer it. Not by hitting back, which is Cain’s way; nor by blending in until there is no difference left; nor by pitying ourselves. If you meet coldness or loss for Christ’s sake, pray for the one who caused it, by name, and look for one way to do him good.

What if the world does not hate me? Does that mean I am compromised? Not necessarily. God often gives his people favour, as Joseph found in Egypt and the early church found with all the people (Acts 2:47), and many unbelievers respect a kind and honest Christian. But ask honestly: do people around me know I follow Christ, and is my life clearly different from theirs at any point? If not, the peace may be the peace of silence. If so, and they still treat you well, thank God for it and use it for the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for our brothers and sisters is how we know we have crossed from death into life; where there is no love, death still reigns.

Passed out of death into life. Crossed over, and remain on the other side: so the verb and its tense mean. It echoes Jesus: whoever hears and believes has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Conversion is a crossing of the frontier (Ephesians 2:1–5).

Because we love the brothers. Love is the evidence, not the cause. A doctor checks for a pulse not to make the patient alive but to find out whether he is.

Abides in death. Without love there is no evidence of new life. Death and life are not only where a person will end up; they are where he lives now.

He crossed first. Christ brought us across the border from the land of death into the country of life by going there himself: the Son of God crossed into death for us and came back out with the keys.

I find some Christians hard to love. Does that mean I have not passed into life? No. The question is not whether loving is easy but whether love is there at all: concern for God’s people, gladness at their good, grief at their harm. Struggling to love a particular brother is part of the Christian life; despising God’s people as such and wanting nothing to do with them would be the alarming sign. That you are troubled by your lack of love itself comes from the new life. Ask God to enlarge it.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settled hatred is murder in the heart, and no one who lives in it has eternal life.

A murderer. Literally a man-killer (anthrōpoktonos). Hatred is the root from which murder grows, as Jesus taught (Matthew 5:21–22): every murder in history was first a hatred somebody did not deal with.

No murderer has eternal life abiding in him. Eternal life and settled hatred cannot live together. This is not a threat against a struggling believer who sometimes feels anger, but a diagnosis of a life marked by settled, unrepented hatred.

The man-killer and the life-giver. John’s word for murderer is the one Jesus used of the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44). Opposite him stands the one who came to give the life that hatred shuts out: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). Eternal life is the life of Christ, for “whoever has the Son has life” (5:12). To nurse hatred is to keep the devil’s likeness while claiming the Son’s life.

What it does not mean. Not that a murderer cannot be saved. Paul was complicit in murder (Acts 8:1; 22:20) and was forgiven. Repentance and faith bring forgiveness for any sin; it is unrepented hatred that shows a person does not have eternal life.

Is anger always hatred? No. “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). There is a righteous anger at injustice and cruelty, which Jesus himself showed (Mark 3:5). Anger becomes hatred when it settles in and turns personal: when you want the other person harmed rather than put right, and you nurse it, rehearse it and refuse to forgive. Ask: do I want this person restored or destroyed? Deal with it before the sun sets, before it hardens.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cross shows us what love is: Christ laid down his life for us, so we owe it to one another to give our lives away.

By this we know love. Love is defined not by a feeling or a theory but by an event. We do not bring our own definition of love to the cross and admire how well it fits; the cross defines love for us. There the Son of God, who owed us nothing, laid down his life for people who owed him everything.

He laid down his life for us. The phrase Jesus used of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11, 15, 17–18): no one took his life from him; he laid it down of his own accord, and took it up again. “For us” means in our place: Christ died the death we deserved.

We ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. “Ought” means we owe it, as debtors. Not that our deaths atone, but that we should be willing to give everything, even life itself, for fellow believers (John 15:12–13). Usually this means daily, practical self-giving (v. 17); sometimes it means literal death, as with the martyrs.

The plague in Alexandria. When an epidemic struck Alexandria in the third century, Bishop Dionysius wrote that while the pagans pushed out the sick and fled from their dearest, the Christians stayed. They nursed the dying, Christian and pagan alike, washed and buried the dead, and many caught the disease and died themselves. He said they took their neighbours’ sickness on themselves, and he counted those who died that way as martyrs. They had learned what love is from the cross.

In everyday life. Laying down your life is usually small: an evening given up, a plan set aside, a cost absorbed quietly. Lay down one such piece of your life on purpose this week, for one particular person.

Does laying down my life mean I must never say no, even to someone who mistreats me? No. Christ laid down his life to save, not to enable evil. Love wills the good of the other, and sometimes that means saying no, setting limits, confronting sin, or getting out of danger. Self-sacrifice for a brother in need is commanded; submitting to abuse is not what this verse means, and abuse must never be tolerated in a home or a church. A wife, a child, or anyone being harmed should seek safety and help, and the church should protect them. Laying down your life is a gift freely given in love, not something taken from you by cruelty.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love that sees a brother in need and shuts its heart against him is not God’s love at all.

The world’s goods. Literally the life of the world: livelihood, possessions. John moves from the dramatic to the everyday. Few will be asked to die for others, but all are asked to share with the brother in front of them now.

Sees his brother in need. Not a passing glance but a clear awareness of the need (so the verb). He knows.

Yet closes his heart against him. Literally he shuts his inward parts against him. The splanchna were the seat of the deepest feelings, and a related word is used of Jesus’ compassion on the crowds. The picture is of a man who feels the stirring of pity and shuts the door on it. Often it is not cruelty but fear: if I give, will I have enough? The gospel answers that fear with a Father who did not spare his own Son, and who will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32).

How does God’s love abide in him? “God’s love” may be love for God, or the love that comes from God. Either way the question answers itself: it does not. Love that refuses to help is not God’s love (James 2:15–16). The love defined by the cross does not stay private; it passes through the hands, the wallet, the time, the presence.

How much should I give, and must I help everyone? Scripture sets no figure but a direction: open-handed, cheerful, in proportion to what you have (2 Corinthians 8:12; 9:7). Your first responsibility is to those nearest: your family (1 Timothy 5:8) and the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). You cannot meet every need in the world. But when God puts a particular brother’s need in front of you and you are able to help, do not close your heart. Help wisely, so that it truly helps, and where you cannot help alone, bring the need to the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real love is shown in what we do, not only in what we say.

Not in word or talk. “Talk” is literally “tongue”: saying “I will pray for you” and then doing nothing. Words alone can deceive the speaker, who confuses saying with doing.

In deed and in truth. Real love acts, and it is genuine, not performed for an audience: it is verified by what the hands do, not by what the mouth says.

A towel, not a speech. On his last night Jesus did not lecture his disciples about humble love. He rose from supper, tied a towel round his waist and washed their feet, Judas’s among them, and then said: “If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). John was at that table. When he writes “in deed and in truth”, he is remembering wet hands on his own feet; and before the next nightfall the same Lord had loved them in the greatest deed of all.

Is it hypocritical to do loving things when I do not feel love? No; it is obedient. Hypocrisy is pretending in order to be admired. A loving act done for someone you do not feel warmly toward, because God commands it, is the opposite: love in deed and truth. Feelings often follow actions; C. S. Lewis advised not to sit waiting for the feeling but to act as if we loved our neighbour, and we would find ourselves coming to love him. The act is itself real love, because love is first a will for another’s good. Do the deed, and ask God for the heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Assurance, Prayer, and the Mutual Indwelling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s children can be at rest before him, even when their own hearts accuse them. After so searching a call to love comes the anxious question: what if my heart condemns me? John answers tenderly that God is greater than our heart and knows everything (vv. 19–20). A heart at rest has confidence before God and freedom in prayer (vv. 21–22). The whole Christian life is then gathered into one commandment, to believe in the name of his Son and love one another (v. 23), and the Spirit he has given assures us that God abides in us (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Greater than Our Heart

On the condemning heart, see vv. 19–20; on the one commandment, see v. 23.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Assurance rested on love in deed and on the Spirit given to them.

Now: A tender conscience can rest in God’s fuller knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real love gives us ground to settle our hearts before God, and when our hearts still condemn us, God, who knows everything, is greater than our hearts. His verdict, not our feelings, has the last word.

By this we shall know that we are of the truth. “By this” most likely looks back to loving in deed and truth (v. 18). Practical love for the brothers is part of the ground on which we settle our hearts.

Reassure our heart before him. Set at rest (so the verb), against a heart that accuses. A life of real love is evidence on the other side, as a lawyer produces the record of a life to answer a charge. John knows there are believers who lie awake rehearsing their failures, who read every warning in Scripture as aimed at them, and who cannot believe that God could be pleased with them.

God is greater than our heart. There are two readings. In the first, God is greater in mercy: he knows everything, including our genuine love and Christ’s atonement, so we can rest even when our hearts accuse us. In the second, God is greater in judgment: if our hearts condemn us, how much more will God. The context (reassurance, v. 19; confidence, v. 21) supports the first. He knows the genuine faith beneath the failures. The tormented conscience finds rest not by arguing itself into peace but by accepting his verdict.

Nothing will surprise him. He knows every sin we have committed and every sin we will commit, and he chose us and sent his Son for us anyway. Nothing will ever come to light about us that surprises him or changes his mind.

Peter on the beach. The best commentary on this verse is a morning by the lake. Peter had denied his Lord three times, with curses. Now the risen Jesus asked him three times, “do you love me?”, and the third time Peter was grieved. He did not point to his record; his record was a disaster. He appealed to the Lord’s knowledge: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). That is exactly the movement of this verse: from a condemning heart to the God who knows everything. And Jesus did not argue. He said, “Feed my sheep.”

What it does not mean. Not that we ignore our conscience when it rightly convicts us of sin; we confess and are forgiven (1:9). But when our hearts go on accusing us after confession, God’s verdict outweighs our feelings.

In everyday life. Write down the accusation, and next to it the verse that answers it (1:9; 2:1–2; Romans 8:1), and read the answer aloud whenever the accusation returns.

My conscience keeps accusing me about sins I have long confessed. What do I do? First, distinguish conviction from accusation. The Spirit’s conviction is specific, leads to confession, and ends in peace. Accusation is vague or endlessly repetitive, leads to despair, and never ends; it is the voice of the accuser, or of an anxious mind. Once you have confessed a sin and, where possible, put it right, God has forgiven it (1:9), and to keep punishing yourself is not humility but a refusal of his verdict. Answer your heart with this verse: God is greater. Some believers suffer from an over-scrupulous conscience as a real affliction; it is wise to talk it through with a pastor and a biblical counsellor, who may also ask you to have a medical check-up. Christ does not want you tormented.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of these verses is compressed. It is uncertain whether “By this” points back to verse 18 or forward; whether the opening of verse 20 should be read “in whatever our heart condemns us” rather than “for whenever”; and why a small linking word is repeated before “God is greater”, perhaps to pick up the thread after a long clause. The ESV gives good sense, and the flow from reassurance (v. 19) to confidence (v. 21) makes the comforting reading the likely one.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
When our hearts are at rest, we may come before God freely, as children come to their father.

If our heart does not condemn us. The other side of verse 20: a conscience at rest through confession and Christ’s blood, not because of sinless perfection but because the life is set toward love and light.

We have confidence before God. Freedom to speak openly: not arrogance, but the freedom of a child approaching a loving father (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19). It is the same word used of confidence at Christ’s coming (2:28) and in prayer (5:14). Think of a child who walks into his father’s study while he is working. A servant would knock and wait; a stranger would not be admitted. The child pushes the door open, climbs on his knee and starts talking. He is not being presumptuous; he is being a son.

The Father who always hears the Son. The Son has always had confidence before his Father. At the tomb of Lazarus he lifted his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:41–42). That freedom is his by nature, and he has shared it with us: by the Spirit he has made his home in us, and we pray in his name, so the Father who always hears the Son hears his brothers and sisters in him. He has never once turned his Son away, and he will not turn away those who come in his name.

Is not confidence before God presumptuous? It would be if it rested on us. But Scripture tells us to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), because our great high priest has opened the way with his own blood (Hebrews 10:19–22). Holding back in fear is not humility; it treats his blood as insufficient. True humility says, I have nothing to bring, so I come with Christ. That is the boldest and the humblest thing a sinner can do at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s obedient children receive what they ask, because they ask as children who want what pleases their Father.

Whatever we ask we receive from him. Keep receiving, as the tense shows. A sweeping promise (John 14:13–14; 15:7; 16:23–24), qualified by 5:14: if we ask according to his will.

Because we keep his commandments. Not that obedience earns answered prayer, but that obedient children ask according to their Father’s will (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; James 5:16). Not a bargain, but being in tune: the person who does what pleases God comes to ask for what pleases God, and God is pleased to give it.

The Son who always pleased him. “Do what pleases him” echoes Jesus’ words about himself: “he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). The Father always hears this perfectly obedient Son, and Christians pray in his name. Our prayers are not heard because of our obedience, which is never perfect, but in the name of the Son whose obedience is counted as ours. Yet the more our lives are shaped like his, the more our asking is shaped like his, until we find ourselves praying what he prays.

Why are some of my prayers not answered, even when I am trying to obey? They are answered, but not always with yes. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and the answer was, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus, perfectly obedient, prayed in Gethsemane that the cup might pass, and the answer was the cross, which saved the world. He may say no because he has something better, wait because the time is not yet, or yes in a form we do not recognise. Keep asking, keep obeying, and trust that your Father hears.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s whole commandment is one: believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another.

This is his commandment. Singular: the commandments of verse 22 are summed up in one with two parts, one response to God, because genuine faith in Christ always produces love for the brothers, and genuine love for the brothers is always grounded in faith in Christ.

Believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ. Faith is the first commandment (John 6:29). The name means his person, all he is, and “his Son Jesus Christ” is the full confession the false teachers denied (2:22–23). This is the first mention of believing in 1 John, and everything John has said, about light, obedience, love and the new birth, rests on it.

And love one another. The two great tests of the letter are inseparable. Faith looks up and receives; love looks out and gives.

What it does not mean. Not that faith and love are equal grounds of salvation. Faith receives salvation; love flows from it (Galatians 5:6).

How can faith be commanded? Is it not a gift? It is both. God commands everyone to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30), and unbelief is sin, not misfortune (John 3:18; 16:9). Yet no one can believe unless God draws him (John 6:44), and faith is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). The command and the gift meet in the gospel: as Christ is offered and the command is heard, the Spirit gives the faith he commands. Lazarus could not obey the command to come out of the tomb by his own power, but the voice that commanded gave the life to obey. So hear the command, ask for the gift, and believe.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who keep God’s commandments live in him and he in them, and the Spirit he has given is how they know it.

Abides in God, and God in him. Each lives in the other (John 15:4–5): God is not merely alongside us or approving from a distance, but in us, and obedience is the sign of it.

By the Spirit whom he has given us. The first mention of the Holy Spirit by name in 1 John. He is the guarantee of God’s presence in us (2 Corinthians 1:22), known by his work: enabling us to confess Christ (4:2), to love (4:13) and to obey. He bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16), and his fruit gives outward evidence.

In the flow. The verse gathers up the chapter: obedience, love, a heart at rest and faith all belong to this life of God in us, which the Spirit makes known. And because the false teachers claimed the Spirit too, John must at once warn that not every spirit is from God (4:1–6).

He has moved in. Jesus promised it at the Last Supper: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23). He has not merely forgiven us at a distance or promised to receive us one day; the Lord of glory has moved in, and he will never move out.

In everyday life. Look for the Spirit’s fingerprints this week: a moment of trusting Christ, a love that was not natural to you, a temptation refused, a verse that suddenly lit up. Thank God for each; they are signs that he lives in you.

Can the Spirit leave me? No. Jesus promised the Helper “to be with you forever” (John 14:16). The Spirit is God’s seal on his people for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and a seal is not broken. You can grieve him by sin, and you may lose for a time the joy and sense of his nearness, as David feared when he prayed “take not your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11). But under the new covenant the Spirit is given to remain: if you have him, you will not lose him. Confess what grieves him, and ask him to restore the joy.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. In 3:1–3 John speaks of being born of God and called his children, one of the high points of the New Testament’s teaching on adoption. It is a real change of standing: we share as children in the inheritance of the Son. And it is both present (v. 1) and still to be completed (v. 2). What we will be is not yet seen, but that does not weaken what we already are (on the hope that purifies, see v. 3).

Love Defined by the Cross. In verse 16 John does not say that love is whatever feels loving. He defines it by one act: the Son laying down his life (see the note on v. 16). A view of love that leaves out the cross will shrink into mere tolerance.
3.examples:
Then: John’s readers had been through the pain of seeing people they loved leave. The temptation in such a time is to turn inward, guard the heart, and love in word only. John points them to the cross as the pattern of what love is, and calls them to love with an openness that made them vulnerable.

Now: Our culture often defines love as acceptance and affirmation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not first whether I feel warmly toward my brother but whether I am laying anything down for him.

keyVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter grows from this verse. Everything John asks of God’s children, purity, righteousness and love in deed, rests on what the Father has already given: not a courtesy title but a new birth, “and so we are”. Holiness and assurance alike begin with a long look at the Father’s love.

3.reflection:
John tells us to “see” the Father’s love: we are his children now, though what we will be has not yet appeared (vv. 1–2). What difference does it make on an ordinary day to know that you are God’s child? When do you most need to remember it?

Verses 4–10 say that no one born of God keeps on sinning, yet 1:8 says that we all sin. How would you explain the difference to a believer who has fought the same sin for years, and to someone who sins and does not mind?

John defines love by the cross (v. 16) and then brings it down to a brother in need (v. 17). What makes us close our hearts, and whose need could you or your group meet in deed and in truth this month?

“God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (v. 20). How does this comfort a troubled conscience, and how can we help one another tell the Spirit’s conviction from the voice of the accuser?

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.<sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,<sup>3</sup>and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.<sup>4</sup>Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.<sup>5</sup>They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.<sup>6</sup>We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.<sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.<sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.<sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.<sup>12</sup>No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.<sup>13</sup>By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.<sup>14</sup>And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.<sup>15</sup>Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.<sup>16</sup>So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.<sup>17</sup>By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.<sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.<sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.<sup>20</sup>If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.<sup>21</sup>And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 opens the letter’s third movement (see the introduction). John returns to two tests he has already sounded, the truth about Christ (2:18–27) and love for the brothers (3:11–18), and takes both deeper.

The message. God has shown what he is, once for all, in the Son he sent: a real man, come in the flesh to be the propitiation for our sins. So listen to no spirit that denies him, and love one another, because the love that saved you is God’s own nature and flows on wherever it is received. And do not dread the day of judgment, for the Judge is the one who bore your punishment.

Why it was said. The teachers who had left were still on the roads, claiming the Spirit, denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh, and winning the world’s ear (vv. 1, 5; see the introduction). The believers left behind felt small and outnumbered, unsure whether they or the confident newcomers had God.

How the chapter makes its case. First the test of truth (vv. 1–6): the spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God, and the believers have already overcome the false prophets, whom the world applauds. Then the source of love (vv. 7–12): God is love, and he defined it by sending his Son as the propitiation for our sins; so we ought to love one another, and when we do, the invisible God is seen. Last, assurance and its evidence (vv. 13–21): the Spirit given, the Son confessed and God’s love believed bring confidence for the day of judgment and drive out fear; and love for the unseen God must show in love for the brother we can see.

Where it leads. Twice the chapter says “God is love” (vv. 8, 16), and each time it ties the sentence to Jesus: the Son come in real flesh (v. 2), God’s only Son (v. 9), bearing the wrath our sins deserved (v. 10), the Saviour of the world (v. 14). Love is what we find at Bethlehem and at Calvary. And because the one who will sit on the throne is the one who died for us, the believer can face even the day of judgment without terror.

For us. Two dangers still meet us: a spirituality that floats free of the real Jesus, and an orthodoxy that has stopped loving. John cures both by sending us back to the cross. Test what you hear by what it says about Jesus. And when love runs dry, do not first try harder: go back to the love that came first (v. 19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Testing the Spirits: Discernment in the Last Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not every voice that claims God’s Spirit speaks for him, so believers must test what they hear, and the test is Jesus. The spirit from God confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh; the spirit of antichrist will not (vv. 1–3). Yet the warning ends in comfort: the believers have already overcome the false prophets, because he who is in them is greater than he who is in the world (v. 4). The world’s applause marks the false prophets as its own (v. 5), and the apostles’ word is the standard by which every spirit is known (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing the Spirits

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: False prophets had gone out into the world.

Now: Ask of any teaching whether it confesses the whole Christ: truly God, truly man, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not believe every voice that claims to speak from God; keep testing, because many false prophets are abroad. John meets the confident teachers who had unsettled his readers not with panic or blanket suspicion but with a habit of discernment.

Do not believe every spirit. The spirit behind a prophet or teacher is either the Holy Spirit or a spirit of error (v. 6). John neither doubts everything nor believes whatever he is told. He believes in spirits, which is exactly why he will not believe all of them.

Test the spirits. Keep testing (the tense is present), as metal was tested to see whether the silver was real: the verb (dokimazete) was used of that testing. Every teaching, however spiritual it seems, must be tested (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21), and the command is plural: discernment is not reserved for leaders but given to every believer.

Many false prophets. The false teachers who had left the church (2:19), claiming to speak for God. Jesus warned of them: beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15; 24:11, 24). As John writes they are travelling the roads between the house churches, and the right response is not panic but testing.

The true Prophet behind the test. A counterfeit exists only because there is a genuine coin. Moses promised a prophet like him, to whom the people must listen (Deuteronomy 18:15), and Peter announced that Jesus is that Prophet (Acts 3:22–23). In these last days God has spoken by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and every other voice is weighed against his. That is why John’s test, in the very next verse, is a question about Jesus. In all the noise of the world, the church is listening for one voice.

The Bereans. When Paul preached in Berea, the Jews there received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so (Acts 17:11). They tested an apostle, not rudely or suspiciously but eagerly, and Luke calls them more noble for it. A good teacher is never threatened by a congregation with open Bibles.

How does an ordinary Christian actually test a teacher? You do not need a theology degree. Start with John’s two tests: what does he say about Jesus (vv. 2–3), and does he submit to the apostles’ word in Scripture (v. 6)? Then ask: does he handle the Bible honestly, in context? Does his life match his teaching (Matthew 7:16)? Does he make much of Christ and his cross, or of himself, money or experience? Does his message lead to holiness and love? Keep your Bible open beside him, and ask your pastor or a mature believer when you are unsure. Testing is not a single event but a habit.

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of God is known by what is confessed about Jesus: that he is the Christ, truly come in the flesh. Any spirit that will not confess him is not from God.

By this you know the Spirit of God. Not by power, feelings, miracles or success. John gives one question: who is Jesus?

Has come in the flesh. To confess is to declare publicly, and the tense means that he came in the flesh and remains in it. The eternal Son became a real man, with a real body, not a temporary appearance. The false teachers said the divine Christ only seemed human, or came on the man Jesus for a time (2:22). The Holy Spirit always glorifies Christ and testifies to who he is (John 15:26; 16:14; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

Does not confess Jesus. Does not acknowledge him as he truly is, the Christ come in the flesh. Mark the name: Jesus, the man from Nazareth. The spirit of antichrist need not deny that there is a Christ; it refuses to confess that the Christ is Jesus. And it is at work already (2:18, 22), in John’s time and in ours.

Still a man. The Son who sits on the throne of the universe is still a man, with a man’s face and a man’s scarred hands. He took our nature into the life of God and will never lay it down.

In everyday life. Your body matters to God; his Son took one. Thank him today for the flesh he wore: the hands that touched lepers, the feet that walked to Calvary, the side that was pierced. And treat your own body, and others’, as something the Son of God was not ashamed to share.

What it does not mean. Not that anyone who mechanically says the words is from God. The confession must be genuine, with the full meaning of who Jesus is: God the Son, truly incarnate, the Christ who died and rose. Even demons acknowledged who Jesus was (Mark 1:24).

Why does it matter so much that Jesus came in the flesh? Because everything he did for us depended on it. Only a real man could stand in the place of men, obey the law we broke, and die the death we deserved (Hebrews 2:14–17). Only a real body could rise from a real grave and guarantee ours. Only one who shares our nature can be a high priest who sympathises with our weakness. And only the eternal Son could make that obedience and death of infinite worth. A Christ who only seemed human could only seem to save: deny this truth, and the gospel dissolves.

Textual note. A few ancient witnesses, chiefly Latin translations and some church fathers, read instead every spirit that annuls Jesus (lyei, dissolves or separates), that is, separates the human Jesus from the divine Christ. The better-supported reading is “does not confess”.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have already overcome the false teachers, not by their own strength but because God, who lives in them, is greater than the devil at work in the world. John does not leave the church on anxious alert; he turns at once to comfort.

You are from God, and have overcome them. “You” is emphatic, in contrast with the false prophets: you belong to God, born of him. As in 2:13–14, they have conquered and remain victorious: they had resisted the false prophets’ teaching and stayed faithful.

Greater than he who is in the world. “He who is in you” is God, by his Spirit (3:24); “he who is in the world” is the devil, the ruler of this world (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11), working through the false prophets. The victory rests not on their strength or cleverness but on the one who is in them, and every believer, however ordinary or doubting, carries him. The devil still rages, but on a chain, and the chain is held by the one who lives in us.

Elisha’s servant. When the Syrian army surrounded Dothan, Elisha’s servant saw horses and chariots everywhere and panicked. Elisha said, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Then he prayed, and the LORD opened the young man’s eyes, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). This verse is that prayer answered for every believer: the enemy is real and visible; what is with you is greater, and invisible.

The stronger man has already entered the house. The victory was won before John’s readers ever met a false prophet. No one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (Mark 3:27), and that is what Jesus came to do: the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil (3:8). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). So John’s “you have overcome” echoes his Master in the upper room: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

In everyday life. Write this verse on a card and put it where you will see it at the moment you usually feel weakest.

If he who is in me is greater, can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No, not in the sense of being owned or controlled by one. A Christian is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and has been transferred out of the domain of darkness into the kingdom of God’s Son (Colossians 1:13). The devil can tempt, accuse, deceive and attack believers, and they must resist him (Ephesians 6:11–13; 1 Peter 5:8–9), but he cannot take possession of one who belongs to Christ. If you are troubled by dark thoughts or fears, do not conclude that you are possessed; bring them to Christ, to Scripture, to prayer and to your pastor, and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up.

verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophets belong to the world, so they speak its language and the world gladly listens; their popularity proves nothing.

They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world. Their source, values and loyalty belong to human society organised against God, so their teaching is shaped by what the world finds respectable, satisfying and acceptable: in John’s day, a spiritual Christ without the embarrassment of a body or a cross.

The world listens to them. Like recognises like (John 15:19). Popularity with the world is no proof of truth; often it is a warning sign.

He who comes from above. John had recorded the same contrast about Jesus: he who is of the earth speaks in an earthly way, but he who comes from heaven is above all (John 3:31). Christ came from above, so he never sounded like the world, and that is why the world that applauds its own prophets hated him: it hates me, he said, because I testify about it that its works are evil (John 7:7). The crowd that would have nodded at a bodiless Christ shouted for Barabbas.

Itching ears. Paul described the same market: people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Timothy 4:3). Health and wealth without repentance, a Jesus who affirms everything and asks nothing, a spirituality without sin or judgment, will always find a crowd. The crowd is not the test.

Should churches then avoid being attractive or relevant? Churches should be welcoming, clear and kind, speaking in language people understand, as Paul became all things to all people, that by all means he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22); being needlessly off-putting is not faithfulness. The danger is changing the message to fit the market: softening sin, removing the cross, promising what Christ never promised. Adapt the packaging freely; never touch the contents. If people are offended by the gospel, that is the gospel’s doing. If they are offended by us, that is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles speak from God, so how a person responds to their word shows whether he knows God; that is how the Spirit of truth is told from the spirit of error.

We are from God. “We” means John and the apostles, the eyewitnesses (1:1–3) whom God made his spokesmen.

Whoever knows God listens to us. Those who know God recognise the apostolic teaching (John 8:47; 18:37), as the sheep know the Shepherd’s voice and will not follow a stranger (John 10:4–5, 27); whoever refuses it shows that he is not from God.

The Spirit of truth and the spirit of error. The Holy Spirit (John 14:17; 15:26), and Satan with his demonic influences, the spirit of deception. This is the second test: does a teacher accept the apostolic witness? Today that word is preserved in the New Testament, and any teaching that contradicts it comes from the spirit of error.

The one who hears you hears me. Why should listening to a handful of apostles reveal whether a person knows God? Because Christ put his own voice in their mouths. The one who hears you hears me, he told them (Luke 10:16), and he promised that the Spirit would bring to their remembrance all that he had said and guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The apostolic word is not one religious opinion among many but the risen Christ speaking through the men he chose. To receive it is to hear the Shepherd himself.

In everyday life. Read one New Testament letter straight through at a sitting this week, as its first hearers did, and note one place where it corrects you.

Is it presumptuous for John to say whoever knows God listens to us? Any group could say it, and many have. The difference is who is speaking: an eyewitness apostle, commissioned by Christ, writing what became Scripture. No church, pastor or movement today can claim that; we can only point to what the apostles wrote. So the verse makes no modern group the judge of truth, but the apostolic word the judge of every group, including ours. The humble church keeps sitting under the New Testament and lets it correct its traditions.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — God Is Love: The Source, the Measure, and the Goal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love comes from God, because God is love, and he has shown what love is by sending his Son. John does not mean a warm feeling or a tolerant mood: love is the life the Father, Son and Spirit have shared from eternity (vv. 7–8). It was made visible when God sent his only Son that we might live through him (v. 9), and defined when he sent him to be the propitiation for our sins (v. 10). Since God so loved us, we ought to love one another (v. 11), and when we do, the God no one has seen is seen in his people (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Love

On the love God showed in sending his Son, see vv. 9–10; on why we ought to love one another, see v. 11.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The departing teachers’ knowledge produced schism, not love.

Now: No one has ever seen God; when we love one another, his love is made complete in us (see v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers should love one another, because love comes from God, and whoever truly loves shows that he has been born of God and knows him. John moves straight from testing teaching to love, for sound teaching and love are two sides of one life.

Let us love one another. Beloved means loved ones: those who are loved should love. The church that tests the spirits must also be the church that loves, not two kinds of Christian but one life.

Love is from God. All genuine love flows from him, not from our natural warmth. A river does not make its own water. Every mother’s tenderness, every friend’s loyalty, every act of self-giving is a stream that rose in God.

Born of God and knows God. “Whoever loves” means whoever goes on loving, with self-giving love. Love is the fingerprint of the new birth and the evidence of knowing God: not knowledge about him but a real meeting with him.

The word the church filled. The Greeks had erōs for desire and philia for friendship; the noun agapē was rare, simply meant love, and could be used of loving the wrong things (2:15). The Christians used it for what they had seen at the cross, so that in their writings it points again and again to the love that gives itself for the undeserving. The meaning came from the cross, not from the word.

The commandment from the upper room. John is repeating what he heard on the night Jesus washed his disciples’ feet: a new commandment, that they love one another just as he had loved them (John 13:34). The command came with a measure, and the measure was Christ. The love that is from God did not arrive as an idea; it arrived kneeling with a towel, and by the next afternoon it hung on a cross.

My unbelieving neighbour is kinder than some Christians I know. How can that be? It can be, and it is humbling. God gives common grace to all: natural affection, a kind temperament, a good upbringing (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). Some unbelievers are naturally gentle, and some Christians were converted from very hard natures and still have far to go; compare each with where he started, not with each other. And John is describing not niceness but love that flows from knowing God through Christ, a love that includes loving God himself. Still, your neighbour’s kindness should shame the church into greater love, and your brother’s unkindness should be gently confronted.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Someone in whom love has left no mark has never known God, because love is not merely something God does; it is what he is.

Does not know God. Has never come to know him, as the tense shows. John is not measuring how warm you feel or how often you fail at love; he describes someone in whom God’s love has left no mark at all. To know the one who is love is to be changed by him, and a believer who grieves over his coldness is already showing the change.

Because God is love. No sentence in the letter says more in fewer words: love is not one of God’s qualities among others but his very nature. Within the Trinity, the Father, Son and Spirit have eternally loved one another (John 17:24). And as God is light (1:5), so God is love: his love is holy, and his holiness is loving.

Why only the Trinity can say this. A god who was a single, solitary person could not be love in himself before creation; there would have been no one to love, and he would need us. The God of the Bible needs nothing. Before the mountains were brought forth, the Father loved the Son and the Son loved the Father in the bond of the Spirit. We were not made because God was lonely, but because his love was so rich he chose to share it. It is that love which made us, came after us when we ran, hung on the cross, and will hold us for ever.

When love becomes god. Our culture has quietly turned the sentence round: “God is love” has become “love is God”, so that whatever is done in love’s name needs no further defence. Watch what it does. The husband who walks out on his family says he had to follow love; the parent who cannot let a grown child go calls the smothering love; the nation that marches to war speaks of love of country. C. S. Lewis, in The Four Loves, took up a line from Denis de Rougemont: love “ceases to be a demon only when he ceases to be a god.” Any human love, made absolute, demands sacrifices it has no right to ask. John lets God define love, and shows us where to look: “not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (v. 10). That love is holy, tells the truth, and pays for what it forgives. Under it our loves can be loved without being worshipped, and so at last become safe to give.

Does God love everyone? Yes, in different ways. He loves all people as his creatures, giving sun and rain to the just and the unjust, kind to the ungrateful and the evil, sincerely calling everyone to repent and believe (Matthew 5:44–45; Luke 6:35; Ezekiel 33:11); every unbeliever has received that love every day of his life. But Scripture also speaks of a special, saving love for his people, chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4–5; 5:25). You need not solve the mystery to enjoy the love: anyone who comes to Christ finds that this saving love was set on him from eternity.

Where Christians differ: if God is love, can he send anyone to hell? Some argue that a God of love could never punish anyone eternally, so that all will be saved, or the wicked annihilated. Those who hold these views often do so out of real concern for God’s goodness, and the question should be faced with tears, not triumph. This commentary’s view: “God is love” does not mean love is God, or that his love overrides his holiness and justice. The same John wrote that the wrath of God remains on those who reject the Son (John 3:36) and described the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10–15). He has already said that God is light (1:5), and he defines love by the cross: God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (v. 10). Propitiation means the turning away of wrath, so God’s love does not cancel his justice; it satisfies it at infinite cost, by bearing his own wrath in his Son. Love that ignored evil would not be true love. Those who refuse this holy love remain under the judgment it was given to remove, and face his just and eternal judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God showed his love in history by sending his one and only Son into the world, so that we, who were dead, might live through him.

Made manifest among us. Verse 8 rests on a deed done at a known time and place: in the reign of Augustus, in the town of Bethlehem.

His only Son. Monogenē means unique, one of a kind, as in John 1:14, 18; 3:16, and it shows what the giving cost. The Father did not send an angel, a prophet or a message; he sent the Son who cannot be replaced, the one he had loved from eternity, into a world that would reject him, to die.

That we might live through him. Eternal life, now and for ever (John 3:16; 10:10), with Christ as its means and source. We were spiritually dead (3:14; Ephesians 2:1); through him we live. Love comes down into the world of the dying and brings life from the only source that has it.

Abraham on the mountain. The phrase reaches back to Moriah. God said to Abraham, take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love (Genesis 22:2). At the last moment God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided a ram. Some two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, God did what he had not allowed Abraham to do. He took his Son, his only Son, whom he loved, and did not hold back his hand. There was no ram for him. He was the Lamb.

What it does not mean. Not that the Son was created or had a beginning. The older translation “only begotten” expresses his unique, eternal relationship with the Father, not a beginning in time.

If believers are also sons of God, why is Jesus called the only Son? Because he is the eternal Son by nature, sharing the Father’s being from all eternity, God from God. We become children of God by grace, by new birth and adoption, through faith in him (John 1:12–13; Galatians 4:4–7). He is the Son; we are sons in the Son. Jesus kept the difference even after the resurrection: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17). Ours is a real sonship, entirely borrowed from his.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is defined not by our love for God but by his love for us, shown when he sent his Son to bear the wrath our sins deserved.

In this is love. Its direction runs from God to us. The sinner is not at the centre straining upward; God is at the centre, moving downward.

Not that we have loved God, but that he loved us. We did not seek God; we were his enemies (Romans 3:11; 5:10). He took the initiative while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8; Ephesians 2:4–5). He did not love us because we were lovely; we become lovely because he loved us.

To be the propitiation. Propitiation, as in 2:2, is the offering that bears God’s wrath in our place and so removes it. The supreme expression of God’s love is that he himself provided the sacrifice to satisfy his own justice (Romans 3:25–26). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son; it is the loving Father sending his Son. When we were enemies, he loved us; when we had nothing to give, he gave his Son; when wrath was due, he bore it himself.

If the Father loved us already, why did he need a propitiation? Because his love is holy. A judge who loved a guilty man and simply let him go would be corrupt, and the victims of the crime would be betrayed. God’s love does not ignore justice; it pays it. The propitiation is not what made God love us but what his love did, at his own cost, so that he could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since God loved us at such cost, we owe it to one another to love in the same way.

If God so loved us. “If” means since: John draws a conclusion, echoing John 3:16. “So” means in this way and to this extent, by sending his Son to be the propitiation (v. 10).

We also ought. We owe it, as in 3:16: not to repay God, which we never could, but to pass his love on. That love gives the power as well as the duty: poured into our hearts through the Spirit (Romans 5:5), it is not only an example to copy but a supply to draw on.

The servant who would not forgive. Jesus told of a servant forgiven ten thousand talents, more than a labourer could earn in many lifetimes, who went straight out, seized a fellow servant who owed him a hundred days’ wages, and threw him in prison (Matthew 18:23–35). The story is absurd, and that is the point. Once you know what you have been forgiven, every debt owed to you shrinks to its real size.

What the pardon cost. The parable does not say what it cost the king to cancel the debt. John does: it cost the Father his Son (v. 10). That is the force of the little word “so”. The love we owe one another is measured not by the size of our brother’s offence but by the price of our own pardon, paid in the blood of Christ. Only those who have stood at the foot of the cross have the heart to forgive like this.

In everyday life. Who is the hardest person in your church to love? God loved you when you were hard to love. Love them this week in one specific way: a greeting, a prayer, an invitation, a kindness they cannot repay.

What if someone has hurt me deeply? Must I love him, and must I trust him again? You must love him: forgive him from the heart, refuse revenge, and wish and pray for his good (Romans 12:17–21). But forgiveness is not trust, and love is not pretending. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by repentance shown over time, and reconciliation needs both sides. Where someone has been abusive, love does not require you to return to danger; abuse must never be tolerated, and the church should protect the vulnerable. You can forgive a person and still keep a safe distance, report a crime, and let the authorities do their work.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God no one has seen becomes visible in a church whose members love one another, for there his love reaches its goal.

No one has ever seen God. Seen means beheld, gazed upon; John 1:18 says the same. God in his essence is invisible (1 Timothy 6:16). John does not boast of visions; he points to a church.

If we love one another, God abides in us. God showed his love once by sending his Son (vv. 9–10); where can it be seen now that the Son has returned to the Father? In a church that loves, and by the Spirit he has given (v. 13). In the Gospel the same sentence led to the Son who made the Father known (John 1:18); here it leads to his people. When believers love one another across differences of taste and background, God is seen more plainly than any private vision could show him.

His love is perfected in us. Brought to its goal, as in 2:5: God’s love for us reaches its goal when it produces love in us for others.

So that the world may believe. All people would know his disciples by their love for one another, Jesus said (John 13:35), and he prayed that they would be one, so that the world may believe that the Father had sent him (John 17:21). In a church that loves, the world sees not God’s essence but the shape of the cross: proud people serving, enemies reconciled, the strong carrying the weak.

What the pagans saw. In the second century the satirist Lucian mocked the Christians as gullible, but noticed how they rushed to care for any brother in prison with food, money and visitors. Tertullian reported the pagans saying of them, see how they love one another. The world could not see God. It could see that.

The invisible God has chosen to be seen. He showed his glory once in his Son, full of grace and truth, and he is painting that likeness now in forgiven sinners who love one another. The portrait is unfinished and the brush strokes are clumsy, but the face is unmistakably his. And the portrait is not the end: his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4), and the God no one has ever seen will be the light of every eye.

What it does not mean. Not that God abides in us only because we love. He abides in us by his Spirit, given at new birth (v. 13); our love is the evidence of his presence.

If no one has seen God, what about Moses, Isaiah and others who saw him? They saw his glory in a form they could bear: the burning bush, the cloud, the throne high and lifted up. Moses was told, you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Exodus 33:20), and saw only the back of his glory. Many think the appearances of the LORD in the Old Testament were the Son before his incarnation. No one has seen God in his essence; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18), and to see Jesus is to see the Father (John 14:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Abiding in Love: Confidence, Fear Cast Out, and the Visible Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who live in God’s love can be sure of him, unafraid of the judgment, and loving towards their brothers. Assurance rests on the Spirit God has given (v. 13), the apostles’ witness to the Son (v. 14), the confession of him (v. 15) and trust in God’s love (v. 16). From that union comes confidence even for the day of judgment, because believers share Christ’s standing, and perfect love casts out the fear of punishment (vv. 17–18). We love only because he first loved us (v. 19), so love for the invisible God is tested by love for the brother we can see (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear Cast Out

On confidence for the day of judgment, see v. 17; on fear cast out, v. 18; on the love that came first, v. 19.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Confidence rested on union with the Son, not on claimed knowledge.

Now: The brother we can see tests our love for the God we cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers can know that they live in God and he in them, because he has given them his Spirit.

We abide in him and he in us. Mutual indwelling, as in 3:24. We do not deduce it from moral achievement or sustained feeling. We know it.

He has given us of his Spirit. Every believer has received the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9), God’s pledge that we belong to him (2 Corinthians 1:22), known by his work: enabling us to confess Christ (v. 2), to love (vv. 7, 12), and to cry “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15–16). So we can say we know, not merely we hope.

The deposit. Paul calls the Spirit the guarantee of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14), the word for a deposit paid on a purchase (in modern Greek it means an engagement ring). The Spirit in us now is the first instalment of heaven: not a sample that might be withdrawn but a down payment that commits the buyer.

Poured out by the exalted Son. The Spirit had not yet been given, John had recorded, because Jesus was not yet glorified (John 7:39); the gift waited for the cross, the resurrection and the ascension. At Pentecost Peter explained the sound and the fire: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33). Every believer who knows that he abides in God knows it by a gift bought at Calvary and given from the throne.

How can I tell the Spirit’s witness from my own wishful thinking? Look at what he produces. His witness never says you are saved while leaving your life unchanged; it comes with his fruit: a heart that confesses Jesus as the Son of God (v. 15), a love for his people (v. 12), a hatred of sin, a desire to obey, a turning to God as Father (Romans 8:15). Wishful thinking can produce a feeling; it cannot produce a new love for holiness and for Christ. If you see these, however weak, the Spirit is at work, and you may trust his witness.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles saw with their own eyes, and bear witness, that the Father sent his Son to save the world.

We have seen and testify. “We” means the apostles, eyewitnesses (1:1–3), and “seen” is the verb of verse 12: no one has ever seen God, but we have seen the Son he sent. That is the gospel in brief.

The Saviour of the world. A rare title in the New Testament. “The world” here means people of every nation who come to him in faith. Emperors were hailed as saviour and benefactor on coins and inscriptions; John gives the title to its true owner.

The Samaritan village. The first to say it were Samaritans, despised by the Jews as half-pagan outsiders, brought to Jesus by a woman with five husbands behind her.
