After two days with him they told her they no longer believed because of what she had said: they had heard for themselves, and knew that this was indeed the Saviour of the world (John 4:42). The title was first spoken by people everyone thought were outside his salvation.

What it does not mean. Not that every person will be saved. Jesus is the Saviour of the world as the only Saviour for all peoples, who saves people from every nation (Revelation 5:9). Those who reject him are not saved (John 3:18, 36).

What does he actually save me from? From sin in every dimension. From its guilt: he bore the penalty, so there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). From God’s wrath (1 Thessalonians 1:10). From sin’s power: he breaks its rule and gives us the Spirit to fight it (Romans 6:14). From the devil, who held us captive (Hebrews 2:14–15). From death, which he defeated by rising (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). And one day from sin’s very presence, when we see him and are made like him (3:2). And he saves us not only from all that but for himself, for fellowship with God, which is eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever truly confesses that Jesus is the Son of God lives in God, and God in him. This is the outward sign of union with God, matching the Spirit’s inward witness in verse 13.

Whoever confesses. The confession the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3): to entrust oneself to him and say, with full personal weight, this Jesus is the Son of God. The baby in the manger, the man on the cross, the body in the tomb, the Lord on the throne: one person, the eternal Son.

God abides in him, and he in God. Confessing Christ does not earn this union, as a work would; it is the open hand of faith receiving a gift.

Peter at Caesarea Philippi. When Peter said, you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus told him that flesh and blood had not revealed it to him, but his Father in heaven (Matthew 16:16–17). No one makes this confession truly by his own insight. Every time a person confesses Jesus as the Son of God from the heart, heaven has been at work.

In everyday life. Look for one opportunity this week to say to someone, simply and without embarrassment, that Jesus is the Son of God. And if you believe but have never been baptised, or are unsure what your baptism meant, speak to your pastor.

Is confession a one-time act, and must it be public? It begins at a point and continues for life. The New Testament expects the first confession to be made openly, and baptism is the appointed way: a believer is baptised on his profession of faith, publicly declaring that he belongs to Christ (Acts 2:41; 8:36–38; Romans 10:9–10). Then it continues in worship, in witness, and in standing for him when it costs; whoever acknowledges him before men, he will acknowledge before his Father (Matthew 10:32). A secret faith that never confesses is in danger. This commentary holds believer’s baptism because in the New Testament baptism follows a person’s own confession of faith; many faithful Christians baptise the children of believers as a sign of God’s covenant promise, and we honour them as brothers and sisters in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have come to know God’s love and to rely on it, and because God is love, whoever lives in that love lives in God.

Come to know and to believe. We have known and believed, and continue to: we know his love because he has shown it (vv. 9–10), and we rely on it by faith.

God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God. Repeated from verse 8, the sentence now explains how God and the believer live in one another: God and love cannot be separated. To abide in love is to live in God’s love, receiving it and showing it. Love is not a virtue we add to our relationship with God; it is the atmosphere in which he dwells, and where his love is received and passed on, there God is.

The same two verbs. John had heard them together before. When many disciples walked away, Peter answered for the Twelve: we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God (John 6:69). Now, at the end of a long life, John uses the same pair in reverse order, and the object has become the love God has for us. That love is known only in the Son. To believe it is to put your weight on Christ; to know it is to have spent a lifetime in his company and found him true.

How do I come to know and believe God’s love when I do not feel loved? By looking where John looks: not inward first, but at the cross. Feelings of being loved are shaped by temperament, illness, upbringing and circumstances, and can lie; the fact of God’s love was settled in history, when he sent his Son (v. 10). Read the accounts of the crucifixion slowly and say: this was for me. Rely on it as you rely on a bridge, by putting your weight on it, not by first feeling confident. Speak it back to God in prayer. And let other believers love you; God often makes his love felt through his people.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Living in God’s love brings that love to its goal: confidence before the Judge on the last day, because believers stand where Christ stands.

Love perfected with us. “Perfected” again means brought to its goal (v. 12); here the goal is confidence on the last day.

Confidence for the day of judgment. Boldness, as in 2:28 and 3:21, at the final judgment when Christ returns.

As he is so also are we. Not as he was, but as he is: the exalted Son, loved by the Father, in whom the believer is hidden (Colossians 3:3). We share his standing, loved as he is loved (John 17:23), and his verdict belongs to those united to him by faith (Romans 8:1). So confidence on the last day is not a reward for the holiest believers but the portion of all who are in Christ.

The judgment already passed. For the believer the verdict of that day was given publicly when God raised Jesus from the dead, declaring the one who stood in our place righteous and his sacrifice accepted. The one who will sit on the throne on that day is the one who died for us. We will be judged by our Saviour.

What it does not mean. Not that believers are now as perfect as Christ in character. They share his acceptance with the Father, and are growing in his likeness.

Will believers be judged at all? Yes, but not to decide whether they are saved. All will stand before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10): what was done for him will be acknowledged and rewarded, and worthless work will be burned up, though the believer himself is saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), and our works will be shown as the evidence of our faith (Matthew 25:31–40). But the question of condemnation is closed (Romans 8:1). It will be a Father’s welcome, not a court deciding our fate.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are compressed. “By this” may point back to abiding in love (v. 16) or forward to the confidence the verse names; either way the two belong together. And “as he is so also are we in this world” does not say how we are like him: in character (we already love as he loves) or in standing (we share the risen Son’s acceptance). Standing fits the day of judgment and verse 18 best, and this commentary takes it so; but the two are not rivals, for the likeness grows from the standing.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where God’s love is truly known, the dread of punishment is driven out, because Christ has already borne the punishment.

There is no fear in love. Fear here is the dread of a criminal before a judge, not the reverent fear of God that Scripture commends (Proverbs 1:7; 1 Peter 1:17).

Perfect love casts out fear. “Casts out” is the word used of Jesus casting out demons. As we take in that Christ bore God’s wrath for us and that we share his standing (v. 17), love drives the dread out.

Fear has to do with punishment. But for believers Christ has borne it (v. 10). The bill has been paid; the creditor has sent the receipt. All the terror that should have been ours fell on the Son in the darkness of Calvary, and he cried out because he was forsaken, so that we never will be. Now the Father’s house is open, and his children come in not cringing but running.

Not perfected in love. Fear of judgment shows that the love that paid the penalty has not yet been fully believed. The cure is not greater willpower but a deeper knowing and believing of his love (v. 16).

Slavish fear and filial fear. The Puritans distinguished a slave’s fear from a son’s. A slave fears his master’s whip; a son fears grieving his father. The slave wants to get away; the son wants to come close. Love casts out the first and deepens the second: the more you know that God will never punish you, the more you will hate to wound him.

I still fear death and judgment. Does that mean I am not a Christian? No. It means you are not yet perfected in love, like every believer this side of glory; John describes what love does as it grows, not an exam to pass first. Fear of death is natural, and even Christ was troubled at its approach (John 12:27). The cure is not to scold yourself but to feed on the gospel: Christ came to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:15). Each time the fear comes, take it to the cross and say, the punishment has been borne. Love is still casting the fear out, and it will finish the job.

verseByVerse.quote: We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All our love, for God and for others, is an answer to his love, which came first.

We love because he first loved us. The gospel’s logic in six English words: probably a statement (we love), not a command (let us love), covering love for God and for others.

The echo. Our love is not self-generated virtue but the echo of a love that reached us first. Augustine, preaching through this letter, made love the mark that tells the children of God from the children of the devil; John says here where that love comes from. A heart at rest in God’s love begins at last to love. Before we were born, before we sinned, before the world was made, he set his love on us, and every flicker of love we have for him reflects a fire that has been burning towards us from eternity.

Simon, do you love me? John had watched this verse happen. By a charcoal fire Peter had denied Jesus three times (John 18:18, 25–27); by another charcoal fire on the shore the risen Lord cooked him breakfast and asked him three times, do you love me (John 21:9, 15–17). Peter’s love had failed completely, and Christ came first: he lit the fire, fed the man who had denied him, and restored him. Every Christian’s story has the same order: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and only then did I love him.

In everyday life. Pride and discouragement often start in the same place: with how much we love God. This verse moves the starting point. On the day you feel pleased with your devotion, and on the day you are ashamed of how little you have, the first word is the same, humbling and glad at once: he loved you first.

Did I choose God, or did he choose me? Both are true, but not in the same way. You really did turn to God and trust Christ; you were not dragged against your will. But your choosing was the fruit of his: you did not choose me, but I chose you, Jesus said (John 15:16), and God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), not for anything he foresaw in us but because of his own love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Scripture calls this election: God’s free choice, before time began, to save particular sinners in Christ and bring them to faith. When you came to him, you found he had been coming to you all along: cause not for confusion but for worship, and a salvation resting on something stronger than your grip.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “him” (we love him, as in the KJV), others “God”; most likely the original simply says we love.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who claims to love God while hating a fellow believer is lying, because love for the unseen God always shows in love for the brother we can see.

He is a liar. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10; 2:4, 6, 9: to love God while hating a fellow believer is not merely inconsistent but impossible.

Whom he has seen. The argument moves from easier to harder. It is easy to love a God you have imagined; it is much harder to love the man in front of you at church, with his irritating habits and disappointing failures, and that is the point.

The brother Christ is not ashamed of. The brother you have seen is Christ’s brother too. The Son is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and whatever is done to the least of them is done to him (Matthew 25:40). The difficult man in the next pew is a brother for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11). Hatred of him cannot sit beside love for God, because it despises the one the Son was glad to call family and bought with his own blood.

Can I love God and still struggle to forgive a brother? Yes, for a time; struggling is not hating. Forgiving a deep wound is often a process, and believers can be truly fighting to forgive while still feeling the pain. John condemns settled hatred that refuses to forgive and does not want to. If you are praying for the grace to forgive, asking God to bless the one who hurt you even through gritted teeth, and refusing revenge, you are not the liar of this verse. You are a Christian doing one of the hardest things a Christian is asked to do. Keep going.

verseByVerse.quote: And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has commanded that love for him and love for our brother go together: whoever loves God must love his children too.

This commandment we have from him. From Christ, or from God. Verse 20 argued that the two loves cannot be separated; now John adds that God commands it.

Must also love his brother. To love God is to love what God loves, and he loves his children. The chapter began by testing the spirits and ends by loving the brothers, and the two belong together: the Spirit of truth always produces love, and the spirit of error always, eventually, produces division.

Both loves in one act. Christ summed up the law as love for God and love for neighbour (Mark 12:29–31), and he did more than command it. On his way out to Gethsemane he said, I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father (John 14:31); and having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1). At the cross his love for the Father and his love for his brothers were one act of obedience. The commandment we have from him is the shape of his own life, now being written into ours.

No brother hard to love. Here our love for God is faint and our love for one another patchy, and we fail where the command presses hardest. But the Son kept it perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours, and by his Spirit he is making us like himself. The God who commands both loves is gathering a family in which both will one day be perfect: no brother hard to love, no heart cold towards the Father, and the whole household of God filling heaven with a love that never grows cold.

What if loving a brother seems to conflict with loving God? Love God first, and you will find it the truest love for your brother too. If a brother asks you to sin, to lie for him, to join in his wrongdoing or to approve what God forbids, love for God says no, and so does real love for him, because it seeks his good, not his comfort (Acts 5:29; Matthew 10:37). Usually there is no conflict at all: the God you love commands you to love, and your brother is best served by your obedience to God.

4.theology:
God is Love. The sentence God is love (vv. 8, 16) is often taken to mean that love is God: that whatever we call love must be divine and approved by him. John means the opposite. God defines love, and he defines it at once by an act (see the note on v. 10). That love is not soft but costly, not vague but given flesh and blood, a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. In verses 17–18 the doctrine of propitiation becomes comfort (see the note on v. 18). Perfect love casts out fear not by denying judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it, and God will not demand payment twice.
4.examples:
Then: The church had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and a more sophisticated knowledge of God. John’s test is not whether they seem spiritual but whether they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh: a test simple enough for a child and sharp enough to unmask a false spirit.

Now: We love because he first loved us, and that answers much Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love to earn God’s approval but a response to a love already given and already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry, the answer is not first to try harder but to go back to the source (v. 10).

keyVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
keyVerse.note: The chapter twice says that God is love; this verse says what that means. It defines love not by our feelings towards God but by his act towards us, and it ties his love to propitiation, so that his love does not cancel his justice but satisfies it. Everything else in the chapter, love for one another, confidence before the Judge and fear cast out, flows from here.

4.reflection:
John’s test of every spirit is what it says about Jesus (vv. 2–3), not how powerful, warm or popular it seems (v. 5). What voices in our culture, or in the church, sound spiritual but leave Jesus vague? How can we test what we hear without becoming suspicious of everyone?

Verse 10 defines love by the cross: “not that we have loved God but that he loved us.” How does that definition differ from the way love is usually spoken of around us? Why does it matter that God’s love includes propitiation?

“Perfect love casts out fear” (v. 18). What fears about God, death or judgment still trouble you or people you know, and how does verse 17 answer them?

John says we cannot love the God we have not seen if we do not love the brother we have seen (v. 20). Who is hard for you to love in your church? What would loving them “because he first loved us” (v. 19) look like this week?

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.<sup>2</sup>By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.<sup>3</sup>For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.<sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.<sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?<sup>6</sup>This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.<sup>7</sup>For there are three that testify:<sup>8</sup>the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.<sup>9</sup>If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.<sup>10</sup>Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.<sup>11</sup>And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.<sup>12</sup>Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.<sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.<sup>14</sup>And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.<sup>15</sup>And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.<sup>16</sup>If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that.<sup>17</sup>All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.<sup>18</sup>We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.<sup>19</sup>We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.<sup>20</sup>And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.<sup>21</sup>Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
5.overview:
Where we are. The last chapter completes the letter’s third movement, faith resting on God’s testimony to his Son (4:1–5:12), and then gathers the whole letter together (vv. 13–21; see the introduction).

The message. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, has been born of God, and that faith has already overcome the world, because it holds the one who overcame it. God himself has testified about his Son, and his testimony is this: eternal life is in the Son, so whoever has the Son has life. You may therefore know, not merely hope, that you have eternal life. So pray boldly, and keep yourselves from every substitute for the true God.

Why it was said. The teachers who had left offered a higher knowledge of God and a Christ who came upon Jesus at his baptism but did not die (see the introduction). The believers left behind were asking whether plain faith in Jesus was enough, whether they really had life, and what to make of brothers who sinned or walked away.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–5 bind faith, new birth, love and obedience into one reality, and name faith in Jesus as the Son of God the victory that overcomes the world. Verses 6–12 call God’s witnesses: the water of Jesus’ baptism and the blood of his death, with the Spirit, three in agreement; and God’s testimony, greater than any human witness, is that life is in his Son. Verse 13 states the purpose of the whole letter. Verses 14–17 turn assurance into prayer, including prayer for a sinning brother. Verses 18–20 give three closing certainties, and verse 21 a last warning.

Where it leads. The letter that began with hands that touched “the word of life” (1:1) ends by naming him: “He is the true God and eternal life” (v. 20). The one who came by water and blood, who keeps his people so that the evil one cannot seize them, is God himself, come in our flesh. To have him is to have life.

For us. Assurance is not arrogance but rest on God’s word about his Son. Ask whether you are looking at the strength of your faith or at the one it holds; whether your confidence shows in prayer for others; and what in your life is quietly competing with the true God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Faith, Love, and the World-Overcoming Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: New birth shows itself in faith, love and obedience, and that faith has already won. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and a child of God loves the Father’s other children (v. 1). That love is proved genuine by love for God shown in obedience (v. 2), and God’s commands do not crush those who love him (v. 3), because the new birth overcomes the world. The victory is faith (v. 4): not faith in general, but faith that Jesus is the Son of God, who has overcome it (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as the Victory

On faith as the sign of new birth, see v. 1; on the faith that overcomes, see vv. 4–5.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ordinary faith in Jesus was being called insufficient.

Now: The faith that overcomes is not heroic; it is trust in the Son of God who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith in Jesus as the Christ is the evidence of a new birth God has already given, and those born of God love his other children. Faith, new birth and love, the letter’s three great themes, meet in this single verse.

Everyone who believes. “Believes” (pisteuōn) is present tense: keeps believing. “That Jesus is the Christ” is the confession the false teachers denied (2:22).

Has been born of God. “Has been born” (gegennētai) is perfect tense: has been born and remains so. The order matters: the person who now believes has already been born of God, so his believing is the evidence of that birth. Regeneration, the Spirit’s giving of life to the spiritually dead, comes first, and faith follows (see the box at the end of this note).

Whoever has been born of him. “The Father” is literally “the one who fathered” (ton gennēsanta). It is a family principle: if you love a father, you love his children.

Lazarus in the tomb. Jesus stood at the grave and called, “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43). Lazarus came, but nobody imagines that he first decided to come out and was then made alive. He could not hear until he was alive, and the voice that called him gave him the life to answer. Every believer is a walking resurrection, a sinner who could not come until Christ made him alive, and then came running.

If new birth comes before faith, should an unbeliever just wait to be born again? No. The command to everyone is to repent and believe now (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30). God gives new birth through the hearing of the gospel (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18), so the place to be is under the word, and the thing to do is to come to Christ. If you find that you want him, that wanting is itself a sign that God is at work. Do not look behind the curtain first: believe, and you will find that you were born again.

Where Christians differ: does faith cause new birth, or does new birth cause faith? Arminians (Protestants who hold that God’s grace enables everyone to believe but leaves the decision to each person) generally hold that a person believes and is then born again, with faith coming from a free choice made possible by prevenient grace, a grace given beforehand to all. Both sides agree that grace comes first and that faith is necessary, and many Arminian believers love Christ deeply. This commentary’s view: the grammar of this verse, and John’s pattern throughout (2:29; 3:9; 4:7), shows that being born of God comes first and produces faith, righteousness and love. Jesus taught that one must be born again to see the kingdom (John 3:3), and that those who believe were born of God (John 1:12–13); dead sinners cannot believe until God gives them life (Ephesians 2:1–5). This is effectual calling, God’s inward call that does not fail to bring a sinner to life: God regenerates, and the regenerate believe. Faith is truly ours, but it is the fruit of God’s prior work.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for God’s children is proved genuine when it flows from love for God shown in obedience. Earlier, love for others proved love for God (4:20); now the test runs the other way, and each checks the other.

When we love God and obey his commandments. Love for people that ignores God’s commands is not genuine love. Sometimes love requires saying no, correcting, or refusing to approve sin, because God commands it.

As I have kept my Father’s commandments. John learned this order from Jesus, who gave himself as the pattern: “If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love” (John 15:10; compare 14:15). In the Son, loving the Father, obeying him and laying down his life for the sheep were never apart (John 10:17–18). His obedience was perfect where ours never is, and it is counted to all who are in him (Romans 5:19), so the Father receives their flawed obedience for his sake.

What if a fellow Christian says I am unloving because I will not approve of his sin? Examine yourself honestly: if you have been harsh, proud or careless in how you spoke, apologise for that. Then stand firm gently. Love does not mean celebrating what God forbids: a friend who watches you walk out onto thin ice and says nothing is not kind. True love keeps the friendship open, speaks the truth with tears rather than contempt, and prays. Jesus, the most loving man who ever lived, told the woman caught in adultery both that he did not condemn her and that she must go and sin no more (John 8:11, in a passage missing from the earliest manuscripts, as most modern Bibles note).

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To love God is to keep his commandments, and his commandments do not crush those who love him.

The love of God. Here it means our love for God, and it is not merely emotion but obedience (John 14:15). That is as old as Moses, who joined loving the LORD to keeping his charge, his statutes, his rules and his commandments always (Deuteronomy 11:1).

Not burdensome. “Burdensome” (bareiai) means heavy, crushing, like the burdens the Pharisees laid on people (Matthew 23:4). They come from a loving Father, who gives the new heart and Spirit to delight in them (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Psalm 119:35).

The wings of a bird. An old preacher’s image: wings add weight to a bird, yet they are not a burden; they are what lift it. Take them off, and the bird can no longer fly. To a heart that loves God, his commandments are the very means of rising toward him.

Why his yoke is easy. The commandments are not burdensome because Christ has carried the crushing part of them. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). What he lays on his people now is not the law as a ladder up to God but his own yoke, and he calls the weary to take it as one who is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:28–29). They ask no less than before, but the one who gives them has already borne their penalty.

Then why does obedience sometimes feel so hard? Because sin still lives in us and pulls against the new nature (Galatians 5:17), and because some obedience costs: forgiving a deep wrong, giving up a relationship, telling the truth at a price. Jesus himself was in anguish in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33–36). “Not burdensome” does not mean effortless, but that the command is good, the Father kind, and the strength to obey given with it. When obedience grinds, ask first not how to try harder but whether the love of God is real and growing in you. Go back to his love, and the load will lighten.

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone born of God shares in Christ’s victory over the world, and the means of it is faith. That is why his commands are not burdensome.

Overcomes the world. “Everyone” (pan) is literally “everything”, which puts the weight on the birth from God, not on the kind of person. God’s children are not crushed by the world (2:15–17) but overcome it.

The victory, our faith. “Victory” (nikē) appears only here in the New Testament; it was also the name of the Greek goddess of victory, whose images were probably familiar across the cities of Asia. “Has overcome” points to a victory already won, which we came to share when we first believed.

He has overcome. “Take heart; I have overcome the world,” Jesus said in the upper room (John 16:33), the night before the world crucified him, and three days later he walked out of the grave to prove it. Faith is the hand that reaches out and holds the one who has already won.

The old man in the arena. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, had been, by early tradition, a disciple of John himself. In about AD 155, as an old man, he was brought into the stadium and urged to swear by the emperor and curse Christ, and he would be released. He answered that for eighty-six years he had served Christ, who had never done him wrong; how could he blaspheme his King who saved him? He was put to death. The crowd had watched faith overcome the world.

In everyday life. The world rarely presses with an arena. It presses with a headline that breeds fear, a feed that breeds envy, an office that rewards quiet compromise. Overcoming looks ordinary: an honest answer, a prayer instead of a panic, a refusal to despair.

I feel defeated by the world, not overcoming it. How is this true of me? Overcoming does not mean winning every skirmish or feeling triumphant. It means the world cannot finally have you: it cannot make you stop trusting Christ for good, or separate you from his love (Romans 8:35–39). Every time you turn back to Christ after failing, refuse a temptation or keep believing through grief, you are overcoming. Victory is often quiet and looks like perseverance, and it rests on his, complete when he rose from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only faith in Jesus as the Son of God overcomes the world, because only he has overcome it. The question has exactly one answer: the eternal Son took flesh, fought the world on its own ground, and won.

Except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? That Jesus, the man, is the divine Son of God is precisely what the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3). What overcomes is not faith in general or a vague spirituality, but faith in this person and the work he did. The question shuts out every other way and invites every person: anyone who believes this overcomes; no one who refuses it does.

What if my faith is weak? Does it still overcome? Yes, because it is not the strength of your faith that wins but the strength of the one you trust. A child crossing a busy road is safe not because his grip is strong but because his father’s is. A weak faith in a strong Christ overcomes; a strong faith in a false Christ does not. Jesus spoke of faith like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 17:20), and when a father cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), Jesus helped him. Bring the faith you have, and ask him to grow it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Three Witnesses and the Life That Is in the Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself has testified that Jesus is his Son, and his testimony is that eternal life is found in the Son alone. Jesus came by the water of his baptism and the blood of his death, not by the first only (v. 6). With the Spirit these make three agreeing witnesses, the number the law required (vv. 7–8; Deuteronomy 19:15). If we accept human testimony, God’s is greater (v. 9); to believe it is to have it within, to refuse it is to call God a liar (v. 10). Its content is simple: life is in his Son, so whoever has the Son has life (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Witnesses

On the three witnesses, see vv. 6–8; on the life that is in the Son, see vv. 11–12.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teaching separated the Christ of the baptism from the Jesus of the cross (see the note on v. 6).

Now: There is no middle ground: life is found in the Son, and nowhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God came through both his baptism and his death, and the Spirit bears true witness to him.

Came by water and blood. “Water and blood” most likely refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death, the public events that open and close his ministry and together declare who he is (see the box at the end of this note). At his baptism the Father declared him Son and the Spirit descended (Mark 1:9–11); at his death he shed his blood for sins (1:7).

Not by the water only. The false teachers apparently taught, as Cerinthus did (see the introduction), that the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism (water) but left before his death (blood), so that only the man Jesus died. John insists that the Son of God himself came through both. The false teaching would happily keep a heavenly Christ who spoke beautiful words; it could not bear a Christ who bled. John will not let the blood be taken away, because the blood is where the salvation is.

The Spirit is the one who testifies. The Spirit of truth (John 14:17) bears witness to Christ at his baptism, through the apostles’ preaching and Scripture, and in believers’ hearts (John 15:26; 16:14), and his witness is not to a divided Christ but to the one Jesus Christ, both God and man.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the water of baptism saves. John speaks of Christ’s own baptism and death as the events that testify to who he is.

Why does it matter that the Son of God himself died, and not only the man Jesus? Because the worth of a sacrifice depends on who offers it. The one who died was the eternal Son, truly God and truly man in one person, so his death has infinite value, enough for all his people of every age (Hebrews 9:14; Acts 20:28). They “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). God did not send someone else to suffer while he stayed safe; he came himself.

Uncertain wording. What John means by “water and blood” is not certain, and it is the most debated phrase in the chapter. Some see the water and blood that flowed from Jesus’ side at the cross (John 19:34); others see the two sacraments, baptism and the Lord’s Supper. But “came by” points to events in Jesus’ own life, and “not by the water only” fits a dispute over whether the Son of God went through death as well as baptism. The baptism-and-death reading fits the context best.
verseByVerse.note: “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death. John says this against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit, the water and the blood give one agreeing testimony that Jesus is the Son of God, the full witness the law required.

Three that testify. The law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides three, and they agree.

The Spirit and the water and the blood. The Spirit’s testimony is the inward, ongoing witness given to believers (v. 10; 4:13); the water and the blood are Jesus’ baptism and death (see v. 6).

These three agree. Literally, they are toward the one thing (eis to hen eisin): all three point to Jesus, the Son of God who came in the flesh and died for sins. Where the Son is refused, it is not for lack of witness.

Textual note. Some late manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven, known as the Johannine Comma or Comma Johanneum (a comma here means a short clause): “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth.” They are not found in the text of any Greek manuscript before about the fourteenth century, and then only in a handful. No Greek church father quotes them, even in the fourth-century debates over the Trinity, when they would have been the obvious verse to cite. They appear to have begun as a comment in the margin of some Latin manuscripts that was later copied into the text.

How they reached the King James Version. Erasmus left them out of the first two editions of his printed Greek New Testament and added them in the third, after a single recent Greek manuscript containing them was produced; from that line of printed texts they passed into the King James Version. However true in itself, the statement is almost certainly not part of what John wrote, which is why most modern Bibles omit it or give it only in a footnote. The doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on it; it is taught clearly throughout Scripture (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; John 1:1; 14:16–17).

Does this mean the Bible has errors, or that I should not use the King James Version? Neither. The Bible as God gave it is without error, and God has preserved it through thousands of manuscripts, more than for any other ancient book; comparing them lets us see almost exactly what the apostles wrote. Most differences are tiny (spelling, word order, a small word added or dropped), the few larger ones are well known and marked in modern Bibles, and no doctrine rests on a doubtful reading. Noticing a later addition is part of honouring the original. The King James Version is a noble translation that has fed believers for four centuries; read it with profit, simply knowing that this one sentence was added later.
verseByVerse.note: Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven (known from the King James Version). They are not in the early Greek manuscripts and the ESV omits them.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we trust human witnesses every day, we should trust far more the testimony God himself has given about his Son.

If we receive the testimony of men. We accept human testimony every day: the doctor’s diagnosis, the map, the friend who tells us the road is closed.

The testimony of God is greater. “Greater” (meizōn) means more reliable, more authoritative, for God “never lies” (Titus 1:2).

Concerning his Son. “Has borne” (memartyrēken) is perfect tense: God has testified and the testimony stands. At the Jordan and on the mountain the Father’s own voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17; 17:5). And in raising him from the dead, God declared him to be the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4).

Where do I hear God’s testimony today? In Scripture, above all, where the Father’s voice, the miracles, the empty tomb and the apostles’ witness are recorded: God’s own testimony in written form (2 Timothy 3:16). The Spirit who inspired it confirms it in your heart as it is read and preached (v. 10). You do not need a private voice or a vision. Open the Gospels, and God himself is testifying to you about his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To believe in the Son is to receive God’s testimony into your own heart; to refuse it is to call God a liar.

Has the testimony in himself. “Believes in” (pisteuōn eis) is literally trusts into. God’s outward testimony becomes an inward witness in the believer, by the Spirit (Romans 8:16; Galatians 4:6): not a feeling of our own making, but God’s testimony confirmed within us.

Has made him a liar. Unbelief is not neutral or merely intellectual; it calls God a liar (1:10), a slander against the God who testified. A sceptic may protest that he is simply unconvinced. John does not call every question wicked, but when the witness is given and the Son is still refused, the deepest reason is usually not in the head but in the heart, which does not want a Lord: “you refuse to come to me that you may have life,” Jesus said (John 5:40).

Honouring the Son. Unbelief is grave because God’s testimony is about the one he loves most. Jesus said that whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (John 5:23), and John had written that whoever receives Christ’s testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true (John 3:33). To refuse Jesus is not to decline one religious option among many; to believe is to say amen to God about his beloved Son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every doubt is calling God a liar. Honest struggles with doubt are different from settled unbelief (Mark 9:24; Jude 22).

What if I do not sense any inner witness? It is usually quieter than people expect: not a voice or a feeling of certainty, but the simple fact that, when you hear the gospel, you find it true and cannot let it go; that Christ is precious to you; that you call God Father; that you want to obey him. That is the Spirit at work (Romans 8:15–16). And the inner witness always rests on the outer one, God’s testimony in Scripture. If your assurance is faint, do not go digging inside yourself for it. Go back to the testimony and believe it; the inner witness grows as you feed on the outer.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s testimony is that he has given us eternal life, and that this life is found in his Son.

God gave us eternal life. “Gave” is past tense: eternal life is a gift already given to believers (John 3:16; 10:28; Romans 6:23).

This life is in his Son. Eternal life is not a thing God hands out apart from Christ; it is found in a person (John 1:4; 14:6), which is why having the Son (v. 12) and having life are the same thing. No ritual, discipline or achievement can pass on the life apart from him. The Father could give no greater gift, because he has nothing greater than his Son.

Were Old Testament believers saved through the Son too? Yes. There has only ever been one way of salvation: by grace, through faith, in Christ. Old Testament believers looked forward to the promised Redeemer, as we look back to him (Romans 4:1–8; Hebrews 11:13, 26). Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56); Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt. They received the same life, in the same Son, whose sacrifice covered his people’s sins before his coming as well as after (Romans 3:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life depends on one thing only: whether you have the Son.

Whoever has the Son has life. “Has” means possesses, through faith. It is the starkest contrast in the letter: not more or less, but has or does not have.

Does not have life. No Christ, no life. There is no other way (John 3:36; 14:6; Acts 4:12). It is both an open invitation, since anyone may have the Son by faith, and an exclusive claim; to soften it would leave people comfortable without life.

No one so dead. Life has a name, and the name is Jesus. All the life of God dwells in him, and he gives himself to beggars, to children, to the dying thief, to anyone who comes. There is no one so dead that he cannot make alive, and no one who has him will ever die.

What about someone I loved who died without professing faith? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian carries, and Scripture gives no other way of salvation to ease the pain. But it gives you things to hold. You do not know what happened in that person’s heart, perhaps in the last hours. The Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and he is kinder and wiser than we are. You may grieve and leave them in his hands. And let the grief make you urgent for the living: tell those still with you about the Son, while there is time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers may know that they have eternal life, and that knowledge makes them bold, prayerful and watchful. John states the purpose of his letter (v. 13), then shows assurance at work in confident prayer according to God’s will (vv. 14–15), and in prayer for a brother who sins, with sober words about sin that leads to death (vv. 16–17). Three certainties follow: Christ keeps those born of God (v. 18); we belong to God while the world lies in the evil one’s power (v. 19); the Son has come, and he is the true God and eternal life (v. 20). So the last word guards against every substitute (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
That You May Know

Assurance leads to bold prayer, to prayer for others, and to rest in what God has made certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter closes on Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life.

Now: Having the true God, refuse every substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John wrote the whole letter so that ordinary believers may know, not merely hope, that they already have eternal life.

I write these things to you who believe. “These things” are the whole letter, written not to evangelise but to assure: his readers already believe, and need confidence in what believing gives them.

That you may know. “Know” (eidēte) means know with settled certainty: not hope, not feel, but know. “Have” is present tense: eternal life is a present possession. So the letter’s tests are meant not to make believers anxious but to assure them, with a plain certainty confirmed by the Spirit, unlike the secret knowledge the false teachers claimed.

Two letters, one purpose. The Gospel brings people to the door (John 20:31); the letter tells them they are inside (see the introduction). God is not a Father who keeps his children in suspense about whether they will be thrown out. He has written it down, sealed it with his Son’s blood, and put his Spirit in our hearts to say it to us.

In the name of the Son of God. Believers can know because eternal life depends not on the strength of their believing but on the one they believe in, who has spoken plainly about his sheep: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). John had heard those words. This certainty is confidence not in ourselves but in Christ’s promise, Christ’s blood and Christ’s grip.

Certainty without arrogance. To many people today, anyone who says “I know” about God sounds dangerous. There is something right in that suspicion: certainty that rests on my intelligence, experience or goodness does make people hard. But John’s certainty rests on the testimony God has given about his Son (vv. 9–11): the certainty of someone handed a gift, not of someone who has won an argument. Here the usual picture turns round. The person who is never sure whether God will have him is often quietly relying on himself, waiting to see whether he has done enough. The person who knows he has eternal life is sure precisely because he has stopped looking at himself. Such assurance makes a believer not proud but restful, and a restful person can afford to listen, because his life does not hang on being right.

If assurance is normal, why do I lack it? There are common reasons, each with a remedy. Some look only at themselves, not at Christ; look first at the promise (vv. 11–12). Some are holding on to a known sin, which clouds the sense of God’s favour; confess it and turn (1:9). Some are going through suffering, depression or exhaustion, which darkens everything; be patient with yourself, and lean on others. Some were taught that doubt is proof of being lost; it is not. The Westminster Confession says that a true believer may wait long and struggle before he has assurance, and may have it shaken, but is never utterly without the seed of faith (Westminster 18.3–4; 1689 18.3–4). Keep coming to Christ. Assurance is the fruit of faith, not its root.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be sure of salvation? Roman Catholic teaching has generally held that, apart from special revelation, no one can be certain of final salvation; some Protestants hold that assurance belongs only to a few mature believers. This commentary’s view: John wrote so that ordinary believers may know they have eternal life. Assurance rests first on God’s promise in Christ (vv. 11–12), is confirmed by the Spirit’s inward witness (v. 10; Romans 8:16), and is supported by the fruit of faith, love and obedience. It is not presumption but the right response to God’s word about his Son: the normal privilege of every Christian, though it may be weak or clouded at times, and it grows as faith grows.
verseByVerse.note: John’s Gospel was written that readers might believe; this letter that believers might know they have eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who know they have eternal life may pray boldly, sure that God hears whatever they ask in line with his will.

This is the confidence that we have toward him. “Confidence” (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech (2:28; 3:21; 4:17). Assurance of eternal life leads at once to boldness in prayer.

According to his will. This is the governing condition of prayer (Matthew 6:10): not bending God to our will but aligning ourselves with his. “Hears” means hears favourably: he who holds the galaxies bends to hear the whisper of a child, intending to give. We learn his will through Scripture, and the Spirit helps us pray (Romans 8:26–27), so we can ask with confidence in the direction God is already moving.

Asking in his name. Jesus promised in the upper room that whatever his disciples asked in his name he would do (John 14:13–14). To pray in his name is not to add a formula but to come on his merit and ask what he would ask. Our prayers are heard because we come in the name of the Son who is always heard.

Should I add “if it be your will” to every prayer? Is that a lack of faith? Not when Scripture leaves the matter open, such as healing or a job; then it is humble trust, as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39; James 4:15). But where God has plainly revealed his will, there is no need to hedge: pray boldly that he will forgive, make you holy, give you wisdom (James 1:5), spread the gospel, and keep his people. The phrase should never be a way of expecting nothing, but the trust of a child who asks freely and lets his Father decide.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God hears such prayers, the answer is as good as given, even before it is seen. For John, to be heard by God is to be answered.

We have the requests. “Have” (echomen) is present tense. If a prayer is according to his will, God hears it and grants it, in his time and way (Mark 11:24). This is not a blank cheque but the confidence of one whose asking has been shaped by the God he knows.

Every promise is Yes in him. The answer is anchored in Christ, not in the strength of the asking. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20), and “he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The cross is the pledge behind every answered prayer.

Daniel’s three weeks. Daniel mourned, prayed and fasted for three weeks, and when the answer finally came, the messenger told him: “from the first day that you set your heart to understand … your words have been heard” (Daniel 10:12). Delay is not refusal, and silence is not deafness.

If God has already heard, why keep praying about the same thing? Because Jesus told us to. He told the parable of the widow who kept coming to the judge to show that we “ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1–8), and he taught us to ask, seek and knock, all continuous (Matthew 7:7). Persistent prayer is not nagging an unwilling God but trusting a willing one, and it changes us as we wait, deepening desire, purifying motives and keeping us dependent. Keep praying until God answers or shows you that his answer is different.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers should pray for a brother caught in sin, and God will give him life; only the settled rejection of Christ lies outside what John commands us to pray for. This is the most contested passage in the letter.

A sin not leading to death. The confident prayer of verses 14–15 is applied at once to a sinning brother in the church. “Not leading to death” (mē pros thanaton) is sin that does not end in spiritual death: most likely the ordinary failures and sins of genuine believers, for which repentance and forgiveness remain available (1:9). God answers such prayer by restoring the sinning believer’s spiritual life: he gives life through the prayers of his people.

There is sin that leads to death. Probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by the false teachers who left the church (2:19, 22): a deliberate, persistent denial of the Son despite knowing the truth, akin to the blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:29) and the apostasy of Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26. John does not forbid praying for such people; he simply does not command it.

All wrongdoing is sin. John makes light of no sin. But the sins of believers who remain in Christ do not lead to spiritual death, because “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1:7).

I have prayed for you. The church’s prayer for a stumbling brother copies something Christ does. On the night Peter would deny him, Jesus said, “Simon, Simon … I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32). Peter fell, but his faith did not die. When believers pray for a sinning brother and God gives life, they pray in step with Christ, our “advocate with the Father” (2:1), who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can know with certainty that someone has committed the sin that leads to death, so that we may give up on them. That judgment belongs to God.

In everyday life. If a fellow believer is struggling with sin, pray for him by name instead of talking about him. And if the Lord gives you the opportunity, go to him gently, as one who could fall the same way (Galatians 6:1).

Could I have committed the sin that leads to death? If you are worried that you have, that worry is strong evidence that you have not. The sin John means is a settled, hardened rejection of Christ by people who no longer care and want nothing more to do with him; a person who fears he has sinned beyond forgiveness and still wants Christ is not that person. The desire to be forgiven is itself the Spirit’s work. Come to Christ now. He has promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37), and that promise has no exception clause.

Where Christians differ: what is the sin that leads to death? Roman Catholic teaching distinguishes mortal sins (which destroy grace and lead to death unless confessed) from venial sins. Others think John means a sin punished by physical death under God’s hand of discipline (Acts 5:1–11, Ananias and Sapphira; 1 Corinthians 11:30), or the unpardonable sin of blaspheming the Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32); and the honest truth is that we cannot be dogmatic about every detail. This commentary’s view: in context, the sin leading to death is not a category of especially bad acts that a believer may commit and so lose salvation, but the settled apostasy of those who deny that Jesus is the Christ, as the false teachers did. True believers, born of God, are kept from it (v. 18). There is no list of mortal sins that sends a genuine believer to hell; all their sins are covered by Christ’s propitiation (2:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: The “sin that leads to death” is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by those who left the church.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those born of God do not go on living in sin, because the Son of God keeps them and the evil one cannot seize them. This is the first of three closing certainties (vv. 18, 19, 20), three hammer blows of assurance.

Does not keep on sinning. As in 3:6, 9, the present tense means habitual, settled sin.

He who was born of God protects him. This is most likely Christ, the eternal Son of the Father (see the box at the end of this note). The believer does not keep himself safe; Christ keeps him (John 10:28; Jude 24), as he said on the last night: “While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost” (John 17:12). The hand that holds us bears the marks of the nails.

The evil one does not touch him. “Touch” (haptetai) means seize so as to harm. Satan may tempt and attack, but he cannot drag the believer back into his power. This is the perseverance of the saints: Christ keeps every true believer to the end, not spared attack but never finally defeated.

Does this mean Satan cannot harm me at all, through illness or persecution? Not quite. Job was afflicted in body, family and possessions with God’s permission, and Paul received “a messenger of Satan to harass me” (2 Corinthians 12:7). Believers are tested and sometimes killed (Revelation 2:10). But Satan works only within the limits God sets. He could take Job’s health but not his God; he could kill the martyrs but not separate them from Christ’s love (Romans 8:38–39). The worst he can do to the body becomes, in God’s hands, the means of bringing his child home.

Uncertain wording. Who is “he who was born of God”? Because John has just used the phrase of believers, some take it to mean the believer, and some manuscripts read “protects himself”. But John changes the verb from “has been born” (believers) to “was born” (ho gennētheis), pointing to a single person, and the better reading, “protects him”, fits Christ keeping his own (John 17:12). The likely meaning is the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers belong to God, while the rest of the world lies, unaware, in the grip of the evil one. This is the second certainty.

We know that we are from God. “From God” (ek tou theou) means born of him, belonging to him.

The whole world lies in the power of the evil one. “Lies” (keitai) pictures passive lying, like someone asleep in another’s arms, and “in the power of the evil one” (en tō ponērō) is literally “in the evil one”. The world is under Satan’s influence (2 Corinthians 4:4; Ephesians 2:2), not fighting him but resting in his embrace, unaware.

Lifted up to draw. The verse that names the world’s captor points to its rescuer. “Now will the ruler of this world be cast out,” Jesus said. “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:31–32). The world cannot climb out of the evil one’s grip, but the Son lifted up on the cross is drawing people out of every nation. To be from God is to have been pulled out by a crucified hand.

How should I treat a world that lies in the evil one? Should I withdraw? No. Jesus prayed not that the Father would take us out of the world but keep us from the evil one, and he sent us into it (John 17:15, 18). The world is not to be feared, despised or imitated, but loved and reached. Your unbelieving neighbours are not the enemy but his captives, asleep in his arms, and the gospel is the voice that wakes them. So be in the world as a light, not a mirror: work well, love well, speak of Christ, and refuse its idols. Separation from sin, yes; separation from sinners, no.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God has come to give us true knowledge of the true God, and he himself is that true God and eternal life. This is the third certainty, and the greatest.

The Son of God has come. “Has come” (hēkei) means has arrived and is here. The incarnation with which the letter opened (1:1–2) is the ground of everything.

Has given us understanding. “Understanding” (dianoian) is mind, insight, the capacity to grasp: not secret knowledge for an elite but a renewed mind given to all believers.

Him who is true. “Him who is true” (ton alēthinon) is the genuine one, the real one: God the Father, in contrast with false gods (John 17:3). We are in him by being in his Son; no one is joined to the one without the other.

He is the true God and eternal life. “He” (houtos, this one) refers to Jesus Christ (see the box at the end of this note). It is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament, alongside John 1:1 and 20:28, and it brings the letter back to where it began: the eternal life that was made manifest (1:2) is the true God himself.

Nothing truer to worship. The baby laid in a manger, the man who wept and slept and bled, is the living and true God, before whom angels veil their faces; and he is eternal life, not merely its giver but its very self. We are in him, held by the one who made the stars and bore our sins, and there is nothing truer to worship.

Thomas’s confession. John’s Gospel reaches its height when Thomas, faced with the risen Jesus and his wounds, says, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Jesus did not correct him, and the letter reaches its height in the same place. The apostle who leaned on his chest at supper ends his letter on his knees.

How can Jesus be the true God when he prayed to the Father? Because God is one being in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet one God (Matthew 28:19). The Son praying to the Father is not one God praying to another, nor God praying to himself, but one divine person speaking to another within the one life of God. And as man, the Son truly prayed, depended and obeyed as our representative; the incarnation did not make him less God, but also man. Scripture holds both together: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and “the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), the second spoken of his humble state as man.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called the true God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some scholars, take “he” to refer to the Father. This commentary’s view: grammatically, “this one” most naturally refers to the nearest person, Jesus Christ. John has already called Jesus the eternal life (1:2), and his Gospel calls Jesus God (John 1:1, 18; 20:28). Jesus is fully God, one with the Father, as the church confesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Jesus Christ is the true God, his children must guard their hearts against every false one. An abrupt close, and exactly right.

Keep yourselves from idols. In Ephesus, where John probably wrote, the temple of Artemis and emperor worship meant literal idols were everywhere (see the introduction). The word also covers the false Christ of the false teachers, a god made in their own image, and anything we put in God’s place: money, pleasure, status, self (Colossians 3:5). Christ keeps us (v. 18), and we are to keep ourselves, and the best protection is to know the one who is true: you cannot treasure the real and be satisfied with the counterfeit.

The last word of an old man. Fathers who know they are dying say the thing that matters most. John ends not with a blessing but with a warning, spoken with the tenderest name he has: little children. He knew how easily the heart drifts to substitutes. Calvin said the human mind is a perpetual forge of idols, a workshop that never stops making them. The old apostle’s final act of love was to stand at its door and warn us.

How do I recognise an idol in my own life? An idol is anything you look to for what only God can give: security, identity, meaning, comfort, approval. Ask: What do I most fear losing? Where does my money go first? What makes me angry when it is threatened? What do I turn to when I am anxious? Whose approval do I most crave? An idol is usually a good thing made into a god thing: a child, a career, a body, a reputation, a cause. The answer is not merely to smash it but to love Christ more, so that it shrinks to its proper size.

How to keep yourself from idols. Keep watch at the door, in ordinary ways. Name them to God. When you notice something you cannot bear to lose, tell him plainly and ask him to put it back in its place. Give him the first share. Idols grow on whatever we hand them first, so put prayer before the inbox, giving before spending, and his people before the rest of the weekend. Enjoy the gift as a gift. Thank God by name for the career, the child, the home; a thing you keep thanking him for is harder to worship. Look longer at the true God. Idols are less often pushed out than crowded out, and a heart that sees how the true God kept nothing back for us, not even his life, has less room for substitutes. And when you find you have bowed again, do not hide it: “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1:7), this sin included.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. In 5:4 the victory that overcomes the world is “our faith.” Faith is not a spiritual achievement but a hand that receives, a trust that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome.

Assurance as Gift. John writes “that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). Assurance is not presumption. Presumption claims safety without grounds; on what assurance rests, see the box “Where Christians differ: can a believer be sure of salvation?” at v. 13.
5.examples:
Then: A church battered by false teaching and painful departures needed to know that the life they had received in the Son was real and eternal. John gave them not a new experience but the settled confidence of those who have the Son.

Now: Assurance in John is not a feeling to be worked up but a knowledge to be received, grounded in God’s testimony about his Son (5:9–10). Whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.

keyVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
keyVerse.note: Here John tells us why he wrote the whole letter: not to unsettle believers but to assure them. Everything in the chapter serves it, from the faith that overcomes (vv. 4–5) to God’s testimony that life is in his Son (vv. 11–12). The certainty rests not on the strength of our believing but on the Son we believe in.

5.reflection:
Verse 1 says that everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ “has been born of God”. How does it change the way you see your own faith to know that it is the fruit of God’s work, not the cause of it?

John says God’s commandments “are not burdensome” and that faith “has overcome the world” (vv. 3–4). Where does obedience feel heavy for you just now, and what would it look like to bring that weight back to Christ’s finished victory?

John wrote “that you may know that you have eternal life” (v. 13). What usually makes Christians unsure, and how do verses 9–13 move the ground of assurance away from ourselves?

The letter ends, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (v. 21), straight after calling Jesus “the true God and eternal life” (v. 20). What good things are most likely to become idols in our lives, and how can we help one another keep them in their place?
